Preparativi.2.full: Complete the standard setup for {0} players as shown in the rulebook, with the exceptions below. *Note that the {icon:AngryMob_Icon} track and starting player will be set by the Storybook in the coming pages.*

Preparativi.3.full: Before shuffling the decks, **set aside**, face up next to the board:

Preparativi.4.full: • the **Teleportation** Masterwork Experiment, before dealing the Masterworks;

Preparativi.5.full: • the Compulsions **"They'll never understand…"** (*Must collect Occult Knowledge*), **"Swing wide the iron gate!…"** (*Must collect a Body*), **"The flora of this region…"** (*Must collect a Chemical*) and **"I will observe these sniveling fools…"** (*Must visit the Town Hall*);

Preparativi.6.full: • the **Existential Crisis** and **Must Be Loved** Maladjustments.

Preparativi.8.full: This unofficial scenario uses some components from the **A Time of War** Scenario Box. Keep it at hand, but **do not open it**: the Storybook will tell you which components to take, one at a time. All the others must stay in the box, hidden.

VSPrologo.3.full: To the heirs of the estate, before they decide.
VSPrologo.3.easy: To the heirs of the estate, before they make their choice.
VSPrologo.3.short: To the heirs of the estate, before they decide.

VSPrologo.4.full: I am sending you my family's Register: three notebooks bound in black cloth, fifty-four years of births, fevers, broken bones and temperatures. My grandmother Hester began it; she was a midwife and was never allowed to call herself a doctor. My father Joost continued it; he was allowed, and never believed in it. I am closing it: I spent four years at the war, and by now I believe almost anything.
VSPrologo.4.easy: I am sending you my family's Register. It is three notebooks with black cloth covers. Inside are fifty-four years of births, fevers, broken bones and temperatures. My grandmother Hester began it. She was a midwife, and nobody let her call herself a doctor. My father Joost went on with it. He was a real doctor, but he never believed in it. Now I am finishing it. I spent four years in the war, and now I believe almost anything.
VSPrologo.4.short: I am sending you my family's Register: fifty-four years of births, fevers and temperatures, begun by my grandmother Hester, kept by my father Joost, closed by me.

VSPrologo.5.full: I do not ask you to believe me. I ask you to count. Count the temperatures that are too low, the recoveries that are too quick, the names that come back twice. Count the people of Brunveen who have stopped dreaming. Then decide.
VSPrologo.5.easy: I do not ask you to believe me. I ask you to count. Count the temperatures that are too low. Count the people who get better too quickly. Count the names that appear twice. Count the people of Brunveen who do not dream any more. Then decide.
VSPrologo.5.short: Do not believe me: count. The cold temperatures, the quick recoveries, the names written twice, the people who no longer dream. Then decide.

VSPrologo.6.full: **The Maas Register – Hester Maas, midwife, *11 November 1865.***

VSPrologo.7.full: Night, a quarter past eleven. On my way back from the miller's wife's lying-in: a boy, healthy. From the dyke road I saw a white light on the tower of the estate, bright as day, with no smoke and no sound. At the same moment, I swear it, another light just like it in the middle of the bog, where there is nothing and no one. They lasted the time of a breath. Then darkness.
VSPrologo.7.easy: Night, a quarter past eleven. I was coming back from the miller's house: his wife had a baby boy, healthy. From the road on the dyke I saw a white light on the tower of the estate. It was as bright as day, with no smoke and no noise. At the same moment, I swear it, there was another light just like it in the middle of the bog, where there is nothing and nobody. Both lights lasted only a breath. Then it was dark.
VSPrologo.7.short: A quarter past eleven at night. From the dyke I saw a white light on the estate's tower, and at the same moment another one in the middle of the empty bog. A breath, then darkness.

VSPrologo.8.full: Morning. Dressed the hands of Fokke Tammer, peat-cutter: second-degree burns on the palms. He says that in the water, where the light was, he found a black stone as hot as a stove, and pulled it out. He will not say where he has put it.
VSPrologo.8.easy: Morning. I put bandages on the hands of Fokke Tammer, who cuts peat. His palms are badly burnt. He says he found a black stone in the water, where the light was. It was as hot as a stove, and he pulled it out. He will not tell me where he has put it.
VSPrologo.8.short: Morning. Fokke Tammer, peat-cutter, has burnt palms: he pulled a hot black stone out of the water where the light was. He will not say where it is.

VSPrologo.10.full: The master of the estate died last night: his heart. I was called too late. In his last days he did not sleep and talked a great deal, always about the tower. He gripped my wrist until it hurt: "Something came through. I do not know what. It must go back where it came from." Pastor Kalf says he was raving. I write his words down here because he asked me to, and because nobody else will.
VSPrologo.10.easy: The master of the estate died last night. It was his heart. They called me too late. In his last days he did not sleep, and he talked a lot, always about the tower. He held my wrist so hard that it hurt. "Something came through," he said. "I do not know what. It must go back where it came from." Pastor Kalf says he was out of his mind. I write his words here because he asked me to, and because nobody else will.
VSPrologo.10.short: The master of the estate died last night. At the end he held my wrist: "Something came through. It must go back where it came from." The pastor says he was raving. I write it down anyway.

PreparaFolla.1.full: Place the Suspicion Marker on space **{0}** and the {icon:AngryMob_Icon} marker one space to its left. Give the {icon:StartPlayerToken} marker to **{1}**.

VociComuni.2.full: When one of your pieces visits a Location with a {icon:S3_ParadoxToken} token, before taking the action you may drink the dark water:

VociComuni.5.full: Whoever visits a Location with a Neighbour {icon:S3_WoodenFigureToken} takes the action as usual, but gains 1 {icon:Creepy_Icon} at the end of the Round. They may instead spend 2 Evidence {icon:S3_WeaponToken} to unmask it:

Traguardi.2.full: The first time a player reaches space 3 of the {icon:Creepy_Icon} track this Generation,

Traguardi.5.full: The first time a player reaches space 3 of the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track this Generation,

Traguardi.8.full: The first time a player reaches Level 2 of the Biology Journal Track this Generation,

Traguardi.11.full: The first time a player reaches 15VP this Generation,

PosaTraguardi.2.full: Place one on **space 3** of the {icon:Creepy_Icon} track, one on **space 3** of the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track and one on **space 15** of the Victory Point track. The fourth goes at the top of the **Level 2 of the Biology Journal Track** column: it counts for all players.

PosaTraguardi.3.full: When a player's marker reaches one of these tokens, that player clicks the matching entry in the Storybook and reads a message. Then the token returns to the supply.

TkCreepy.2.full: For some days now, every morning, Smit the washerwoman has stopped in front of the estate's gate and waved to you. She had never done it, in thirty years: Smit the washerwoman greets nobody, and last year she threw a bucket of dirty water after you. Now she smiles, and asks how you are, and waits for the answer. Her hands are red with cold, she says, but she does not put them in her pockets.
TkCreepy.2.easy: For some days now, every morning, Smit the washerwoman stops at the gate of the estate and waves to you. In thirty years she has never done this. She never says hello to anyone. Last year she even threw a bucket of dirty water at you. Now she smiles, asks how you are, and waits for your answer. She says her hands are red with cold, but she does not put them in her pockets.
TkCreepy.2.short: Every morning Smit the washerwoman, who greets nobody, stops at your gate to wave and smile. Her hands are red with cold, but she never puts them in her pockets.

TkCreepy.3.full: The new neighbour, the one who moved into the house across the road last spring, brings you a basket of apples every Sunday, and every Sunday asks whether you need anything. They mend the roof tiles without being asked. They have learned the names of all your dogs. In the evening they stay at the window opposite, with the lamp unlit, and watch yours.
TkCreepy.3.easy: The new neighbour moved into the house across the road last spring. Every Sunday they bring you a basket of apples, and every Sunday they ask if you need anything. They mend the roof tiles before anyone asks. They know the names of all your dogs. In the evening they stand at their window, with the lamp off, and look at yours.
TkCreepy.3.short: The new neighbour across the road brings apples every Sunday and knows your dogs' names. In the evening they stand at their dark window and watch yours.

TkCreepy.4.full: Back from town, you find your house clean, the windows washed, the firewood cut and stacked. A note on the table, in a round, kindly hand: *We found you a little neglected. Think nothing of it. Your neighbours.* The door was locked. There are only two keys, and both are in your pocket.
TkCreepy.4.easy: When you come back from town, your house is clean. The windows are washed, and the firewood is cut and stacked. There is a note on the table, in round, friendly handwriting: *We found you a little neglected. Think nothing of it. Your neighbours.* The door was locked. There are only two keys, and you have both of them in your pocket.
TkCreepy.4.short: Back from town, you find the house cleaned and a note: *We found you a little neglected. Your neighbours.* The door was locked, and both keys are in your pocket.

TkCreepy.8.full: You return it: a greeting, a cake, an invitation to dinner. The neighbour accepts everything, gives thanks for everything and forgets nothing. From that day on, in the village, your family are "decent folk", and the tradesmen give you credit.
TkCreepy.8.easy: You are kind in return: a greeting, a cake, an invitation to dinner. The neighbour accepts everything, says thank you for everything, and forgets nothing. From that day, in the village, people call your family "decent folk", and the shops let you pay later.
TkCreepy.8.short: You return the kindness. From then on your family are "decent folk", and the shops give you credit.

TkCreepy.9.full: Gain $2. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkCreepy.10.full: You close the shutters and slide the bolt. The neighbour does not knock, does not call out, does not take offence. They stay there until evening, patient, like someone who knows how to wait. When at last they leave, the print of a hand remains on the windowpane, misted, and it does not fade for an hour.
TkCreepy.10.easy: You close the shutters and lock the door. The neighbour does not knock, does not call, and is not offended. They stay outside until evening, patient, like someone who knows how to wait. When they finally go away, there is the print of a hand on the window glass, all misty. It stays there for an hour.
TkCreepy.10.short: You close the shutters. The neighbour waits outside until evening, patient, and leaves a misty handprint on the glass that lasts an hour.

TkCreepy.11.full: Gain 1 Evidence {icon:S3_WeaponToken}. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkInsanity.2.full: You wake before dawn with your hands frozen, as if you had kept them in water all night. The bed is dry. The room is warm, the fire lit. Your hands are not: they stay cold and damp until noon, and when you smell them they smell of peat smoke.
TkInsanity.2.easy: You wake up before dawn with icy hands, as if they had been in water all night. The bed is dry. The room is warm and the fire is lit. But your hands stay cold and damp until midday. When you smell them, they smell of peat smoke.
TkInsanity.2.short: You wake with icy, damp hands in a warm, dry bed. They stay cold until noon, and smell of peat smoke.

TkInsanity.3.full: You shake a client's hand, and he snatches it back. "Forgive me," he says, "your hands are frozen." You smile at him. He does not smile back. On the way home you look at your fingers under a street lamp: they are white, clean, steady. Too steady. They no longer tremble even when you are afraid.
TkInsanity.3.easy: You shake hands with a client, and he pulls his hand away fast. "Sorry," he says, "your hands are ice cold." You smile at him. He does not smile back. On the way home you look at your fingers under a street lamp. They are white, clean and still. Too still. They do not shake any more, not even when you are afraid.
TkInsanity.3.short: A client pulls his hand away: "Your hands are frozen." Under a street lamp your fingers look white and steady. Too steady: they no longer shake even when you are afraid.

TkInsanity.4.full: At the front, the doctors used to say that cold feet were the first sign of gangrene. In Brunveen the cold begins with the hands. This morning you warmed a cup of milk and held it tight until it had gone completely cold. The milk. Not your hands.
TkInsanity.4.easy: At the front, the doctors said that cold feet were the first sign of gangrene. In Brunveen the cold starts in the hands. This morning you warmed a cup of milk and held it tight until it was completely cold. The milk got cold. Your hands did not get warm.
TkInsanity.4.short: At the front, cold feet meant gangrene. In Brunveen it starts with the hands: this morning a hot cup of milk went cold in yours, and your hands stayed cold.

TkInsanity.6.full: You warm them at the fire.

TkInsanity.8.full: You hold them near the flame until the skin turns red and begins to hurt. The pain is good news: it means they are still yours. In the evening, writing, you catch yourself checking the temperature of the ink.
TkInsanity.8.easy: You hold your hands near the fire until the skin is red and starts to hurt. The pain is good news: it means they are still yours. In the evening, while you write, you notice that you are checking how warm the ink is.
TkInsanity.8.short: You hold them to the flame until they hurt: good, they are still yours. That evening you catch yourself checking the temperature of the ink.

TkInsanity.9.full: Move back 1 space on the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkInsanity.10.full: The doctor puts the thermometer under your arm, waits, looks, and writes a number in the Register without telling you. Then he asks whether you have drunk water from the bog. You say no. He writes that down too.
TkInsanity.10.easy: The doctor puts a thermometer under your arm. He waits, looks at it, and writes a number in the Register. He does not tell you the number. Then he asks if you have drunk water from the bog. You say no. He writes that down too.
TkInsanity.10.short: The doctor takes your temperature and writes it in the Register without telling you. He asks if you have drunk bog water. You say no. He writes that down too.

TkInsanity.11.full: Pay $1 and gain 1 Evidence {icon:S3_WeaponToken}. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkBiology.2.full: You have put a handful of peat from the dyke, where the light was, under the lens. Fibres, roots, black seeds, the wing of an insect dead who knows how long ago. Then, as you watch, one of the fibres moves. It stretches towards the light of the lamp, slowly, like a finger.
TkBiology.2.easy: You put a handful of peat under the lens. It comes from the dyke, where the light was. You see fibres, roots, black seeds and the wing of an insect that died long ago. Then, while you watch, one of the fibres moves. It reaches slowly towards the lamp, like a finger.
TkBiology.2.short: Under the lens, the peat from the dyke shows fibres, roots and seeds. Then one fibre moves, and reaches slowly towards the lamp like a finger.

TkBiology.3.full: The new microscope, the one bought in the city, magnifies three hundred times. In the drop of dark water there are things the books do not name: filaments that knot and untie themselves, in a precise order. If you watch them long enough, the order calls to mind a face. Yours.
TkBiology.3.easy: The new microscope, which you bought in the city, makes things three hundred times bigger. In the drop of dark water there are things that no book describes. Thin threads tie and untie themselves, always in the same order. If you watch them long enough, the order looks like a face. Your face.
TkBiology.3.short: Under the new microscope, threads in the dark water knot and untie in a precise order. Watch long enough, and the order becomes a face. Yours.

TkBiology.4.full: The University laboratory lends you a German instrument and an assistant who asks no questions. Under the lens, a fragment of a Neighbour, taken from the peat in the street where it crumbled: the cells are perfect, orderly, identical to a man's. They are simply made of something else.
TkBiology.4.easy: The University laboratory lends you a German machine and an assistant who asks no questions. Under the lens you put a piece of a Neighbour. You took it from the peat in the street where the Neighbour fell apart. The cells are perfect, in neat rows, the same as a person's cells. They are just made of something different.
TkBiology.4.short: At the University, under a German lens, a fragment of a crumbled Neighbour shows perfect human cells. They are just made of something else.

TkBiology.8.full: You study it for days, until you know it by heart. You learn a great deal. And you have the impression, absurd and precise, that in the meantime it has learned something about you too.
TkBiology.8.easy: You study it for days, until you know it by heart. You learn a lot. And you have a strange, clear feeling that, at the same time, it has learned something about you.
TkBiology.8.short: You study it for days and learn a great deal. You feel, absurdly, that it has learned something about you too.

TkBiology.9.full: Gain 1 Biology Knowledge and 1 {icon:Insanity_Icon}. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkBiology.10.full: You burn it in the stove. It burns slowly, without a flame, the way peat burns, and gives off a sweetish smoke that lingers in the room for a week. What you saw, though, you remember.
TkBiology.10.easy: You burn it in the stove. It burns slowly, with no flame, like peat. The smoke smells sweet and stays in the room for a week. But you still remember what you saw.
TkBiology.10.short: You burn it. It smoulders like peat, and its sweet smoke stays for a week. You still remember what you saw.

TkBiology.11.full: Gain 1VP. Return the {icon:StorybookToken} token to the supply.

TkVP.2.full: Mayor Wessel invites you to the council luncheon, on the first Thursday of the month, and seats you at his right hand. They talk of peat, of dykes, of the price of butter. Nobody mentions the two lights. When the pudding comes, the mayor raises his glass "to the family of the estate, who will carry Brunveen into the future". Everyone drinks water.
TkVP.2.easy: Mayor Wessel invites you to the council lunch, on the first Thursday of the month, and you sit at his right. People talk about peat, dykes and the price of butter. Nobody talks about the two lights. At dessert the mayor raises his glass "to the family of the estate, who will take Brunveen into the future". Everyone drinks water.
TkVP.2.short: At the council lunch Mayor Wessel seats you at his right and toasts your family, "who will carry Brunveen into the future". Nobody mentions the lights. Everyone drinks water.

TkVP.3.full: The council offers you a seat. The sittings are very short: nobody argues, nobody objects, the accounts balance to the penny. At the end of the first sitting the clerk shakes your hand and tells you that you are "just like them". In Brunveen, it is a compliment.
TkVP.3.easy: The council offers you a seat. The meetings are very short. Nobody argues, nobody says no, and the accounts are right to the last penny. At the end of the first meeting the clerk shakes your hand and says you are "just like them". In Brunveen, that is a compliment.
TkVP.3.short: You join the council. Nobody ever argues, and the accounts balance to the penny. The clerk says you are "just like them". In Brunveen, that is a compliment.

TkVP.4.full: The town makes you chair of the committee for the war memorial. The bronze is already ordered, the names already chosen, the unveiling already set. All they ask of you is a signature and a speech. In the speech, they beg you, not a word about the bog: "Our boys came home. That is what matters."
TkVP.4.easy: The town makes you the head of the committee for the war memorial. The bronze is already ordered. The names are already chosen. The day of the ceremony is already fixed. They only want your signature and a speech. In the speech, they ask, please say nothing about the bog: "Our boys came home. That is what matters."
TkVP.4.short: The town puts you in charge of the war memorial: everything is decided, they only want your signature and a speech. Not a word about the bog, please: "Our boys came home."

TkVP.8.full: You accept, give thanks, do what they ask of you. They welcome you the way one welcomes family, with a warmth that has no cracks. It is pleasant. It is so pleasant that, on the way home, you have to stop for a moment to remember what you wanted to ask.
TkVP.8.easy: You accept, you say thank you, and you do what they ask. They welcome you like one of the family, with a warmth that has no cracks. It feels nice. It feels so nice that, on the way home, you have to stop for a moment to remember the question you wanted to ask.
TkVP.8.short: You accept. They welcome you like family, so warmly that on the way home you cannot remember what you wanted to ask.

TkVP.10.full: You decline, with all the good manners you have. Nobody takes offence. In Brunveen nobody takes offence any more: they smile at you, they thank you all the same, and they watch you leave the way one watches a guest who has come to the wrong house.
TkVP.10.easy: You say no, as politely as you can. Nobody is offended. In Brunveen nobody is ever offended now. They smile at you, they thank you anyway, and they watch you go, like a guest who came to the wrong house.
TkVP.10.short: You decline politely. Nobody in Brunveen takes offence any more: they smile, thank you, and watch you go like a guest at the wrong house.

Bevi.2.full: The water of the bog is dark as tea left to steep too long, and cold even in summer. Those who have drunk it say it tastes of smoke and earth, and clears the head better than coffee. The pastor says it is the devil's water. The pastor drinks only wine.
Bevi.2.easy: The water of the bog is as dark as tea that has been left too long, and it is cold even in summer. People who have drunk it say it tastes of smoke and earth. They say it clears your head better than coffee. The pastor says it is the devil's water. The pastor only drinks wine.
Bevi.2.short: The bog water is dark as stewed tea and cold even in summer. They say it clears the head better than coffee. The pastor calls it the devil's water, and drinks wine.

Bevi.3.full: In Brunveen the water of the bog is sold in labelled bottles, "Brunveen Water, for health and serenity". The chemist recommends it for sleeplessness, the schoolmistress for inattention, the mayor for everything else. Nobody in the village has been ill for years.
Bevi.3.easy: In Brunveen they sell the bog water in bottles with a label: "Brunveen Water, for health and serenity". The chemist says it is good if you cannot sleep. The schoolmistress says it is good if you cannot pay attention. The mayor says it is good for everything else. Nobody in the village has been ill for years.
Bevi.3.short: The bog water is sold in bottles, "Brunveen Water, for health and serenity", and recommended for everything. Nobody in the village has been ill for years.

Bevi.4.full: In the glass the dark water does not move, not even when you knock on the table. At the front you drank water from puddles, from snow, from radiators. This is different: it is looking at you.
Bevi.4.easy: The dark water in the glass does not move, not even when you hit the table. At the front you drank water from puddles, from snow, even from radiators. This water is different. It is looking at you.
Bevi.4.short: The dark water in the glass does not move, even when you knock the table. You drank worse at the front. But this water looks back.

Bevi.5.full: *Whoever drinks gains knowledge, but everyone sees how much water they have drunk, and the village grows quieter.*

Bevi.8.full: The cold goes down to your stomach and spreads, slowly, like ink in a glass. Then comes a new clarity: your thoughts line up by themselves, your worries grow small and far away. For a few hours you are afraid of nothing. It is the most pleasant feeling you have ever had, and that, more than anything else, frightens you.
Bevi.8.easy: The cold goes down into your stomach and spreads slowly, like ink in a glass of water. Then your mind becomes very clear. Your thoughts put themselves in order. Your worries become small and far away. For a few hours you are not afraid of anything. It is the nicest feeling of your life, and that is what frightens you most.
Bevi.8.short: The cold spreads through you like ink, and your mind turns clear and calm. For a few hours you fear nothing. That, more than anything, frightens you.

Bevi.9.full: Immediately gain 1 Knowledge cube of your choice. Take the {icon:S3_ParadoxToken} token from that Location and keep it in front of you: everyone must see how much water you have drunk.

Bevi.10.full: You look at your reflection in the dark water for a long time. Then you leave the glass where it is. As you walk away you have the impression that the reflection has stayed there, watching you go.
Bevi.10.easy: You look at your reflection in the dark water for a long time. Then you leave the glass where it is. As you walk away, you feel that the reflection is still there, watching you leave.
Bevi.10.short: You stare at your reflection, then leave the glass. Walking away, you feel the reflection is still watching you.

BeviEffetti.2.full: Nobody had drunk the dark water before you: take the set-aside Compulsion **"The flora of this region…"**.

BeviEffetti.3.full: This morning, in the mirror, you had to think for a moment before you recognised yourself. Only a moment.
BeviEffetti.3.easy: This morning, in the mirror, you needed a moment to know who you were looking at. Only a moment.
BeviEffetti.3.short: This morning, in the mirror, it took you a moment to recognise yourself.

BeviEffetti.4.full: This is the third time you have drunk: take the set-aside Maladjustment **Existential Crisis**.

BeviEffetti.11.full: Outside, the village seems a little quieter than before. Or perhaps it is you.
BeviEffetti.11.easy: Outside, the village seems a little quieter than before. Or maybe you are the one who is quieter.
BeviEffetti.11.short: Outside, the village seems quieter. Or perhaps you are.

PosaVicino.1.full: There are no more Neighbours {icon:S3_WoodenFigureToken} in the supply: leave the board as it is. The village has changed more than it shows.

PosaVicino.2.full: Take a **Wooden Figure token** {icon:S3_WoodenFigureToken} from the **A Time of War** Box and place it on the **{0}**: it is a **Neighbour**.

Smaschera.2.full: In front of everyone you take its hand and squeeze hard, until the skin splits. No blood comes out of the wound: dark water comes out, slowly, smelling of smoke.
Smaschera.2.easy: In front of everyone, you take its hand and squeeze it hard, until the skin breaks. No blood comes out of the cut. Dark water comes out, slowly, and it smells of smoke.
Smaschera.2.short: You squeeze its hand in front of everyone until the skin splits. Out comes not blood but dark water, smelling of smoke.

Smaschera.3.full: Before the gathered crowd you show it the Evidence, one piece at a time: the temperature, the scar that is no longer there, the name that appears twice in the Register. It listens, kindly, denying nothing.
Smaschera.3.easy: In front of the crowd you show it the Evidence, one piece after another: the temperature, the scar that has disappeared, the name that is written twice in the Register. It listens kindly and does not deny anything.
Smaschera.3.short: Before the crowd you lay out the Evidence: the temperature, the missing scar, the name written twice. It listens kindly, denying nothing.

Smaschera.4.full: Wil Maas pricks its finger with a needle, in front of everyone. A black drop comes out of the prick. The Neighbour looks at it, then looks at you, and smiles like someone caught cheating at cards.
Smaschera.4.easy: In front of everyone, Wil Maas pricks its finger with a needle. A black drop comes out. The Neighbour looks at the drop, then at you, and smiles like someone caught cheating at cards.
Smaschera.4.short: Wil Maas pricks its finger before everyone: a black drop. The Neighbour smiles like a card cheat caught out.

Smaschera.8.full: The Neighbour does not run and does not defend itself. It sits down on the ground, looks at its hands, and begins to lose its shape, like an earthen statue in the rain. In a few minutes there is nothing left but a heap of wet peat, with a button and a pair of spectacles in it. The village watches in silence. Nobody thanks you.
Smaschera.8.easy: The Neighbour does not run away and does not fight. It sits on the ground, looks at its hands, and starts to lose its shape, like a statue made of earth in the rain. After a few minutes there is only a pile of wet peat, with a button and a pair of glasses in it. The village watches in silence. Nobody thanks you.
Smaschera.8.short: The Neighbour sits down and melts like earth in the rain, leaving wet peat, a button and a pair of spectacles. The village watches in silence. Nobody thanks you.

Smaschera.9.full: Spend 2 Evidence {icon:S3_WeaponToken} and return the Neighbour {icon:S3_WoodenFigureToken} to the supply. Gain 2VP.

Smaschera.10.full: You let it go. The Neighbour wishes you a good day, and means it.
Smaschera.10.easy: You let it go. The Neighbour wishes you a good day, and really means it.
Smaschera.10.short: You let it go. The Neighbour wishes you a good day, and means it.

VSG1Intro.3.full: Buried today, the master of the estate, in the cemetery on the dyke, in the rain. Few present: his children, Pastor Kalf, the notary come from the city, a few onlookers. Mayor Wessel sent a wreath and sent word of his gout. Fokke Tammer stood at the back, with his hands bandaged, and did not take off his hat.
VSG1Intro.3.easy: Today they buried the master of the estate, in the cemetery on the dyke. It was raining. Only a few people came: his children, Pastor Kalf, the notary from the city and a few curious people. Mayor Wessel sent flowers and said he could not come because of his gout. Fokke Tammer stood at the back with his bandaged hands. He did not take off his hat.
VSG1Intro.3.short: The master of the estate was buried today, in the rain. Few came. Fokke Tammer stood at the back, hands bandaged, and kept his hat on.

VSG1Intro.4.full: The master was a strange man, but he paid for the births on time and never called me "the woman". In his last months he spent his nights in the tower, a brick building he had had raised behind the house, as tall as the church steeple; and at night, from the dyke, one could see blue flashes at its windows. The village said he was doing alchemy. I said he was keeping late hours.
VSG1Intro.4.easy: The master was a strange man, but he always paid me on time for the births, and he never called me "the woman". In his last months he spent his nights in the tower. It is a brick building that he had built behind the house, as tall as the church tower. At night, from the dyke, people saw blue flashes at its windows. The village said he was doing alchemy. I said he was just staying up late.
VSG1Intro.4.short: The master was strange, but he paid on time. In his last months he spent his nights in his brick tower, where blue flashes lit the windows. The village said alchemy. I said late hours.

VSG1Intro.5.full: Now the tower is shut. The lock, the smith says, is melted, as if someone had welded it from the inside; and there is nobody inside, because its only occupant is in the coffin we have just lowered.
VSG1Intro.5.easy: Now the tower is closed. The smith says the lock has melted, as if someone had welded it from the inside. But nobody is inside, because the only person who lived there is in the coffin we have just put in the ground.
VSG1Intro.5.short: Now the tower is shut, its lock melted as if welded from inside. Yet its only occupant is in the coffin we just lowered.

VSG1Intro.6.full: After the funeral the notary gave each of the children a sheet from their father's Journal, torn out and folded, with a name on it. They were in the will. One of the children showed me theirs, at the church door, and asked me whether their father had still been in his right mind when he wrote it. I told the truth: I do not know.
VSG1Intro.6.easy: After the funeral the notary gave each child a page from their father's Journal. Each page was torn out and folded, with a name on it. The will said so. At the church door, one of the children showed me their page and asked me if their father was still in his right mind when he wrote it. I told the truth: I do not know.
VSG1Intro.6.short: After the funeral the notary gave each child a folded page of their father's Journal. One asked me if he was still sane when he wrote it. I do not know.

G1JournalA.3.full: **With your name on it, in your father's hand, more and more crooked.**

G1JournalA.4.full: *11 November, night. The ring lit up by itself. I did not touch it, I swear: I was at the window, with my pipe out. White light, no heat, a hum like bees inside a wall. Then nothing. I sent nothing, and it lit up all the same. It was made for sending, not for receiving. What has it received?*
G1JournalA.4.easy: *11 November, night. The ring turned on by itself. I did not touch it, I swear. I was at the window, and my pipe was out. White light, no heat, a hum like bees inside a wall. Then nothing. I did not send anything, but it turned on anyway. It was made to send things, not to receive them. What has it received?*
G1JournalA.4.short: *11 November, night. The ring lit up by itself: white light, a hum like bees. I sent nothing. It was made to send, not to receive. What has it received?*

G1JournalA.5.full: Below, a pencil drawing: the tower, the ring at its top, and a dotted line that starts at the ring and ends, straight as a thread, in the middle of a stretch of little dashes. The bog.
G1JournalA.5.easy: Under the words there is a pencil drawing: the tower, the ring at the top, and a dotted line. The line starts at the ring and goes, straight as a thread, to the middle of an area full of little dashes. The bog.
G1JournalA.5.short: Below, a pencil drawing: a dotted line runs straight from the ring on the tower into the middle of the bog.

G1JournalA.6.full: *Tammer is not Tammer. Look at his hands. He burnt them that night, and the next day the bandages were dry. He has stopped drinking. He has stopped cursing. He has cut more peat in a month than in a year, and he greets everyone by name, even the ones he hated. His wife sleeps at her sister's.*
G1JournalA.6.easy: *Tammer is not Tammer. Look at his hands. He burnt them that night, and the next day the bandages were dry. He does not drink any more. He does not curse any more. He has cut more peat in one month than in a whole year. He says hello to everyone by name, even to the people he hated. His wife now sleeps at her sister's house.*
G1JournalA.6.short: *Tammer is not Tammer. His bandages were dry the day after. He no longer drinks or curses, greets everyone by name. His wife sleeps at her sister's.*

G1JournalA.7.full: Below, smaller, underlined twice: *He is not wicked. It is worse: he is content.*
G1JournalA.7.easy: Under it, in smaller letters, underlined twice: *He is not wicked. It is worse than that: he is happy.*
G1JournalA.7.short: Underlined twice: *He is not wicked. It is worse: he is content.*

G1JournalA.8.full: *On the floor of the tower, the next morning, there was my watch. But mine is in my waistcoat: I took it out and held them both in my palm. Identical. Same crest, same scratch on the lid. The one from the floor is old, worn, with its glass cracked. As if it had been through a war.*
G1JournalA.8.easy: *The next morning, on the floor of the tower, I found my watch. But my watch is in my waistcoat pocket. I took it out and held both of them in my hand. They are the same: the same crest, the same scratch on the lid. But the one from the floor is old and worn, and its glass is cracked. As if it had been through a war.*
G1JournalA.8.short: *On the tower floor I found my watch, though mine was in my waistcoat. Identical, scratch and all. But the one from the floor is old and cracked, as if it had been through a war.*

G1JournalA.9.full: Below, in a different pen: *I gave it to the midwife as payment. I do not want it in the house.*
G1JournalA.9.easy: Under it, written with a different pen: *I gave it to the midwife to pay her. I do not want it in the house.*
G1JournalA.9.short: In another pen: *I gave it to the midwife. I do not want it in the house.*

G1JournalA.10.full: *Something came through. I do not know what. I do not know from where. I have done the sums a hundred times and they do not add up: the Machine was not on, so nobody sent it from here. Then who?*
G1JournalA.10.easy: *Something came through. I do not know what it is. I do not know where it came from. I have done the calculations a hundred times, and they are wrong every time. The Machine was not on, so nobody sent it from here. So who sent it?*
G1JournalA.10.short: *Something came through, from I know not where. The Machine was off: nobody sent it from here. Then who?*

G1JournalA.11.full: *Whatever it is, this land is not its own. It must go back where it came from. If I cannot do it, tell my children. Tell my children's children.*
G1JournalA.11.easy: *Whatever it is, it does not belong in this land. It must go back where it came from. If I cannot send it back, tell my children. Tell my children's children.*
G1JournalA.11.short: *Whatever it is, it does not belong here. It must go back. If I fail, tell my children, and theirs.*

G1JournalA.12.full: What do you do with the sheet?

G1JournalA.13.full: You keep it to yourself, among your papers.

G1JournalA.14.full: You read it to everyone, at breakfast.

G1JournalA.15.full: You fold the sheet in four and slip it among your papers. It is yours, after all: your name is on it. You will tell the others what you like, when you like. For now it seems to you only the ravings of a lonely old man, shut in a tower talking to his gears.
G1JournalA.15.easy: You fold the page in four and put it with your papers. It is yours, after all: your name is on it. You will tell the others what you want, when you want. For now, you think it is only the crazy talk of a lonely old man, shut in a tower, talking to his machines.
G1JournalA.15.short: You fold the sheet away among your papers. It has your name on it. For now it seems the ravings of a lonely old man in a tower.

G1JournalA.16.full: Gain 1 Occult Knowledge. You may tell the others what you have read: all of it, some of it or none of it.

G1JournalA.17.full: The next morning, at breakfast, you read the sheet aloud. Someone laughs, then stops. Someone shakes their head: their father had not been well in his last months, everyone knew it. Someone else says nothing and looks at the tower through the window.
G1JournalA.17.easy: The next morning, at breakfast, you read the page out loud. Someone laughs, then stops. Someone shakes their head: everyone knew that their father was not well in his last months. Someone else says nothing and looks out of the window at the tower.
G1JournalA.17.short: At breakfast you read it aloud. One laughs, then stops. One shakes their head. One looks out at the tower and says nothing.

G1JournalA.18.full: Read the text in italics above aloud to the other players. Gain 1VP.

G1JournalFine.2.full: The estate is a long, low house on the edge of the village, with a reed roof and windows facing the bog. Behind the house stands the tower: red brick, no windows up to half its height, and at the top a room with four glazed walls, shut. In the morning the crows settle on it. They do not stay long.
G1JournalFine.2.easy: The estate is a long, low house at the edge of the village. It has a roof of reeds and windows that look out over the bog. Behind the house is the tower. It is made of red bricks, with no windows on the lower half, and at the top there is a closed room with four big windows. In the morning the crows land on it. They never stay long.
G1JournalFine.2.short: The estate is a long, low house facing the bog. Behind it rises the red-brick tower, with a shut glass room at the top. Crows land there in the morning, but never stay.

G1JournalFine.3.full: Brunveen is a village of peat-cutters: a hundred or so wooden houses around the church, a market, a mill, a dyke that keeps the river away, and all around it the bog, flat and dark to the horizon, where in winter the fog rises and in summer the mosquitoes. For centuries the people here have cut the peat into bricks, dried it and burnt it. Peat gives little heat and a great deal of smoke. But it is free, and it belongs to everyone.
G1JournalFine.3.easy: Brunveen is a village of peat-cutters. There are about a hundred wooden houses around the church, a market, a mill, and a dyke that keeps the river out. All around is the bog, flat and dark as far as you can see. In winter it is full of fog, and in summer it is full of mosquitoes. For hundreds of years the people here have cut the peat into bricks, dried it and burnt it. Peat does not give much heat, and it makes a lot of smoke. But it is free, and it belongs to everyone.
G1JournalFine.3.short: Brunveen is a village of peat-cutters: wooden houses, a church, a mill, a dyke, and the flat dark bog all around. Peat gives little heat and much smoke, but it is free, and everyone's.

G1JournalFine.4.full: In the middle of the morning someone knocks at the gate. It is Fokke Tammer, the peat-cutter, with his hands bandaged and a barrow full of bricks of dark peat, almost black. He offers them as a gift, "for the master's family, as a mark of respect". He says this peat heats better than any other. He says it makes no smoke. He smiles: nobody in the village remembers ever seeing him smile.
G1JournalFine.4.easy: In the middle of the morning someone knocks at the gate. It is Fokke Tammer, the peat-cutter. His hands are bandaged, and he has a wheelbarrow full of bricks of dark peat, almost black. He offers them as a gift, "for the master's family, to show respect". He says this peat is warmer than any other. He says it makes no smoke. And he smiles. Nobody in the village remembers ever seeing him smile.
G1JournalFine.4.short: Fokke Tammer comes to the gate with a barrow of almost black peat, a gift "for the master's family". It makes no smoke, he says. He smiles, and nobody has ever seen him smile.

G1JournalFine.6.full: You let him in and accept the gift.

G1JournalFine.7.full: You thank him and send him home.

G1JournalFine.8.full: Fokke comes in, sits in the kitchen and accepts a glass of water, not of gin. He speaks of the master with affection, of the weather, of peat. When the cook lights the fire with his bricks, the flame is low and silent and the room warms up in a few minutes. Fokke never goes near the hearth. He keeps his hands in his lap, and leaves with three thank-yous.
G1JournalFine.8.easy: Fokke comes in, sits in the kitchen and accepts a glass of water, not gin. He talks kindly about the master, about the weather and about peat. The cook lights the fire with his bricks. The flame is low and quiet, and the room gets warm in a few minutes. Fokke never goes near the fire. He keeps his hands in his lap, and when he leaves he says thank you three times.
G1JournalFine.8.short: Fokke sits in the kitchen and drinks water, not gin. His peat burns low and silent and warms the room in minutes. He never goes near the fire.

G1JournalFine.9.full: Each player gains $1: Fokke's peat saves you firewood all winter.

G1JournalFine.10.full: You thank him at the gate and tell him there is no need. Fokke does not insist, does not take offence. He nods, turns the barrow round and goes off along the dyke, slowly. After a hundred paces he stops, turns and stands looking at the tower for a long moment, the way one looks at a house one lived in as a child.
G1JournalFine.10.easy: You thank him at the gate and tell him there is no need. Fokke does not insist and is not offended. He nods, turns his wheelbarrow and walks slowly away along the dyke. After a hundred steps he stops, turns and looks at the tower for a long time, the way you look at a house where you lived as a child.
G1JournalFine.10.short: You thank him and send him away. He goes without a word, but stops on the dyke to gaze at the tower, as one gazes at a childhood home.

G1R1.26.full: At the market they talk of nothing but the two lights. The miller swears they were will-o'-the-wisps, the schoolmaster that it was a shooting star, the widow Brink that it was the devil come to fetch the master of the estate who, finding him not ready, waited four months.
G1R1.26.easy: At the market everyone talks about the two lights. The miller swears they were marsh lights. The schoolmaster says it was a shooting star. The widow Brink says it was the devil, who came to take the master of the estate. He was not ready, she says, so the devil waited four months.
G1R1.26.short: The market talks only of the two lights: marsh lights, says the miller; a shooting star, says the schoolmaster; the devil, says the widow Brink, who waited four months for the master.

G1Fokke.2.full: At the Farmer's Market, among the baskets of herring and the cheeses, stands Fokke Tammer's stall, and in front of the stall there is a queue. He is selling his new peat, the black kind, at half a penny a brick: it burns slowly, makes no smoke, and they say a single stack lasts a week. The other peat-cutters look at him sideways, hands in their pockets, their carts full of ordinary peat that nobody buys.
G1Fokke.2.easy: At the Farmer's Market, between the baskets of herring and the cheeses, there is Fokke Tammer's stall, and people are queuing in front of it. He sells his new black peat for half a penny a brick. It burns slowly and makes no smoke, and people say one stack is enough for a week. The other peat-cutters look at him unkindly. They stand with their hands in their pockets, next to carts full of normal peat that nobody buys.
G1Fokke.2.short: At the market there is a queue for Fokke Tammer's black peat: smokeless, half a penny a brick. The other peat-cutters glare, their ordinary peat unsold.

G1Fokke.3.full: Fokke serves everyone patiently, without raising his voice, and gives the right change down to the last penny, he who a year ago could not count past ten. The bandages on his hands are clean. When he sees you he smiles and waves you to the front: "The master's family does not queue."
G1Fokke.3.easy: Fokke serves everyone with patience. He never raises his voice, and he gives the right change to the last penny. A year ago he could not count past ten. The bandages on his hands are clean. When he sees you, he smiles and waves you to the front: "The master's family does not wait in line."
G1Fokke.3.short: Fokke, who could not count past ten a year ago, gives exact change. Seeing you, he smiles and waves you forward: "The master's family does not queue."

G1Fokke.6.full: You ask him to take off his bandages.

G1Fokke.7.full: You ask the other peat-cutters what they think.

G1Fokke.8.full: You buy a stack of black bricks, and Fokke has a boy carry it to your house. It burns exactly as promised: no smoke, no crackling, for days. The house is so warm that in winter you sleep with the windows open. You sleep wonderfully, besides. Nobody in the family remembers their dreams any more.
G1Fokke.8.easy: You buy a stack of black bricks, and Fokke sends a boy to carry it to your house. It burns just as he promised: no smoke, no noise, for days. The house is so warm that in winter you sleep with the windows open. And you sleep very well. Nobody in the family remembers their dreams any more.
G1Fokke.8.short: The black peat burns for days without smoke, and the house is warm all winter. Everyone sleeps very well. Nobody remembers their dreams any more.

G1Fokke.10.full: Fokke looks at you for a moment, then unwinds the bandages without a word, in front of everyone. Underneath there is no burn at all. The skin of his palms is smooth, pink, perfect as a newborn's. The lines of the hand, the ones the fortune teller at the market reads for a penny, are gone. Fokke winds the bandages back, carefully, and wishes you a good day.
G1Fokke.10.easy: Fokke looks at you for a moment. Then, without a word, he unwraps the bandages in front of everyone. There is no burn under them. The skin of his palms is smooth, pink and perfect, like a baby's skin. The lines on his hands, the ones the fortune teller at the market reads for a penny, are not there any more. Fokke wraps the bandages again, carefully, and wishes you a good day.
G1Fokke.10.short: Without a word Fokke unwraps his bandages. No burns: his palms are smooth as a baby's, and the lines of his hands are gone. He wraps them again and wishes you a good day.

G1Fokke.12.full: The peat-cutters offer you a sip of gin and plenty of opinions. The black peat, they say, comes from the place of the light, where none of them sets foot. Fokke goes there alone, at night, and comes back with his cart full and his clothes dry. "Fokke was the worst of us all," says the oldest. "Now he is the best. I do not like it."
G1Fokke.12.easy: The peat-cutters give you a sip of gin and lots of opinions. They say the black peat comes from the place where the light was, and none of them goes there. Fokke goes there alone, at night, and comes back with a full cart and dry clothes. "Fokke was the worst of us all," says the oldest one. "Now he is the best. I do not like it."
G1Fokke.12.short: The peat-cutters say the black peat comes from where the light was. Fokke goes alone at night and comes back dry. "He was the worst of us. Now he is the best. I do not like it."

G1Cane.2.full: In the Park, under the willow by the pond, there is a big black dog, thin, its coat caked with mud. It is Bruin, Fokke Tammer's dog: everyone knows him, because for ten years he followed his master home from the inn, every night, keeping him on his feet. Since Fokke was "cured", Bruin will not go home. He sleeps under the willow, eats what the children throw him, and when Fokke passes on the road he growls at him, hackles up, until he is out of sight.
G1Cane.2.easy: In the Park, under the willow near the pond, there is a big black dog. He is thin, and his fur is covered in dry mud. It is Bruin, Fokke Tammer's dog. Everyone knows him, because for ten years he walked his master home from the inn every night and kept him standing. Since Fokke got "better", Bruin does not go home. He sleeps under the willow and eats what the children throw to him. When Fokke walks along the road, Bruin growls at him, with the fur on his back standing up, until Fokke is gone.
G1Cane.2.short: Under the willow in the Park lives Bruin, Fokke Tammer's dog, who for ten years walked his drunken master home. Since Fokke was "cured", Bruin will not go home, and growls whenever Fokke passes.

G1Cane.4.full: You take Bruin to the estate.

G1Cane.5.full: You take him back to Fokke.

G1Cane.6.full: Bruin follows you with no need of a lead, as if he had been waiting for you. At the estate he eats for three, sleeps in front of the tower door and never barks, at anyone. Except at certain people, when they pass on the road. You soon learn to pay attention to who they are.
G1Cane.6.easy: Bruin follows you without a lead, as if he was waiting for you. At the estate he eats enough for three dogs, sleeps in front of the tower door and never barks at anyone. Only at some people, when they walk past on the road. You soon learn to notice who they are.
G1Cane.6.short: Bruin follows you home, sleeps by the tower door and never barks. Except at certain people on the road. You learn to notice who.

G1Cane.8.full: You take Bruin to Fokke's house, with a rope round his neck. The dog digs in his paws the whole way. Fokke thanks you, offers you a coffee, and shuts the door. The next day Bruin is gone: Fokke says he ran away. The week after, at the market, Fokke has a new dog, black, big, identical. It growls at nobody.
G1Cane.8.easy: You take Bruin to Fokke's house with a rope around his neck. The dog pulls back the whole way. Fokke thanks you, offers you a coffee and closes the door. The next day Bruin is not there: Fokke says he ran away. The week after, at the market, Fokke has a new dog. It is black and big, exactly the same as Bruin. It does not growl at anyone.
G1Cane.8.short: You drag Bruin back to Fokke. Next day the dog has "run away". A week later Fokke has a new one, black, big, identical. It growls at nobody.

G1Levatrice.2.full: In church, after the christening of the miller's son, Hester Maas takes you aside. She is a tall, spare woman, her leather bag always in her hand, with the air of someone who has seen half the village born and the other half die. From the bag she takes a silver pocket watch: old, worn, its glass cracked and the crest of the estate engraved on the lid.
G1Levatrice.2.easy: In church, after the christening of the miller's son, Hester Maas takes you to one side. She is a tall, thin woman. She always carries her leather bag, and she looks like someone who has seen half the village born and the other half die. From the bag she takes a silver pocket watch. It is old and worn. The glass is cracked, and the crest of the estate is engraved on the lid.
G1Levatrice.2.short: After the christening, Hester Maas the midwife takes you aside and shows you a silver pocket watch: old, worn, cracked, with the estate's crest on the lid.

G1Levatrice.3.full: "Your father gave it to me, in payment for the last visit," she says. "He said it was his. But he had his own in his waistcoat, I saw it myself: new, shiny, with the same crest. He found this one on the floor of the tower. I do not want it, if it is yours." The watch has stopped at a quarter past eleven.
G1Levatrice.3.easy: "Your father gave it to me to pay for his last visit," she says. "He said it was his. But his watch was in his waistcoat pocket. I saw it myself: new and shiny, with the same crest. He found this one on the floor of the tower. I do not want it, if it belongs to you." The watch has stopped at a quarter past eleven.
G1Levatrice.3.short: "Your father paid me with it. He had his own in his waistcoat, the same, but new. This one he found on the tower floor." It has stopped at a quarter past eleven.

G1Levatrice.5.full: You offer to buy it back.

G1Levatrice.6.full: You tell her to keep it.

G1Levatrice.7.full: You ask her to write down everything she sees.

G1Levatrice.8.full: Hester refuses the money, offended: it was a payment, and she is an honest woman. She does let you look at the watch closely, though. Inside the lid, under the crest, someone has scratched initials and a date with the point of a knife, but the metal is so worn that nothing can be read any more. The movement is of a workmanship you have never seen: finer, denser. More modern.
G1Levatrice.8.easy: Hester will not take the money. She is offended: it was a payment, and she is an honest woman. But she lets you look closely at the watch. Inside the lid, under the crest, someone has scratched some letters and a date with a knife. But the metal is so worn that you cannot read them. The works inside are made in a way you have never seen. They are finer and smaller. More modern.
G1Levatrice.8.short: Hester refuses the money, offended. Inside the lid someone scratched initials and a date, worn unreadable. The works are finer than any you know. More modern.

G1Levatrice.10.full: Hester nods, puts the watch back in her bag and takes it home, where she locks it in the drawer with the Register, along with the birth certificates and the receipts. From that day on, when she meets you in the street, she greets you first.
G1Levatrice.10.easy: Hester nods, puts the watch back in her bag and takes it home. There she locks it in the drawer where she keeps the Register, the birth certificates and the receipts. From that day, when she meets you in the street, she is the first to say hello.
G1Levatrice.10.short: Hester locks the watch in the drawer with her Register. From then on she always greets you first.

G1Levatrice.12.full: Hester looks at you for a long time. Then she says she does it already: the temperatures, the recoveries, the cold hands. She does not know why, she says: it just seems to her that someone, one day, will need it. She promises you she will not miss a name.
G1Levatrice.12.easy: Hester looks at you for a long time. Then she says she already does it: the temperatures, the people who get better, the cold hands. She does not know why. She just feels that one day someone will need it. She promises she will not miss a single name.
G1Levatrice.12.short: Hester says she already does: temperatures, recoveries, cold hands. Someone will need it one day. She will not miss a name.

G1Torre.2.full: At the Builder's Office, Lambert the master builder shows you his drawing of the tower door, traced on tracing paper: wrought iron, three locks, hinges fit for a fortress. He sent two lads with crowbars and a smith with a file. The door did not move a hair. "The lock is melted from the inside," he says. "Someone welded it with a heat you cannot get from coal. And your father was outside when he died: we found him at the foot of the tower, with the key in his hand."
G1Torre.2.easy: At the Builder's Office, Lambert the master builder shows you his drawing of the tower door. It is made of iron, with three locks and very strong hinges, like the door of a castle. He sent two young workers with iron bars and a smith with a file. The door did not move at all. "The lock has melted from the inside," he says. "Someone welded it with a heat you cannot make with coal. And your father was outside when he died. We found him at the bottom of the tower, with the key in his hand."
G1Torre.2.short: Lambert the master builder could not move the tower door. "The lock is melted from inside, by a heat no coal can make. And your father died outside, at the foot of the tower, with the key in his hand."

G1Torre.4.full: You pay Lambert to break through the wall.

G1Torre.5.full: You leave the tower shut, for now.

G1Torre.6.full: The lads work for two days with chisels, and in the end they open a hole in the wall as big as a fist, level with the stairs. Inside it is dark. Lambert puts his ear to it and turns white: inside, he says, something is humming, softly, like a beehive. Then it stops. The lads refuse to come back.
G1Torre.6.easy: The young workers use their chisels for two days. In the end they make a hole in the wall as big as a fist, next to the stairs. It is dark inside. Lambert puts his ear to the hole and goes pale. He says something inside is humming, softly, like a beehive. Then it stops. The workers do not want to come back.
G1Torre.6.short: After two days of chiselling there is a fist-sized hole. Lambert listens and turns white: something inside hums like a beehive. Then it stops. The lads will not come back.

G1Torre.8.full: Lambert is relieved, and does not hide it. He charges you only for the lads' half day, and advises you to leave the dead's belongings to the dead. On your way out of the office you notice that his hands are bandaged too. He burnt himself, he says, on the stove.
G1Torre.8.easy: Lambert is relieved, and he shows it. He only asks you to pay for half a day of work, and he tells you to leave the things of the dead to the dead. As you leave the office, you notice that his hands are bandaged too. He says he burnt them on the stove.
G1Torre.8.short: Lambert, relieved, charges only half a day and advises leaving the dead alone. On the way out you notice his hands are bandaged too. The stove, he says.

G1Tomba.2.full: The Brunveen cemetery is built on the dyke, the only dry place in the village, and even there, a yard down, you strike water. New graves fill up in a single night. Siebe the gravedigger, a slight man with one leg shorter than the other, is waiting for you beside your father's grave, still covered with loose earth.
G1Tomba.2.easy: The Brunveen cemetery is on the dyke, because it is the only dry place in the village. But even there, if you dig one metre down, you find water. New graves fill with water in one night. Siebe the gravedigger is a small man with one leg shorter than the other. He is waiting for you next to your father's grave, which is still covered with fresh earth.
G1Tomba.2.short: The cemetery is on the dyke, the only dry ground, and even there graves fill with water overnight. Siebe the gravedigger waits for you by your father's fresh grave.

G1Tomba.3.full: Fokke Tammer, he tells you, has offered to cover the grave with his black peat, free of charge: the peat of the bog, the old folk say, preserves the dead for ever, and the master of the estate deserves to be preserved. Siebe waits for an answer, leaning on his spade. He looks like someone who hopes you will say no.
G1Tomba.3.easy: He tells you that Fokke Tammer has offered to cover the grave with his black peat, for free. The old people say that bog peat keeps the dead for ever, and the master of the estate deserves to be kept. Siebe waits for your answer, leaning on his spade. He looks like he hopes you will say no.
G1Tomba.3.short: Fokke Tammer has offered to cover the grave with his black peat, which "keeps the dead for ever". Siebe, leaning on his spade, clearly hopes you will refuse.

G1Tomba.6.full: You pay for a stone slab.

G1Tomba.7.full: Fokke brings the peat himself, the next day, and spreads it over the grave with his bandaged hands, brick by brick, the way one tucks in a blanket. When he has finished he stays on his knees a moment, looking. Siebe says Brunveen has never seen a grave so well made.
G1Tomba.7.easy: The next day Fokke brings the peat himself. With his bandaged hands he lays it on the grave, brick by brick, like someone tucking in a blanket. When he finishes, he stays on his knees for a moment and looks. Siebe says that nobody in Brunveen has ever seen such a well-made grave.
G1Tomba.7.short: Fokke lays the peat on the grave brick by brick, like tucking in a blanket, and kneels a moment to look. Siebe has never seen a finer grave.

G1Tomba.9.full: Siebe has a granite slab brought from the city, heavy, smooth, with your father's name and the two dates. It takes four men to set it in place. When they have finished Siebe shakes your hand, relieved: "That will keep him down," he says. Then he blushes, as if he had said too much.
G1Tomba.9.easy: Siebe has a granite stone brought from the city. It is heavy and smooth, with your father's name and the two dates. Four men are needed to put it in place. When they finish, Siebe shakes your hand. He looks relieved. "That will keep him down," he says. Then his face goes red, as if he has said too much.
G1Tomba.9.short: Four men set the heavy granite slab in place. Siebe shakes your hand, relieved: "That will keep him down." Then he blushes.

G1Carovana.2.full: At the Traveling Caravan, between a travelling dentist and a man selling almanacs, there is a cart painted blue with a sign in gold letters: STAR WATER – FROM BRUNVEEN – CURES ALL ILLS. The seller is a little man with a battered top hat, not from these parts. He sells phials of dark water at a florin apiece, and he has already sold fifty in the village. He draws it, he says, laughing, "where the star fell".
G1Carovana.2.easy: At the Traveling Caravan, between a travelling dentist and a man who sells almanacs, there is a blue cart with a sign in gold letters: STAR WATER – FROM BRUNVEEN – CURES ALL ILLS. The seller is a small man in an old, dented top hat. He is not from here. He sells little bottles of dark water for a florin each, and he has already sold fifty in the village. He laughs and says he takes the water "where the star fell".
G1Carovana.2.short: A stranger in a battered top hat sells STAR WATER – CURES ALL ILLS at a florin a phial. He has sold fifty already. He draws it, he laughs, "where the star fell".

G1Carovana.5.full: You report him to the mayor.

G1Carovana.7.full: The phial is of green glass, with a cork stopper and a hand-drawn label: a star falling on a meadow. At home you uncork it and sniff: smoke, earth, iron. In your laboratory the water stays cloudy for weeks, never settling, and every so often, when nobody is looking at it, the level drops by a finger.
G1Carovana.7.easy: The little bottle is made of green glass, with a cork and a label drawn by hand: a star falling on a field. At home you open it and smell it: smoke, earth, iron. In your laboratory the water stays cloudy for weeks and never clears. And sometimes, when nobody is looking, the water level goes down by a finger.
G1Carovana.7.short: The green phial smells of smoke, earth and iron. In your laboratory the water stays cloudy for weeks, and when nobody is watching, the level drops.

G1Carovana.8.full: Pay $1 and gain 1 {icon:Chemical_Icon} and 1 Chemistry Knowledge.

G1Carovana.9.full: Mayor Wessel listens to your complaint with great attention and promises to see to it. The next day the blue cart is gone. In the village they say the seller left in the night, without paying the innkeeper. On his bed, at the inn, the landlady found only a heap of wet peat, in the shape of a man.
G1Carovana.9.easy: Mayor Wessel listens to your complaint very carefully and promises to deal with it. The next day the blue cart is not there. People in the village say the seller left in the night without paying the innkeeper. At the inn, on his bed, the landlady found only a pile of wet peat in the shape of a man.
G1Carovana.9.short: The mayor promises to deal with it. Next day the cart is gone, the inn unpaid, and on the seller's bed lies a heap of wet peat in the shape of a man.

G1Carovana.11.full: You follow him to the dyke, in the dark, keeping your distance. The little man wades into the bog up to his knees, at the exact place of the light, and fills the phials one by one, singing. Then he stops singing. He stays motionless in the water for a whole hour, arms at his sides, as if he were listening to someone. When he comes out, the top hat is gone, and he walks straight, without a limp.
G1Carovana.11.easy: In the dark you follow him to the dyke, staying far behind. The little man walks into the bog up to his knees, at the exact place where the light was. He fills the bottles one by one, singing. Then he stops singing. He stands still in the water for a whole hour, with his arms by his sides, as if someone were talking to him. When he comes out, his top hat is gone, and he walks straight. He does not limp any more.
G1Carovana.11.short: You follow him to the bog. He fills his phials where the light was, singing, then stands silent in the water for an hour, as if listening. He comes out without his hat, and without his limp.

G1Asta.3.full: Today Fokke Tammer brought to market the thing he found in the water, the one that burnt him. He had kept it hidden in his shed. It is a black stone, smooth, as big as a loaf, heavier than it looks; and warm, always, even in the rain. Those who touch it say it makes them thirsty.
G1Asta.3.easy: Today Fokke Tammer brought to the market the thing he found in the water, the thing that burnt his hands. He had hidden it in his shed. It is a smooth black stone, as big as a loaf of bread, and heavier than it looks. It is always warm, even in the rain. People who touch it say it makes them thirsty.
G1Asta.3.short: Today Fokke Tammer brought the thing from the water to market: a smooth black stone the size of a loaf, always warm, even in the rain. Touching it makes you thirsty.

G1Asta.4.full: Fokke is putting it up for auction. He says it is not right for him to keep it: it must go "to whoever will know what to do with it". The professor from the city museum arrived on the morning train with a fat wallet. But everyone at the market was looking at the family of the estate.
G1Asta.4.easy: Fokke is selling it at an auction. He says it is not right for him to keep it. It must go "to someone who will know what to do with it". The professor from the city museum came on the morning train with a lot of money. But at the market, everyone was looking at the family of the estate.
G1Asta.4.short: Fokke is auctioning it, "for whoever will know what to do with it". The museum professor came with a fat wallet. But everyone was looking at the family of the estate.

G1Asta.5.full: Each player secretly bids a sum of money. The highest bidder pays and takes the **stone**: the **Crown token** {icon:S3_CrownToken} from the **A Time of War** Box. The others pay nothing. *(In case of a tie, the Start Player wins.)*

G1Asta.6.full: Whoever has the stone, once per Round, draws one extra Experiment when they draw Experiments. But at the end of each Round the stone makes them thirsty.

G1AstaVinta.2.full: Fokke hands you the stone wrapped in a jute sack, with both hands, the way one hands over a baby. He urges you to keep it dry. Then, softly, so that only you can hear: "Never leave it near water. It wants to go back."
G1AstaVinta.2.easy: Fokke gives you the stone, wrapped in a jute sack. He holds it with both hands, like someone giving you a baby. He tells you to keep it dry. Then he speaks quietly, so that only you can hear: "Never leave it near water. It wants to go back."
G1AstaVinta.2.short: Fokke hands you the stone in a sack, like a baby, and whispers: "Never leave it near water. It wants to go back."

G1AstaVinta.3.full: At home the stone is warm on the laboratory table, and the room, within a few minutes, fills with a smell of bog. On its smooth surface there is not a scratch, a vein, a flaw. It is no mineral you know. That night you get up three times to drink.
G1AstaVinta.3.easy: At home the stone is warm on the laboratory table. In a few minutes the room smells of the bog. Its smooth surface has no scratches, no lines, no faults. It is not a mineral you know. That night you get up three times to drink.
G1AstaVinta.3.short: On your laboratory table the warm stone fills the room with the smell of the bog. It is no mineral you know. That night you get up three times to drink.

G1AstaVinta.4.full: **{0}** takes the Crown token {icon:S3_CrownToken} and keeps it in front of them.

G1R2.3.full: *It is Fokke Tammer: he is the first.*

G1R2.4.full: Take the **Paradox tokens** {icon:S3_ParadoxToken} from the **A Time of War** Box: in this scenario they are the bog's **dark water**. Place one on the **Park**.

G1R2.9.full: The first player who sends one of their pieces to the Laborer's Union

G1R2.15.full: The first player who sends one of their pieces to the Blacksmith

G1R2.24.full: This year nobody in Brunveen has died. Siebe the gravedigger, to make ends meet, has taken up carpentry as well, and Pastor Kalf has celebrated more weddings than in all the previous years put together. The couples marry without haste, without quarrels, and without inviting relatives from outside.
G1R2.24.easy: This year nobody in Brunveen has died. Siebe the gravedigger needs money, so now he works as a carpenter too. Pastor Kalf has had more weddings this year than in all the other years together. The couples get married calmly, without fighting, and without inviting any family from outside the village.
G1R2.24.short: Nobody in Brunveen died this year. The gravedigger now does carpentry, and the pastor has married more couples than ever: calm, quiet weddings, with no relatives from outside.

G1R2.25.full: At the estate, Bruin, Fokke's dog, has taken to sitting in front of the gate whenever a wedding procession goes by, and growling, softly, at only one of the couple. Never at both.
G1R2.25.easy: At the estate, Bruin, Fokke's dog, now sits in front of the gate every time a wedding procession goes past. He growls softly, but only at one of the two people getting married. Never at both.
G1R2.25.short: When a wedding goes past the estate, Bruin growls softly at one of the couple. Never at both.

G1R2.26.full: At the estate, meanwhile, {0}'s stone warms its felt box, and in the laboratory the water jugs are empty every morning.
G1R2.26.easy: At the estate, meanwhile, {0}'s stone keeps its felt box warm, and in the laboratory the water jugs are empty every morning.
G1R2.26.short: At the estate {0}'s stone warms its box, and every night the water jugs empty.

round.G1R2.end.full: The Middle Years of the First Generation have ended.

round.G1R2.then.full: Then perform all Start of Round actions for the Late Years before continuing.

G1Mani.2.full: At the Town Hall the council meets on the first Thursday of the month, in a wood-panelled room with a portrait of the king. Today Hester Maas has asked to speak, something a midwife never does. She has brought her Register. She reads aloud: nine people in the village have a body temperature a full two degrees below normal. All nine are perfectly well. All nine have drunk water from the bog.
G1Mani.2.easy: At the Town Hall the council meets on the first Thursday of every month, in a room with wooden walls and a picture of the king. Today Hester Maas has asked to speak. A midwife never does that. She has brought her Register, and she reads from it. Nine people in the village have a body temperature two whole degrees lower than normal. All nine are very healthy. All nine have drunk water from the bog.
G1Mani.2.short: At the council, Hester Maas reads from her Register: nine villagers are two degrees colder than normal. All nine are perfectly healthy. All nine drank bog water.

G1Mani.3.full: Mayor Aldert Wessel listens to her with his hands folded over his belly. He is a big, red-faced man, with gout and a cough that will not go away. When Hester has finished, he thanks her for her zeal and asks whether she also has an illness to report, or only good health.
G1Mani.3.easy: Mayor Aldert Wessel listens with his hands crossed on his belly. He is a big man with a red face, gout and a cough that never goes away. When Hester finishes, he thanks her for working so hard. Then he asks if she has an illness to report, or only good health.
G1Mani.3.short: Mayor Wessel, big, red and gouty, thanks her for her zeal, and asks whether she has an illness to report, or only good health.

G1Mani.5.full: You back her before the council.

G1Mani.6.full: You ask her for the names, in private.

G1Mani.7.full: You make a joke and ease the tension.

G1Mani.8.full: You stand up and say the midwife is right, and that the council should forbid the bog water until it is known what it is. The silence lasts a long time. Then the mayor thanks you too, puts the proposal to the vote, and the proposal fails: everyone against, except the two of you. The councillors who voted against smile at you on their way out, one by one.
G1Mani.8.easy: You stand up and say that the midwife is right. The council should forbid the bog water until they know what it is. There is a long silence. Then the mayor thanks you too and asks for a vote. Everyone votes no, except you and Hester. As they leave, the councillors who voted no smile at you, one by one.
G1Mani.8.short: You say the council should ban the bog water. Long silence. Everyone votes against, except you and Hester, and they all smile at you on the way out.

G1Mani.10.full: Outside, under the portico, Hester shows you the page. The first name is Fokke Tammer. Then Lambert the master builder, Smit the washerwoman, two peat-cutters, a smith's lad, the Mulder boy, the miller's wife, and the last, written last week, with a question mark: Wessel, Aldert, mayor.
G1Mani.10.easy: Outside, under the arches, Hester shows you the page. The first name is Fokke Tammer. Then come Lambert the master builder, Smit the washerwoman, two peat-cutters, a boy who works for the smith, the Mulder boy and the miller's wife. The last name was written last week, with a question mark: Wessel, Aldert, mayor.
G1Mani.10.short: Outside, Hester shows you the names: Fokke Tammer first, then Lambert, Smit the washerwoman, the miller's wife... and last, with a question mark, the mayor.

G1Mani.12.full: You say that if good health were a disease, Brunveen would have an epidemic, and the council laughs, all together, for too long. Hester closes the Register and leaves without saying goodbye to you. The mayor, on the other hand, invites you to dinner.
G1Mani.12.easy: You say that if good health were an illness, Brunveen would have an epidemic. The whole council laughs, all at the same time, for too long. Hester closes the Register and leaves without saying goodbye. But the mayor invites you to dinner.
G1Mani.12.short: "If good health were a disease, Brunveen would have an epidemic." The council laughs together, too long. Hester leaves without a word. The mayor invites you to dinner.

G1Pozzo.2.full: At the Laborer's Union, the room above the stable where day labourers are hired, the drinking water is brought from a canal that runs straight from the bog. Until last year nobody touched it: it tasted of rust and gave you stomach ache. Now everybody drinks it, because it is good, fresh, and takes away tiredness. The labourers work from dawn to dusk without complaint. The head of the union is worried: for six months nobody has asked for a rise.
G1Pozzo.2.easy: The Laborer's Union is a room over the stable, where farm workers are hired by the day. Their drinking water comes from a canal that runs straight from the bog. Until last year nobody drank it: it tasted of rust and gave people stomach ache. Now everyone drinks it, because it is good and fresh, and it takes away tiredness. The workers work from morning to night and never complain. The head of the union is worried: for six months nobody has asked for more pay.
G1Pozzo.2.short: At the Laborer's Union everyone now drinks the bog canal's water, once undrinkable. The labourers work dawn to dusk without complaint. For six months nobody has asked for a rise.

G1Pozzo.4.full: You pay to close the canal and dig a well.

G1Pozzo.6.full: The new well costs dear and gives hard water that tastes of lime. The labourers grumble, cough, complain of the heat and of their pay. The head of the union thanks you with tears in his eyes.
G1Pozzo.6.easy: The new well is expensive, and its water is hard and tastes of lime. The workers grumble and cough, and they complain about the heat and about their pay. The head of the union thanks you with tears in his eyes.
G1Pozzo.6.short: The new well's water tastes of lime. The labourers grumble about the heat and the pay again. The union head thanks you with tears in his eyes.
