G1Pozzo.8.full: It really is good. It is cold as melted snow, and leaves in the mouth a taste of smoke that is not unpleasant. All afternoon you work without tiring, and in the evening you cannot quite remember what you were thinking about. Nothing bad, at any rate.
G1Pozzo.8.easy: It really is good. It is as cold as melted snow, and it leaves a taste of smoke in your mouth that is quite nice. All afternoon you work without getting tired. In the evening you cannot really remember what you were thinking about. Nothing bad, anyway.
G1Pozzo.8.short: It is good: cold as snowmelt, with a pleasant taste of smoke. You work all afternoon without tiring, and cannot remember what you thought about. Nothing bad.

G1Pastore.2.full: The Brunveen church is made of wood, like everything else, with a crooked steeple and worn pews. Pastor Ewout Kalf is a thin, stern man with a voice bigger than he is. This Sunday he preaches on Lot's wife and the things one must not look at. Then, without changing his tone, he speaks of the stone from the bog: it came from the sky, he says, and what comes from the sky without being called does not come from God. It must be taken back where it was found. As he speaks, he looks at your pew.
G1Pastore.2.easy: The Brunveen church is made of wood, like everything else. Its steeple is crooked and its benches are old. Pastor Ewout Kalf is a thin, strict man with a very big voice. This Sunday he talks about Lot's wife and about the things you must not look at. Then, in the same voice, he talks about the stone from the bog. He says it came from the sky, and what comes from the sky when nobody called it does not come from God. It must go back to where they found it. While he speaks, he looks at your bench.
G1Pastore.2.short: Pastor Kalf, thin and stern, preaches that the stone came from the sky uncalled, and so not from God: it must go back where it was found. He looks at your pew as he says it.

G1Pastore.4.full: After the service, you agree with him.

G1Pastore.5.full: You contradict him, on the church steps.

G1Pastore.6.full: The pastor holds your hand between his, for a long time, the way one holds a convert's. He tells you that you are not the only person in Brunveen who thinks so, but that you are few, and fewer every month. He asks you to pray for them. He does not say for whom.
G1Pastore.6.easy: The pastor holds your hand in both of his for a long time, like the hand of someone who has just found God. He tells you that you are not the only person in Brunveen who thinks this way. But there are few of you, and fewer every month. He asks you to pray for them. He does not say who they are.
G1Pastore.6.short: The pastor clasps your hand: you are not alone in thinking so, he says, but you are few, and fewer every month. Pray for them. He does not say whom.

G1Pastore.8.full: You answer him, in front of everyone, that a stone is a stone, and that science is not done with sermons. The pastor goes red, then white. Around you, people nod, politely: many more than you expected. They all have their hands in their pockets.
G1Pastore.8.easy: In front of everyone you tell him that a stone is just a stone, and that you cannot do science with sermons. The pastor's face goes red, then white. Around you, people nod politely. There are many more of them than you thought. They all have their hands in their pockets.
G1Pastore.8.short: You tell him a stone is a stone, and science is not made of sermons. Around you, far more people than you expected nod politely, all with their hands in their pockets.

G1Fabbro.2.full: Jaap Mol, the smith, fell into the bog canal at Easter, drunk, and stayed under water until his lads fished him out, half an hour later, given up for dead. He got up by himself, shook the water off and went back to work. Since then he has not missed a stroke. The horseshoes he makes are so perfect that the horses of the city come to Brunveen to be shod. Jaap no longer drinks, no longer sings, and has apologised to everyone he owed money.
G1Fabbro.2.easy: At Easter, Jaap Mol the smith fell into the bog canal. He was drunk. He stayed under the water until his workers pulled him out, half an hour later. Everyone thought he was dead. But he stood up by himself, shook off the water and went back to work. Since then he has never missed a blow with his hammer. His horseshoes are so perfect that horses come from the city to Brunveen to get them. Jaap does not drink or sing any more, and he has said sorry to everyone he owed money to.
G1Fabbro.2.short: At Easter Jaap Mol the smith fell drunk into the canal and stayed under for half an hour. He got up and went back to work. Now he never misses a stroke, no longer drinks or sings, and has paid all his debts.

G1Fabbro.4.full: You order a key for the tower from him.

G1Fabbro.5.full: You ask him what he remembers of the canal.

G1Fabbro.6.full: Jaap looks at your drawing of the lock, turns it round, and says a welded door cannot be opened with a key. But a key can be made that heats it, from outside, until it melts again. He works on it for three days. The result is an iron rod as long as an arm, with a wooden handle and a copper tip. He hands it over without charging: "For your father," he says. "He was a good man."
G1Fabbro.6.easy: Jaap looks at your drawing of the lock and turns it around. He says you cannot open a welded door with a key. But he can make a key that heats the lock from the outside, until it melts again. He works on it for three days. In the end there is an iron bar as long as an arm, with a wooden handle and a copper tip. He does not ask for money: "For your father," he says. "He was a good man."
G1Fabbro.6.short: A welded door needs no key, says Jaap, but a rod that will melt the lock again. After three days he gives you one, free: "For your father. He was a good man."

G1Fabbro.8.full: Jaap thinks about it, hammering. He remembers the cold, he says, and then the dark, and then a great silence, like in church when the pastor stops talking. And someone, down there, who looked like him, and who was asleep. "I let him sleep," he says. "He was tired. I was not." Then he goes back to hammering, and does not miss a stroke.
G1Fabbro.8.easy: Jaap thinks while he hammers. He says he remembers the cold, then the dark, then a great silence, like in church when the pastor stops talking. And down there was someone who looked like him, sleeping. "I let him sleep," he says. "He was tired. I was not." Then he goes back to his hammering, and he does not miss once.
G1Fabbro.8.short: Jaap remembers the cold, the dark, a great silence, and someone down there who looked like him, asleep. "I let him sleep. He was tired. I was not."

G1Fosse.2.full: At the cemetery on the dyke, Siebe the gravedigger has a problem. He had to move three old graves to make room for the new wall, and the coffins, opened, were full of dark water. Inside, the dead of twenty years ago: intact, their skin brown as leather, in their Sunday clothes, hands folded. As if they were asleep. Siebe has seen plenty, he says: it is the peat, which preserves everything. But in the third grave, under the coffin, in the water, there was another face, young, white, eyes closed, which nobody ever buried there. Siebe swears it was the miller's wife. The miller's wife, this morning, was at the market.
G1Fosse.2.easy: At the cemetery on the dyke, Siebe the gravedigger has a problem. He had to move three old graves for the new wall. When he opened the coffins, they were full of dark water. Inside were people who died twenty years ago. They were whole, with skin brown like leather, in their best clothes, with their hands together. They looked asleep. Siebe says he has seen many like that: the peat keeps everything. But in the third grave, under the coffin, in the water, there was another face. It was young and white, with its eyes closed, and nobody ever buried anyone there. Siebe swears it was the miller's wife. This morning the miller's wife was at the market.
G1Fosse.2.short: Moving three old graves, Siebe found the dead intact in dark water, as if asleep: the peat keeps everything. But under the third coffin lay a young face nobody buried there. The miller's wife. Who was at the market this morning.

G1Fosse.5.full: You call Hester to examine them.

G1Fosse.6.full: You rebury them at sunset, in a hurry, with dry earth brought from the hill, so that the water will not reach them. Before filling the third grave, Siebe does not look, and says a prayer that is not in the pastor's book. When you have finished he washes his hands three times at the fountain, and asks you not to tell anyone.
G1Fosse.6.easy: You bury them again at sunset, quickly, with dry earth from the hill, so that the water cannot reach them. Before he fills the third grave, Siebe looks away and says a prayer that is not in the pastor's book. When you finish, he washes his hands three times at the fountain and asks you not to tell anyone.
G1Fosse.6.short: You rebury them at sunset in dry earth. At the third grave Siebe looks away and says a prayer not in the pastor's book, then asks you to tell nobody.

G1Fosse.8.full: Hester arrives with her bag and her lantern. In the third grave the water has clouded, and the face can no longer be seen. Hester dips her thermometer in, waits, and draws it out: the water down there is as lukewarm as a sleeping body. She notes it in the Register, then closes the notebook and says she has seen nothing, and that it is better so.
G1Fosse.8.easy: Hester comes with her bag and her lantern. In the third grave the water is cloudy now, and you cannot see the face. Hester puts her thermometer in the water, waits, and takes it out. The water down there is as warm as a sleeping body. She writes it in the Register. Then she closes the book and says she has seen nothing, and that it is better this way.
G1Fosse.8.short: In the third grave the water has clouded over the face. Hester's thermometer says it is as warm as a sleeping body. She writes it down, then says she saw nothing.

G1Cronaca.3.full: Four years since the night of the two lights. Nobody in Brunveen has died of illness since: only two old people, in their sleep, and a child who fell from the hayloft. The marsh fevers, which every summer carried someone off, did not come this year. The doctor from the city says it is the air. I count the temperatures.
G1Cronaca.3.easy: It is four years since the night of the two lights. Since then nobody in Brunveen has died of an illness. Only two old people died in their sleep, and a child fell from the hayloft. Every summer the marsh fever used to kill someone, but this year it did not come. The doctor from the city says it is thanks to the air. I count the temperatures.
G1Cronaca.3.short: Four years since the two lights, and nobody in Brunveen has died of illness. Even the marsh fever stayed away. The city doctor says it is the air. I count the temperatures.

G1Cronaca.4.full: The cold hands, in the Register, number forty-one. I have stopped telling the council.
G1Cronaca.4.easy: There are forty-one cold hands in the Register now. I do not tell the council any more.
G1Cronaca.4.short: Forty-one cold hands in the Register. I no longer tell the council.

G1Cronaca.5.full: Fokke Tammer's dog lives at the estate, and growls at the same people I mark in the Register. I have started taking him with me when I do my rounds of the houses. He is never wrong.
G1Cronaca.5.easy: Fokke Tammer's dog lives at the estate. He growls at the same people that I write in the Register. Now I take him with me when I visit the houses. He is never wrong.
G1Cronaca.5.short: Fokke's dog growls at the very people I mark in the Register. I take him on my rounds now. He is never wrong.

G1Cronaca.6.full: Fokke Tammer's new dog, the one identical to the old, follows its master everywhere, without a sound. It does not bark, does not eat, does not grow old. The children no longer play with it.
G1Cronaca.6.easy: Fokke Tammer's new dog, the one that looks exactly like the old one, follows its master everywhere without a sound. It does not bark, it does not eat, and it does not get older. The children do not play with it any more.
G1Cronaca.6.short: Fokke's new dog follows him everywhere in silence. It does not bark, eat or age. The children no longer play with it.

G1Cronaca.7.full: The star water, the one from the seller in the top hat, can now be found in every kitchen. One of the phials, I am told, is on the laboratory table at the estate.
G1Cronaca.7.easy: The star water, from the seller in the top hat, is now in every kitchen. People tell me that one of the little bottles is on the laboratory table at the estate.
G1Cronaca.7.short: The star water is in every kitchen now. One phial, I am told, is in the estate's laboratory.

G1Cronaca.8.full: The star water seller has vanished, but the water has not: now the innkeeper's son sells it, with the same label.
G1Cronaca.8.easy: The seller of the star water has gone, but the water has not. Now the innkeeper's son sells it, with the same label.
G1Cronaca.8.short: The seller is gone, but the innkeeper's son sells his star water, same label.

G1Cronaca.9.full: The star water seller came back this year, without his top hat, without his limp, and without the accent he had before. He talks like us.
G1Cronaca.9.easy: The seller of the star water came back this year. He has no top hat, no limp, and not the same accent as before. He talks like us.
G1Cronaca.9.short: The star water seller is back, without hat, limp or accent. He talks like us.

G1Cronaca.10.full: On the grave of the master of the estate, Fokke's peat has grown no grass, nor moss. It is as black and smooth as on the first day.
G1Cronaca.10.easy: On the grave of the master of the estate, no grass or moss has grown on Fokke's peat. It is still black and smooth, like on the first day.
G1Cronaca.10.short: On the master's grave Fokke's peat grows nothing. It is as black as the first day.

G1Cronaca.11.full: The granite slab on the master's grave has tilted by a finger's breadth, as if something were pushing from below. Siebe says it is the ground settling.
G1Cronaca.11.easy: The granite stone on the master's grave has moved a little to one side, as if something under it were pushing. Siebe says it is only the ground settling.
G1Cronaca.11.short: The granite slab on the master's grave has tilted, as if pushed from below. Siebe says it is the ground settling.

G1Cronaca.12.full: The family of the estate is well liked now. They are invited to parties, greeted by name. I am afraid for them.
G1Cronaca.12.easy: Now people like the family of the estate. They invite them to parties and say hello to them by name. I am afraid for them.
G1Cronaca.12.short: The estate family is well liked now. I am afraid for them.

G1Cronaca.13.full: The family of the estate asks questions, and the village has stopped answering. They are greeted all the same, always politely. But nobody visits them any more.
G1Cronaca.13.easy: The family of the estate asks questions, and the village does not answer any more. People still say hello to them, always politely. But nobody goes to visit them now.
G1Cronaca.13.short: The estate family asks questions; the village no longer answers. Polite greetings, and no visits.

G1R3.2.full: Open the Village Chronicle to the **Fear of the Unknown** section ({icon:S2_ScenarioIcon}) and turn to **page 12**.

G1R3.4.full: Place a {icon:S3_ParadoxToken} token on the **Farmer's Apprentice**.

G1R3.6.full: The first player who sends one of their pieces to the Bank

G1R3.9.full: The first player who sends one of their pieces to the Church Library

G1R3.15.full: The first player who sends one of their pieces to the Foundry

G1R3.18.full: The first player who sends one of their pieces to the Farmer's Apprentice

G1R3.27.full: Mayor Wessel no longer coughs and has stopped limping. He lost forty pounds in one winter, with no diet and no medicine, and his gout went in a single night. At the council, these days, sittings last ten minutes. Nobody objects to anything any more.
G1R3.27.easy: Mayor Wessel does not cough any more, and he does not limp. In one winter he lost forty pounds, with no diet and no medicine, and his gout disappeared in one night. Now the council meetings last ten minutes. Nobody says no to anything any more.
G1R3.27.short: Mayor Wessel no longer coughs or limps: he lost forty pounds in a winter, and his gout vanished overnight. Council sittings now last ten minutes. Nobody objects to anything.

G1R3.28.full: The mill, without Harm Visser, grinds better than before. Grietje runs it on her own, and never gets the weight of a sack wrong.
G1R3.28.easy: Without Harm Visser, the mill works better than before. Grietje runs it alone, and she never gets the weight of a sack wrong.
G1R3.28.short: Without Harm Visser the mill grinds better. Grietje runs it alone, and never misweighs a sack.

G1R3.29.full: At the mill Harm Visser and his wife Grietje sing together as they work, in two parts. Perfectly in tune.
G1R3.29.easy: At the mill Harm Visser and his wife Grietje sing together while they work, with two voices. They are perfectly in tune.
G1R3.29.short: At the mill Harm and Grietje Visser sing in two parts as they work. Perfectly in tune.

round.G1R3.end.full: The Late Years of the First Generation have ended.

round.G1R3.then.full: Perform the End of Round actions, then continue with the Storybook before the End of the Generation.

G1Banca.2.full: At the Bank, the sturdiest house in the village, with the only safe in the province, Professor Ostrander of the city's natural history museum is waiting for you: an elderly gentleman with gold spectacles and a starched collar. He did not manage to buy the stone at the auction, he says, and he blames nobody for it. But science has its rights. A chip would be enough for him, as small as a fingernail, for his analyses. He has already prepared the money, in an envelope.
G1Banca.2.easy: At the Bank, the strongest house in the village, with the only safe in the province, Professor Ostrander is waiting for you. He works at the natural history museum in the city. He is an old gentleman with gold glasses and a stiff white collar. He says he could not buy the stone at the auction, and he does not blame anyone. But science has its rights. He only needs a tiny piece, as small as a fingernail, to study it. He already has the money ready in an envelope.
G1Banca.2.short: At the Bank, Professor Ostrander of the city museum asks politely for a chip of the stone, no bigger than a fingernail, for science. The money is ready in an envelope.

G1Banca.6.full: The stone will not be scratched by anything: not the knife, not the file, not the hammer. In the end Jaap Mol, the smith, manages it, with a single precise blow. The professor tucks the chip into a little velvet box and leaves on the evening train. A few months later you read in the city paper that the museum's caretaker, after years of illness, has recovered, and that the professor no longer drinks.
G1Banca.6.easy: Nothing can scratch the stone: not a knife, not a file, not a hammer. In the end Jaap Mol the smith does it, with one exact blow. The professor puts the chip in a little velvet box and leaves on the evening train. A few months later you read in the city newspaper that the museum's caretaker, who was ill for years, is now well. And the professor does not drink any more.
G1Banca.6.short: Only Jaap Mol's single precise blow can chip the stone. The professor leaves with it in a velvet box. Months later the city paper says the museum caretaker is cured, and the professor has stopped drinking.

G1Banca.8.full: The professor puts the envelope away, disappointed but polite, and leaves you his visiting card, "in case you change your mind". On his way back to the station he stops on the dyke to look at the bog. He stays a long time. Then he takes the train.
G1Banca.8.easy: The professor puts the envelope away. He is disappointed but polite. He gives you his card, "in case you change your mind". On the way back to the station he stops on the dyke and looks at the bog. He stays there a long time. Then he gets on the train.
G1Banca.8.short: The professor leaves his card, "in case you change your mind". On the way to the station he stops a long time on the dyke, looking at the bog.

G1Libri.2.full: The Church Library is a room behind the sacristy, with three hundred volumes and a smoking stove. Pastor Kalf has left you the keys and a book open on the lectern: a German treatise from a hundred years ago on the bog men. Bodies found in the peat, the book says, with skin and hair intact after a thousand years, as if they were asleep. Some with a rope round their necks, others with their hands tied. All of them, the book says, buried alive. Nobody knows why.
G1Libri.2.easy: The Church Library is a room behind the sacristy, with three hundred books and a stove that smokes. Pastor Kalf has left you the keys and a book open on the reading stand. It is a German book from a hundred years ago about the bog people. It says that bodies have been found in the peat after a thousand years, with their skin and hair still whole, as if they were sleeping. Some had a rope around the neck, others had their hands tied. The book says they were all buried alive. Nobody knows why.
G1Libri.2.short: The pastor has left a German treatise open for you: bodies found in the peat after a thousand years, intact, as if asleep. All buried alive, it says. Nobody knows why.

G1Libri.3.full: In the margin, in the pastor's hand: *What if they were not buried? What if they went in of their own accord?*
G1Libri.3.easy: In the margin, in the pastor's handwriting: *What if nobody buried them? What if they went in by themselves?*
G1Libri.3.short: In the margin, in the pastor's hand: *What if they went in by themselves?*

G1Libri.6.full: You ask the pastor to organise a watch.

G1Libri.7.full: You study for three evenings, by candlelight. You learn how peat preserves flesh, how the dark water tans it, how to tell a body centuries old from one of yesterday. You also learn to recognise the smell. On your way home you smell it everywhere.
G1Libri.7.easy: You study for three evenings by candlelight. You learn how peat keeps a body, how the dark water turns it into leather, and how to tell a body hundreds of years old from one that died yesterday. You also learn to know the smell. On your way home, you smell it everywhere.
G1Libri.7.short: Three evenings by candlelight teach you how peat preserves the dead, and the smell of it. On the way home you smell it everywhere.

G1Libri.9.full: The pastor agrees at once, as if he had only been waiting for someone to ask. Brunveen's first night watch goes out the following Saturday: the pastor, three peat-cutters, Siebe the gravedigger and a lantern. They find nothing. But all night long, from the houses, people watch them pass, behind the windowpanes, without lighting a lamp.
G1Libri.9.easy: The pastor says yes immediately, as if he was only waiting for someone to ask. The first night watch of Brunveen goes out the next Saturday: the pastor, three peat-cutters, Siebe the gravedigger and a lantern. They find nothing. But all night, from the houses, people watch them walk past, behind the windows, in the dark.
G1Libri.9.short: The pastor agrees at once. The first night watch, five men and a lantern, finds nothing. But all night people watch them from dark windows.

G1Sindaco.2.full: Mayor Aldert Wessel receives you in his office at the Town Hall: thin, upright, rosy, his collar too loose. He offers you a glass of water and asks you, with great courtesy, what you need. He remembers your mother's name, the day of your birthday, the exact price the estate paid for its hay last year. When you shake his hand, it is cold. Old Wessel always had sweaty hands: in the village they called him "the fish".
G1Sindaco.2.easy: Mayor Aldert Wessel meets you in his office at the Town Hall. He is thin, he stands straight, his face is pink, and his collar is too big for him. He offers you a glass of water and asks, very politely, what you need. He remembers your mother's name, your birthday, and the exact price the estate paid for hay last year. When you shake his hand, it is cold. Old Wessel always had sweaty hands. In the village they called him "the fish".
G1Sindaco.2.short: Mayor Wessel, thin and rosy now, remembers your mother's name, your birthday, the price of your hay. His hand is cold. Old Wessel's hands were always sweaty: they called him "the fish".

G1Sindaco.4.full: You point it out to him, in front of the councillors.

G1Sindaco.5.full: You say nothing, and make a note of it.

G1Sindaco.6.full: You ask him about his wife.

G1Sindaco.7.full: You say it aloud, laughing, as a joke: "Mayor, have you caught a chill?" Nobody laughs. The mayor looks at you with clear, patient eyes, and answers that the doctor from the city has prescribed him cold baths, and that he feels reborn. The councillors nod, one after another. On your way out, you count seven with their hands in their pockets.
G1Sindaco.7.easy: You say it out loud, laughing, like a joke: "Mayor, have you caught a cold?" Nobody laughs. The mayor looks at you with pale, patient eyes. He says the doctor from the city told him to take cold baths, and he feels like a new man. The councillors nod, one after the other. As you leave, you count seven of them with their hands in their pockets.
G1Sindaco.7.short: "Mayor, have you caught a chill?" Nobody laughs. Cold baths, he says patiently: he feels reborn. On your way out you count seven councillors with their hands in their pockets.

G1Sindaco.9.full: You smile, thank him, drink half the glass of water. At home, in your notebook, under Fokke Tammer's name, you write the mayor's. The list is already long. You notice that you are writing the names in order of kindness.
G1Sindaco.9.easy: You smile, you say thank you, and you drink half the glass of water. At home, in your notebook, you write the mayor's name under Fokke Tammer's. The list is already long. You notice that you are writing the names in order of how kind they are.
G1Sindaco.9.short: At home you add the mayor to the list under Fokke Tammer. It is already long. You realise you are writing the names in order of kindness.

G1Sindaco.11.full: The mayor smiles: Mrs Wessel is very well, thank you. She left for the city in the spring, to her sister's, for a rest. She writes to him every week. He shows you the letters: a neat pile, tied with a ribbon. The envelopes are all alike, the handwriting all alike, the postmark always the same: Brunveen.
G1Sindaco.11.easy: The mayor smiles: Mrs Wessel is very well, thank you. In the spring she went to the city, to her sister's house, to rest. She writes to him every week. He shows you the letters: a tidy pile, tied with a ribbon. All the envelopes are the same. All the handwriting is the same. And the postmark is always the same: Brunveen.
G1Sindaco.11.short: Mrs Wessel is resting at her sister's in the city, he smiles, and writes every week. He shows you the letters: identical envelopes, identical hand, and every postmark says Brunveen.

G1Fonderia.2.full: At the Foundry, on the canal, the owner Dirk Haverkamp shows you an unpaid bill, dated 1864 and signed by your father, which his old man left him along with the foundry: a brass ring three metres across, in twelve sections; thirty-six panes of black glass, brought from Bohemia; two hundred metres of copper wire. The bill is high. Haverkamp still keeps the original drawings, with your father's measurements and notes, and a twelfth spare segment that your father never came to collect.
G1Fonderia.2.easy: At the Foundry, on the canal, the owner Dirk Haverkamp shows you a bill that was never paid. It is from 1864, and your father signed it. Haverkamp's father left it to him together with the foundry. The bill is for a brass ring three metres wide, in twelve parts; thirty-six pieces of black glass from Bohemia; and two hundred metres of copper wire. It is a lot of money. Haverkamp still has the original drawings, with your father's measurements and notes, and a twelfth spare part that your father never came to take.
G1Fonderia.2.short: At the Foundry, Dirk Haverkamp shows you your father's unpaid bill of 1864: a brass ring in twelve sections, black glass, copper wire. He still has the drawings, and a spare segment never collected.

G1Fonderia.4.full: You pay the bill and take the drawings.

G1Fonderia.5.full: You say the bill belongs to a dead man.

G1Fonderia.6.full: Haverkamp hands you a roll of drawings tied with string and the spare segment, wrapped in oilcloth. On the drawings, beside the measurements, your father has written in pencil words you do not understand: *resonance*, *return*, *receiver*, and at the bottom of the sheet a question, circled three times: *who transmits?*
G1Fonderia.6.easy: Haverkamp gives you a roll of drawings tied with string, and the spare part wrapped in oilcloth. On the drawings, next to the measurements, your father wrote some words in pencil that you do not understand: *resonance*, *return*, *receiver*. At the bottom of the page there is a question, with three circles around it: *who transmits?*
G1Fonderia.6.short: Haverkamp gives you the drawings and the spare segment. Beside the measurements your father wrote *resonance*, *return*, *receiver*, and, circled three times: *who transmits?*

G1Fonderia.8.full: Haverkamp does not insist. He says he will keep the drawings himself, in a drawer, until someone from the family comes to pay. "You will come sooner or later," he says, sure of it. "Your old man always said so: the sums add up. Even the ones that do not."
G1Fonderia.8.easy: Haverkamp does not insist. He says he will keep the drawings in a drawer until someone from the family comes to pay. "Sooner or later you will come," he says, very sure. "Your father always said it: the numbers add up in the end. Even the ones that do not."
G1Fonderia.8.short: Haverkamp will keep the drawings until the family pays. "You will come. Your old man always said: the sums add up. Even the ones that do not."

G1Apprendista.2.full: At the Farmer's Apprentice, the farm where the village children learn to milk and to mow, the widow Brink is waiting for you, her apron clutched in her hands. Her son Piet, fifteen, fell into the bog in September chasing a calf, and came home the next morning, alone, dry. Since then he has been the best boy on the farm: he obeys, he works, he learns everything at the first try. He has not answered her back once. He has not cried once. Last night she asked him whether he loved her, and he said yes, at once, with a lovely smile.
G1Apprendista.2.easy: At the Farmer's Apprentice, the farm where the village children learn to milk cows and cut hay, the widow Brink is waiting for you. She is holding her apron tight in her hands. Her son Piet is fifteen. In September he fell into the bog while he was running after a calf. He came home the next morning, alone and dry. Since then he is the best boy on the farm. He obeys, he works, and he learns everything the first time. He has never been rude to her again. He has never cried again. Last night she asked him if he loved her. He said yes, at once, with a beautiful smile.
G1Apprendista.2.short: The widow Brink's son Piet, fifteen, fell into the bog in September and came home next morning, dry. Now he is the best boy on the farm: obedient, tireless, never rude, never in tears. "Do you love me?" "Yes," at once, with a lovely smile.

G1Apprendista.3.full: "It is not him," says the widow. "I know it is him. But it is not him."
G1Apprendista.3.easy: "It is not him," says the widow. "I know it is him. But it is not him."
G1Apprendista.3.short: "I know it is him," says the widow. "But it is not him."

G1Apprendista.5.full: You tell her Piet is fine, and that he has grown up.

G1Apprendista.6.full: You take Piet to Hester Maas.

G1Apprendista.7.full: You go with her to the bog, where he fell.

G1Apprendista.8.full: The widow looks at you the way one looks at someone who has lied out of kindness, and thanks you all the same. Piet, behind her, smiles. From that day on the widow no longer comes to the farm. Piet does: he always arrives first, and always leaves last.
G1Apprendista.8.easy: The widow looks at you like someone who knows you lied to be kind, and she thanks you anyway. Behind her, Piet smiles. From that day the widow does not come to the farm any more. Piet does. He is always the first to arrive and the last to leave.
G1Apprendista.8.short: The widow thanks you as one thanks a kind liar. Behind her, Piet smiles. She never comes back to the farm. Piet is always first to arrive, last to leave.

G1Apprendista.10.full: Hester examines Piet in the Brinks' kitchen, with the door closed. She comes out after an hour and writes in the Register a temperature and a sentence she will not let you read. Then she sits down beside the widow, takes her hands, and they stay like that, without speaking, while outside Piet splits wood, stroke after stroke, always at the same rhythm.
G1Apprendista.10.easy: Hester examines Piet in the Brinks' kitchen with the door closed. After an hour she comes out. She writes a temperature and a sentence in the Register, and she does not let you read it. Then she sits next to the widow and holds her hands. They stay like that, without talking, while outside Piet chops wood, again and again, always at the same speed.
G1Apprendista.10.short: After an hour with Piet behind a closed door, Hester writes something she will not show you. Then she holds the widow's hands in silence, while outside Piet chops wood at an unchanging rhythm.

G1Apprendista.12.full: At the place where Piet fell, the water is still and black, and on the surface float bubbles that do not burst. The widow kneels on the bank and calls her son by name, softly, the way she called him as a child. For a moment, under the water, you seem to see a face, white, eyes closed, turn towards the voice. Then nothing.
G1Apprendista.12.easy: At the place where Piet fell, the water is still and black. There are bubbles on top of it that do not burst. The widow kneels on the bank and softly calls her son's name, the way she did when he was little. For a moment you think you see a white face under the water, with its eyes closed, turning towards her voice. Then nothing.
G1Apprendista.12.short: Where Piet fell, the water is black and still. The widow kneels and softly calls his name. For a moment a white face under the water seems to turn towards her voice. Then nothing.

G1PietraVoto.3.full: Pastor Kalf came to the estate, old, with his stick and his hat in his hand, and asked to speak to the whole family. He said he too has been counting, these years: the weddings, the christenings, the confessions. Nobody in Brunveen confesses any more. They have no sins.
G1PietraVoto.3.easy: Pastor Kalf came to the estate. He is old now, with his walking stick and his hat in his hand. He asked to speak to the whole family. He said that he has also been counting, all these years: the weddings, the christenings, the confessions. Nobody in Brunveen confesses any more. They have no sins.
G1PietraVoto.3.short: Old Pastor Kalf came to the estate to speak to the whole family. He too has been counting. Nobody in Brunveen confesses any more. They have no sins.

G1PietraVoto.4.full: He asked the family to take the stone back to the bog, to the exact place of the light, and to leave it there: "We do not know what it does, but we know it does it better near water. Then at least let it do it far from your houses." Then he waited for the answer standing, because the chair they had offered him was by the fire.
G1PietraVoto.4.easy: He asked the family to take the stone back to the bog, to the exact place where the light was, and to leave it there. "We do not know what it does," he said, "but we know it works better near water. So at least let it work far from your houses." Then he waited for the answer standing up, because the chair they offered him was next to the fire.
G1PietraVoto.4.short: He asked you to return the stone to the place of the light: "We do not know what it does, but it does it better near water. Let it do it far from your houses." He waited standing, because the chair was by the fire.

G1PietraVoto.5.full: Before leaving he blessed the house, room by room, even the shut tower, and said that the family, whatever it decides, has always been on the right side.
G1PietraVoto.5.easy: Before he left, he blessed the house, room by room, even the closed tower. He said that the family, whatever it decides, has always been on the right side.
G1PietraVoto.5.short: Before leaving he blessed every room, even the tower: whatever you decide, he said, you have always been on the right side.

G1PietraVoto.6.full: Before leaving he looked for a long time at whoever had contradicted him, years ago, on the church steps. He said nothing. He was more sad than angry.
G1PietraVoto.6.easy: Before he left, he looked for a long time at the person who argued with him years ago, on the church steps. He said nothing. He looked more sad than angry.
G1PietraVoto.6.short: Before leaving he looked long at whoever had argued with him on the church steps, years ago. More sad than angry.

G1PietraVoto.7.full: Each player takes a Voting token and chooses in secret. When everyone has chosen, reveal your votes together.

G1PietraVoto.8.full: YAY: take the stone back to the bog.

G1PietraVoto.10.full: Tally the votes *(in case of a tie, the Start Player decides)*.

G1PietraEsito.3.full: The stone goes back to the bog. (YAY)

G1PietraEsito.4.full: The stone stays in the family. (NAY)

G1PietraEsito.5.full: At dawn you carry the stone to the dyke, wrapped in its sack, and hand it to Pastor Kalf, who wades into the bog up to his waist, his cassock floating, as far as the place of the light. He lets it go. The stone sinks without a sound and without a bubble, as if the water had been waiting for it. For a moment the surface, all around, turns smooth as glass. Then the wind breaks it.
G1PietraEsito.5.easy: At dawn you carry the stone to the dyke in its sack and give it to Pastor Kalf. He walks into the bog up to his waist, with his long black robe floating on the water, to the place where the light was. He lets the stone go. It sinks with no sound and no bubbles, as if the water was waiting for it. For a moment the water all around becomes as smooth as glass. Then the wind moves it again.
G1PietraEsito.5.short: At dawn Pastor Kalf wades waist-deep to the place of the light and lets the stone go. It sinks without a bubble, as if expected. For a moment the water turns to glass. Then the wind breaks it.

G1PietraEsito.6.full: That night, in Brunveen, nobody is thirsty.

G1PietraEsito.7.full: {0} puts the Crown token {icon:S3_CrownToken} back on the **Park**: the stone is in the bog.

G1PietraEsito.8.full: You thank the pastor and tell him no: the stone is an object of study, and the family of the estate is a family of scientists. The pastor nods, puts his hat back on and goes off along the dyke, slowly. That evening the stone stays on the laboratory shelf, warm, in its felt-lined box. In the house, at night, everyone gets up to drink. Nobody tells the others.
G1PietraEsito.8.easy: You thank the pastor and say no. The stone is something to study, and the family of the estate is a family of scientists. The pastor nods, puts his hat on and walks slowly away along the dyke. That evening the stone stays on the shelf in the laboratory, warm, in its box lined with felt. At night, everyone in the house gets up to drink. Nobody tells the others.
G1PietraEsito.8.short: You refuse: the stone is for study. The pastor leaves without a word. That night the stone stays warm on the laboratory shelf, and everyone in the house gets up to drink. Nobody tells the others.

G1Torre2.2.full: Jaap Mol the smith's iron heats the lock in an hour, until the metal turns red and runs like wax. The tower door opens with a groan of hinges, twenty-three years later.
G1Torre2.2.easy: The iron rod of Jaap Mol the smith heats the lock for an hour, until the metal is red and melts like wax. The tower door opens, with a cry from its hinges, twenty-three years later.
G1Torre2.2.short: Jaap Mol's iron melts the lock like wax. The tower door groans open, twenty-three years later.

G1Torre2.3.full: Lambert, the master builder, widens the old hole in the wall until a person can get through. He does not want to go in first. Nobody does.
G1Torre2.3.easy: Lambert the master builder makes the old hole in the wall bigger, until a person can get through. He does not want to go in first. Nobody wants to.
G1Torre2.3.short: Lambert widens the old hole until a person fits. Nobody wants to go in first.

G1Torre2.4.full: It takes four men, two crowbars and a whole day to open a gap in the wall of the tower, beside the welded door. The workmen leave as soon as they have finished, without waiting for their pay.
G1Torre2.4.easy: Four men with two iron bars need a whole day to make a hole in the tower wall, next to the welded door. As soon as they finish, the workers leave, without waiting for their money.
G1Torre2.4.short: Four men take a whole day to break through beside the welded door, and leave without waiting for their pay.

G1Torre2.5.full: The stair spirals up into the dark, to the room of the four glass walls. Dust, cobwebs, a smell of burnt copper. In the middle of the room, on a wooden scaffold, there is a brass ring twice the height of a man, made of twelve sections, its inner rim lined with panes of black glass. It is dark. One of the panes is cracked, and caught in the crack is a chip of black stone, smooth, identical to the stone from the bog.
G1Torre2.5.easy: The stairs go round and round up into the dark, to the room with the four big windows. There is dust, there are cobwebs, and there is a smell of burnt copper. In the middle of the room, on a wooden frame, there is a brass ring twice as tall as a man. It is made of twelve parts, and the inside edge is covered with pieces of black glass. It is not working. One of the glass pieces is broken, and in the crack there is a small piece of smooth black stone, exactly like the stone from the bog.
G1Torre2.5.short: At the top of the spiral stair, among dust and the smell of burnt copper, stands a brass ring twice a man's height, lined with black glass. One pane is cracked, and in the crack is a chip of black stone, like the stone from the bog.

G1Torre2.6.full: The floor beneath the ring is burnt in a perfect circle. On the table, by the window that looks out on the bog, lies your father's notebook, open at a page marked with a ribbon. Calculations, distances, angles. Then, at the bottom, a line that is no raving:
G1Torre2.6.easy: Under the ring, the floor is burnt in a perfect circle. On the table, next to the window that looks at the bog, is your father's notebook. It is open at a page with a ribbon in it. There are calculations, distances and angles. Then, at the bottom, there is a line that is not crazy at all:
G1Torre2.6.short: Under the ring the floor is burnt in a perfect circle. By the window, your father's notebook lies open at a marked page. At the bottom, a line that is no raving:

G1Torre2.7.full: *11 November, fourteen minutes past eleven. Light on the ring. At the same instant, light on the bog, at twelve hundred metres, north-north-east. The Machine is a bridge: one end here, one there. Something crossed the bridge from the other side, and I opened no bridge.*
G1Torre2.7.easy: *11 November, fourteen minutes past eleven. Light on the ring. At the same moment, light on the bog, twelve hundred metres away, to the north-north-east. The Machine is a bridge: one end is here, the other is there. Something came over the bridge from the other side. And I did not open any bridge.*
G1Torre2.7.short: *11 November, 11:14. Light on the ring, and at the same instant on the bog, twelve hundred metres away. The Machine is a bridge. Something crossed it from the other side, and I opened no bridge.*

G1Torre2.8.full: **The two lights were one and the same. The stone did not fall from the sky: your father's Machine, a machine for moving things from one place to another, brought it into the bog on the night it turned on by itself.** The old man's ravings were true: something came through. It remains to find out from where.
G1Torre2.8.easy: **The two lights were one thing. The stone did not fall from the sky. Your father's Machine, a machine that moves things from one place to another, put it in the bog on the night it turned on by itself.** The old man was not crazy: something came through. Now you must find out where it came from.
G1Torre2.8.short: **The two lights were one. Your father's Machine, which moves things from place to place, put the stone in the bog the night it turned on by itself.** Something did come through. But from where?

G1Torre2.9.full: On the table, beside the notebook, you unroll the drawings bought at the foundry. They match the ring section by section. Only one segment is missing, the cracked one. The spare, luckily, is yours.
G1Torre2.9.easy: On the table, next to the notebook, you open the drawings you bought at the foundry. They match the ring, part by part. Only one part is missing: the broken one. Luckily, you have the spare part.
G1Torre2.9.short: The foundry drawings match the ring exactly. Only the cracked segment is missing, and luckily you have the spare.

G1Torre2.10.full: What do you do with your father's notebook? *(Decide together.)*

G1Torre2.11.full: You read all of it, that very night.

G1Torre2.12.full: You make a copy for Hester Maas.

G1Torre2.13.full: You take turns reading it until dawn, by candlelight, in the room of the ring. Three hundred pages of calculations, sketches, failed trials, curses. In the last twenty, after the night of the two lights, the handwriting changes: it becomes small, cramped, obsessive. The old man tried to turn the Machine on again every night, for four months, always at a quarter past eleven. He never managed it. The last page, written a few days before he died, has a single line: *perhaps it is not for me to do.*
G1Torre2.13.easy: You take turns reading it until morning, by candlelight, in the room with the ring. There are three hundred pages of calculations, drawings, failed tests and curses. In the last twenty pages, after the night of the two lights, the handwriting changes. It becomes small, tight and obsessed. Every night for four months the old man tried to turn the Machine on again, always at a quarter past eleven. He never did it. The last page, written a few days before he died, has only one line: *perhaps it is not for me to do.*
G1Torre2.13.short: You read it in turns until dawn. After the two lights the hand turns small and obsessive: every night for four months, at a quarter past eleven, he tried to turn the Machine on again. The last page says only: *perhaps it is not for me to do.*

G1Torre2.14.full: Each player gains 1 {icon:Insanity_Icon} and 1 Occult Knowledge.

G1Torre2.15.full: You copy out by hand the most important pages, those of the two lights and the months after, and take them to Hester Maas, who slips them into the Register without reading them, between a birth certificate and a receipt. "Someone after me will read them," she says. "Someone who will have more time than I do."
G1Torre2.15.easy: You copy by hand the most important pages, about the two lights and the months after, and you take them to Hester Maas. She puts them in the Register without reading them, between a birth certificate and a receipt. "Someone after me will read them," she says. "Someone who will have more time than me."
G1Torre2.15.short: You copy the key pages for Hester Maas, who slips them unread into the Register. "Someone after me will read them. Someone with more time."

G1TorreFine.2.full: The stone is in the bog, and nobody in the family holds it any longer. The Machine, though, must have someone to keep it.
G1TorreFine.2.easy: The stone is in the bog, and nobody in the family has it now. But someone must take care of the Machine.
G1TorreFine.2.short: The stone is in the bog. But someone must keep the Machine.

G1TorreFine.3.full: Who takes the Machine into their keeping? *(Decide together.)*

G1Macchina.2.full: The keeping of the tower, the notebook and the Machine falls to whoever held the stone longest, or to whoever the family chooses. Together with the notebook there is something else, which your father left on the table, beside his pen: his silver pocket watch, the one from his waistcoat, new, shiny, with the crest of the estate. Stopped at a quarter past eleven. You wind it, and it starts again.
G1Macchina.2.easy: The tower, the notebook and the Machine go to the person who had the stone for the longest time, or to the person the family chooses. Next to the notebook there is something else that your father left on the table, near his pen. It is his silver pocket watch, the one from his waistcoat. It is new and shiny, with the crest of the estate. It has stopped at a quarter past eleven. You wind it up, and it starts again.
G1Macchina.2.short: The Machine goes to whoever kept the stone longest, or whom the family chooses. Beside the notebook lies your father's own watch, new and shiny, stopped at a quarter past eleven. You wind it, and it runs.

G1Macchina.3.full: From that day on, whoever has the Machine always carries it. Nobody in the family finds anything strange in it. Only Hester Maas, when she sees it, turns pale, and goes home to check the drawer with the Register.
G1Macchina.3.easy: From that day, the person who has the Machine always carries the watch. Nobody in the family thinks this is strange. Only Hester Maas goes pale when she sees it. She goes home to look in the drawer where she keeps the Register.
G1Macchina.3.short: Whoever keeps the Machine now carries the watch. Only Hester Maas, seeing it, turns pale and hurries home to check her drawer.

G1Macchina.4.full: **{0}** takes the set-aside **Teleportation** Masterwork and puts it in place of their own Masterwork, which goes back in the box: repairing the Machine means completing this Masterwork. They also take the set-aside Compulsion **"They'll never understand…"**.

G1Macchina.5.full: *The Machine and your father's watch stay with {0}, and then with their heirs, for the whole game.*

G1Chiusura.3.full: I am old, and my hand no longer helps me. This is the last page I shall write. I leave the Register to my son Joost, who took his degree in medicine in the city and is coming back to Brunveen as the village doctor. He laughs at my cold hands. He has studied, and those who have studied do not count: they measure.
G1Chiusura.3.easy: I am old, and my hand does not help me any more. This is the last page I will write. I leave the Register to my son Joost. He studied medicine in the city, and now he is coming back to Brunveen as the village doctor. He laughs at my cold hands. He has studied, and people who have studied do not count. They measure.
G1Chiusura.3.short: I am old; this is my last page. I leave the Register to my son Joost, the new village doctor. He laughs at my cold hands. He has studied: he does not count, he measures.

G1Chiusura.4.full: The heirs of the estate have grown old, like me. Some have died, in their beds, of old age, with warm hands: I touched them myself. The Machine has stayed in the tower, silent. Their children have grown up in Brunveen, and do not know what Brunveen was before.
G1Chiusura.4.easy: The heirs of the estate are old now, like me. Some of them have died of old age, in their beds, with warm hands. I touched them myself. The Machine is still in the tower, silent. Their children grew up in Brunveen, and they do not know what Brunveen was like before.
G1Chiusura.4.short: The heirs of the estate have grown old. Some died in their beds, hands warm: I checked. The Machine stands silent. Their children do not know what Brunveen was before.

G1Chiusura.5.full: The stone has gone back into the bog. This winter the place of the light has not frozen, not even on the coldest nights.
G1Chiusura.5.easy: The stone is back in the bog. This winter the place where the light was did not freeze, not even on the coldest nights.
G1Chiusura.5.short: The stone is back in the bog. This winter the place of the light never froze.

G1Chiusura.6.full: The stone is still at the estate, on the laboratory shelf. The family drinks a great deal of water. They buy it in the city.
G1Chiusura.6.easy: The stone is still at the estate, on the shelf in the laboratory. The family drinks a lot of water. They buy it in the city.
G1Chiusura.6.short: The stone is still on the laboratory shelf. The family drinks a lot of water, bought in the city.

G1Chiusura.7.full: The names in the Register, those with cold hands, number one hundred and fourteen. The village has three hundred and twenty inhabitants. I tell nobody: who would I tell, anyway?
G1Chiusura.7.easy: In the Register there are one hundred and fourteen names with cold hands. The village has three hundred and twenty people. I do not tell anyone. Who could I tell?
G1Chiusura.7.short: One hundred and fourteen cold hands in the Register, out of three hundred and twenty villagers. Who would I tell?

G1Chiusura.8.full: Remove all pieces from the board and perform the End of a Generation. Return the unused {icon:StorybookToken} tokens to the supply. The Neighbours {icon:S3_WoodenFigureToken} and the {icon:S3_ParadoxToken} tokens left on the board go back to the supply; whoever has drunk keeps their {icon:S3_ParadoxToken} tokens in front of them.

G1Ostrander.2.full: **Letter from Professor Ostrander to the director of the natural history museum – *June 1866.***

G1Ostrander.3.full: My distinguished colleague, I write to you from Brunveen, a village of peat-cutters half a day away by train, where I came for the object I told you of: the so-called "stone of the light". I return empty-handed. The object was knocked down to a member of the family of the estate, {0}, for a sum the museum would never have approved. I give you a description of it all the same, for the record.
G1Ostrander.3.easy: Dear colleague, I am writing to you from Brunveen, a village of peat-cutters half a day away by train. I came here for the object I told you about: the so-called "stone of the light". I am coming back with nothing. A member of the family of the estate, {0}, bought it at the auction, for a price the museum would never accept. But I will describe it to you anyway, so that we have a record.
G1Ostrander.3.short: Dear colleague, I return from Brunveen empty-handed: the "stone of the light" went to {0}, of the estate, for a sum the museum would never approve. For the record, a description.

G1Ostrander.4.full: Black stone, smooth, as big as a loaf, of anomalous specific gravity. Constant temperature, above that of its surroundings: one feels it warm through the sack. No visible crystallisation, no fracture. It is not a meteorite of any kind known to me. The peat-cutter who found it, one Tammer, handled it like a living thing.
G1Ostrander.4.easy: A black stone, smooth, as big as a loaf of bread, and strangely heavy. Its temperature never changes, and it is warmer than the air around it: you can feel the heat through the sack. You cannot see any crystals or any cracks. It is not any kind of meteorite I know. The peat-cutter who found it, a man called Tammer, held it like a living thing.
G1Ostrander.4.short: Black, smooth, oddly heavy, always warm. No crystals, no cracks: no meteorite I know of. The peat-cutter who found it held it like a living thing.

G1Ostrander.5.full: I add a personal impression, which you need not mention to the board. Brunveen is the quietest village I have ever visited. Nobody at the auction raised their voice. Nobody haggled. When the auctioneer brought down the hammer, the crowd applauded all together, and stopped all together. At the inn they served me water, though I had asked for beer, and the innkeeper told me, with a smile, that "it is better for everyone".
G1Ostrander.5.easy: I add a personal feeling, but please do not talk about it to the board. Brunveen is the quietest village I have ever seen. At the auction nobody raised their voice. Nobody tried to get a lower price. When the auctioneer hit the table with his hammer, the whole crowd clapped at the same moment, and stopped at the same moment. At the inn I asked for beer, but they gave me water. The innkeeper smiled and said that "it is better for everyone".
G1Ostrander.5.short: Privately: Brunveen is the quietest village I have known. The crowd clapped all at once and stopped all at once. I asked for beer and was served water: "better for everyone", smiled the innkeeper.

G1Ostrander.6.full: I left my visiting card with the family. I mean to return. Your most devoted, J. Ostrander.
G1Ostrander.6.easy: I left my card with the family. I plan to come back. Yours most faithfully, J. Ostrander.
G1Ostrander.6.short: I left my card with the family. I shall return. J. Ostrander.

G1Mugnaio.2.full: At the Traveling Caravan, in front of the cart that sells tickets for the city coach, stands Harm Visser, the miller, with a bundle in his hand and the face of a man who has not slept for weeks. He wants to leave, he says, but cannot find the courage to buy the ticket. His wife Grietje, since the winter, has not been herself. She sings as she works, and she used to sing out of tune. She no longer quarrels with her mother-in-law, and she used to hate her. She kisses him on the forehead every evening, and she had never done so, not even as newlyweds. She is perfect. He is afraid of her as he has never been afraid of anything.
G1Mugnaio.2.easy: At the Traveling Caravan, in front of the cart that sells tickets for the coach to the city, there is Harm Visser, the miller. He has a bundle in his hand and looks like he has not slept for weeks. He wants to leave, he says, but he is not brave enough to buy the ticket. Since the winter, his wife Grietje is different. She sings while she works, and before she always sang out of tune. She does not fight with his mother any more, and before she hated her. Every evening she kisses him on the forehead. She never did that before, not even when they were just married. She is perfect. He is more afraid of her than he has ever been of anything.
G1Mugnaio.2.short: Harm Visser the miller stands by the coach-ticket cart with a bundle, not daring to buy. Since winter his wife Grietje sings in tune, loves her mother-in-law, kisses him goodnight. She is perfect, and he has never been so afraid.

G1Mugnaio.3.full: "Tell me I am mad," he asks you. "You at the estate have studied. Tell me so, and I will go home."
G1Mugnaio.3.easy: "Tell me that I am mad," he asks you. "You people at the estate have studied. Tell me, and I will go home."
G1Mugnaio.3.short: "Tell me I am mad. You have studied. Tell me, and I will go home."

G1Mugnaio.5.full: You tell him he is tired, and must go home.

G1Mugnaio.7.full: You ask him where his wife was, the night before she changed.

G1Mugnaio.8.full: Harm thanks you, relieved, like a patient whose doctor says it is nothing. He goes home with the bundle under his arm. The next month you run into him at the market: shirt ironed, hands clean, a calm smile. He greets you with a nod, kindly. He no longer thanks you.
G1Mugnaio.8.easy: Harm thanks you. He is relieved, like a sick man when the doctor tells him it is nothing. He goes home with his bundle under his arm. The next month you see him at the market. His shirt is ironed, his hands are clean, and he has a calm smile. He nods to you, kindly. He does not thank you any more.
G1Mugnaio.8.short: Harm goes home relieved. A month later, at the market, he has an ironed shirt, clean hands and a calm smile. He nods to you kindly. He no longer thanks you.

G1Mugnaio.10.full: You buy him the ticket and walk him to the coach. Harm sits at the back, clutching his bundle, and does not look back. Grietje does not come to see him off. She comes to the estate the next day instead, with a cake, to thank the family "for helping poor Harm, who was not well". The cake is perfect.
G1Mugnaio.10.easy: You buy his ticket and walk with him to the coach. Harm sits at the back, holding his bundle tight, and does not look back. Grietje does not come to say goodbye. But the next day she comes to the estate with a cake, to thank the family "for helping poor Harm, who was not well". The cake is perfect.
G1Mugnaio.10.short: Harm leaves on the coach without looking back. Next day Grietje brings the estate a cake, "for helping poor Harm, who was not well". The cake is perfect.

G1Mugnaio.12.full: Harm thinks. On Saint Nicholas' night, he says, Grietje went out to fetch water from the canal, because the well was frozen. She came back an hour later, dry, without the bucket. She said the canal was beautiful at night, and that she was not cold. Then she went to bed and slept without a sigh. That night he cried without knowing why.
G1Mugnaio.12.easy: Harm thinks. On Saint Nicholas' night, he says, Grietje went out to get water from the canal, because the well was frozen. She came back an hour later, dry, without the bucket. She said the canal was beautiful at night, and she was not cold. Then she went to bed and slept very quietly. That night he cried, and he did not know why.
G1Mugnaio.12.short: On Saint Nicholas' night Grietje went to the canal for water. She came back an hour later, dry, without the bucket, saying it was beautiful there. That night Harm cried without knowing why.

G1Lambert.2.full: At the Builder's Office, Lambert the master builder has unrolled on the table a council resolution, signed and stamped: the tower of the estate is "unsafe", and must be pulled down within the year, at the town's expense, for the safety of the citizens. Lambert reads it aloud, in his calm voice. He has not worn bandages on his hands for years. He offers to see to it in person, with his men, free of charge. "Then you need not think about it any more," he says. "Then nobody need think about it any more."
G1Lambert.2.easy: At the Builder's Office, Lambert the master builder has opened a council decision on the table. It is signed and stamped. It says the tower of the estate is "unsafe" and must be knocked down before the end of the year, paid for by the town, to keep people safe. Lambert reads it out in his calm voice. He has not had bandages on his hands for years. He offers to do the job himself, with his men, for free. "Then you will not have to think about it," he says. "Then nobody will have to think about it."
G1Lambert.2.short: Lambert reads out a council resolution: the estate's tower is "unsafe" and must come down this year. He offers to do it himself, free. "Then nobody need think about it any more."

G1Lambert.4.full: You refuse, and threaten to go to court.

G1Lambert.5.full: You ask him to shore it up instead, at your expense.

G1Lambert.6.full: You ask him who put the resolution forward.

G1Lambert.7.full: Lambert does not insist. He rolls the resolution up again carefully, ties it with string and puts it away in the drawer. The council will not speak of it again. But in the evening, from the window of the estate, you see Lambert standing in the road, looking at the tower for an hour, motionless, the way one looks at an old enemy or an old friend.
G1Lambert.7.easy: Lambert does not insist. He rolls up the paper carefully, ties it with string and puts it in the drawer. The council will not talk about it again. But in the evening, from the window of the estate, you see Lambert standing in the road. He looks at the tower for an hour without moving, the way you look at an old enemy, or an old friend.
G1Lambert.7.short: Lambert puts the resolution away without a word. But that evening he stands in the road for an hour, motionless, looking at the tower like an old enemy, or an old friend.

G1Lambert.9.full: Lambert agrees, with the same calm. His men work for a month: iron chains around the walls, a new staircase, oak beams. They work well, better than anyone has ever worked in Brunveen. They never go higher than the stairs, though. The room at the top, they say, is not their concern.
G1Lambert.9.easy: Lambert says yes, just as calmly. His men work for a month: iron chains around the walls, new stairs, oak beams. They work very well, better than anyone has ever worked in Brunveen. But they never go above the stairs. They say the room at the top is not their business.
G1Lambert.9.short: Lambert's men shore up the tower beautifully in a month. But they never go above the stairs. The room at the top, they say, is not their concern.

G1Lambert.11.full: Lambert shows you the first page of the resolution. The proposal is signed by three councillors: Mayor Wessel, the clerk, and a new councillor, elected this year with every vote in the village. The new councillor's name is Fokke Tammer. Twenty years ago he could not write his own name. The signature is elegant, regular, slanted like a notary's.
G1Lambert.11.easy: Lambert shows you the first page of the decision. Three councillors signed the proposal: Mayor Wessel, the clerk and a new councillor. The whole village voted for him this year. The new councillor is Fokke Tammer. Twenty years ago he could not write his name. Now his signature is elegant and even, like a notary's.
G1Lambert.11.short: The resolution is signed by the mayor, the clerk and a new councillor elected unanimously: Fokke Tammer. Twenty years ago he could not write his name. His signature is a notary's.

G1Wessel.2.full: At the Town Hall, Mayor Aldert Wessel receives you with his bandaged foot on a stool and a handkerchief in his hand, with which he mops his brow every two minutes. He is a big, red, sweaty man who talks too much and laughs at his own jokes. In the village they call him "the fish" for his ever-damp hands, and he knows it, and laughs about it. He has a proposal: the town would buy the tower of the estate, "to make a water tank of it", and would pay well. Your father, he says, owed him money. A lot. And besides, that tower at night, with its blue flashes, frightened his wife.
G1Wessel.2.easy: At the Town Hall, Mayor Aldert Wessel meets you with his bandaged foot on a stool. He holds a handkerchief and wipes his forehead every two minutes. He is a big, red, sweaty man who talks too much and laughs at his own jokes. In the village they call him "the fish" because his hands are always wet. He knows it, and he laughs about it. He has an offer: the town wants to buy the tower of the estate, "to make a water tank", and will pay well. He says your father owed him money. A lot of money. And that tower, at night, with its blue flashes, frightened his wife.
G1Wessel.2.short: Mayor Wessel, big, red and sweaty, his gouty foot on a stool, offers to buy the tower "for a water tank". Your father owed him money, he says. And its blue flashes frightened his wife.

G1Wessel.5.full: You tell him the tower is not for sale.

G1Wessel.6.full: You ask him about the night of the two lights.

G1Wessel.7.full: The mayor counts the money twice, with sweaty fingers, and signs your receipt with a flourish. Then he offers you a cigar and tells you, laughing, three dirty jokes about Pastor Kalf. They are dreadful. You leave the Town Hall with a headache and a strange fondness for that noisy man.
G1Wessel.7.easy: The mayor counts the money twice with his sweaty fingers and signs the receipt with a big flourish. Then he gives you a cigar and, laughing, tells you three rude jokes about Pastor Kalf. They are terrible. You leave the Town Hall with a headache and a strange feeling of affection for this loud man.
G1Wessel.7.short: The mayor counts the money twice, signs with a flourish and tells three dreadful jokes about the pastor. You leave with a headache and a strange fondness for him.

G1Wessel.9.full: The mayor takes offence, goes redder, raises his voice. He says the estate is not above the law, and that the council has its means. Then, as always, he calms down, mops his brow and apologises: it is the gout, he says, that makes him short-tempered. He sees you to the door, limping, and shakes your hand. It is damp and warm.
G1Wessel.9.easy: The mayor is offended. His face gets redder and he raises his voice. He says the estate is not above the law, and the council has ways to get what it wants. Then, as always, he calms down, wipes his forehead and says sorry. It is the gout, he says, that makes him nervous. He limps with you to the door and shakes your hand. His hand is wet and warm.
G1Wessel.9.short: The mayor shouts that the estate is not above the law, then calms down and blames his gout. At the door he shakes your hand. It is damp and warm.

G1Wessel.11.full: The mayor stops laughing. That night, he says, he was awake with the pain in his foot, and from the window he saw everything: the light on the tower and the one on the bog, at the same instant, like two lanterns signalling to each other. He was afraid. He told nobody, because a mayor is not afraid. "But you are the family," he says. "You must know what you have in your house."
G1Wessel.11.easy: The mayor stops laughing. That night, he says, his foot hurt and he could not sleep. From the window he saw everything: the light on the tower and the light on the bog, at the same moment, like two lanterns sending signals to each other. He was afraid. He did not tell anyone, because a mayor is never afraid. "But you are the family," he says. "You must know what you have in your house."
G1Wessel.11.short: The mayor stops laughing. That night he saw both lights at once, like two lanterns signalling. He was afraid, and told nobody. "But you are the family. You must know what is in your house."

G1Bagno.2.full: At the Park, on Easter morning, there is a crowd in white shirts on the bank of the pond. It is a new tradition, born two years ago without anyone deciding it: whoever wants to begin the year "clean" wades into the water, which comes straight from the bog there, up to the waist, and comes out in silence. Pastor Kalf is not there: he has said it is a pagan rite. Mayor Wessel is, in the front row, holding the hand of those who are afraid. Someone holds out a hand to you. They smile.
G1Bagno.2.easy: At the Park, on Easter morning, a crowd in white shirts stands by the pond. It is a new tradition. It started two years ago, but nobody decided it. People who want to start the year "clean" walk into the water up to their waist and come out in silence. The water there comes straight from the bog. Pastor Kalf is not there: he says it is a pagan custom. Mayor Wessel is there, at the front, holding hands with the people who are afraid. Someone reaches out a hand to you. They smile.
G1Bagno.2.short: On Easter morning a crowd in white wades waist-deep into the pond, fed by the bog, to begin the year "clean". The pastor stays away; the mayor holds the frightened by the hand. Someone smiles and reaches out to you.

G1Bagno.4.full: You go into the water with them.

G1Bagno.5.full: You stay on the bank, counting who comes out.

G1Bagno.6.full: The water is icy, then it is not. You stand there, waist-deep, a stranger's hand in yours, and for a long moment nobody breathes. When you come out, people embrace you, one after another. You go home light, without a care. Not a single one.
G1Bagno.6.easy: The water is ice cold, and then it is not. You stand there with the water up to your waist and a stranger's hand in yours. For a long moment nobody breathes. When you come out, people hug you, one after the other. You go home feeling light, with no worries. Not even one.
G1Bagno.6.short: The water is icy, then not. For a long moment nobody breathes. Coming out, you are embraced by everyone, and go home without a single care.

G1Bagno.8.full: You stay on the bank with your notebook. Forty-two go in. Forty-two come out. But three of them were coughing as they went in, and coming out they cough no more; one was limping, and now walks straight; a girl was crying, and now she smiles. You note the names. When you look up, those who came out of the water are watching you, in a row, kindly.
G1Bagno.8.easy: You stay on the bank with your notebook. Forty-two people go in. Forty-two come out. But three of them were coughing when they went in, and when they come out they are not coughing. One was limping, and now walks straight. A girl was crying, and now she is smiling. You write down the names. When you look up, the people who came out of the water are standing in a line, looking at you kindly.
G1Bagno.8.short: Forty-two go in, forty-two come out. But the coughs, a limp, a girl's tears are gone. You note the names. When you look up, they stand in a row, watching you kindly.

VSG2Intro.2.full: **The Maas Register – Dr Joost Maas, village doctor, *January 1891.***

VSG2Intro.3.full: I take up my mother's Register, out of respect and out of habit, and with one intention: I shall write in it only what can be measured. My mother was an intelligent woman and an excellent midwife, but in her last years she counted cold hands the way others count rosaries. I studied in the city. Cold hands, in medicine, are called poor circulation.
VSG2Intro.3.easy: I continue my mother's Register, out of respect and out of habit, and with one plan: I will only write things that can be measured. My mother was a clever woman and a very good midwife. But in her last years she counted cold hands the way other people count prayers. I studied in the city. In medicine, cold hands are called bad circulation.
VSG2Intro.3.short: I take up my mother's Register, and will write only what can be measured. In her last years she counted cold hands like rosary beads. In medicine, cold hands are poor circulation.

VSG2Intro.4.full: Brunveen is no longer the village I was born in. The wooden houses have been rebuilt in brick, with exposed beams and tiled roofs; the dyke has been raised, the mill rebuilt, the church enlarged. The council has named it the tidiest village in the province three years running. There are no thefts, no debts, no brawls at the inn, because nobody goes to the inn any more. The church choir is the best in the diocese.
VSG2Intro.4.easy: Brunveen is not the village where I was born. The wooden houses are now brick houses, with wooden beams and tiled roofs. The dyke is higher, the mill is new, the church is bigger. Three years in a row, the council has given the village the prize for the tidiest village in the province. There are no thieves, no debts and no fights at the inn, because nobody goes to the inn any more. The church choir is the best in the diocese.
VSG2Intro.4.short: Brunveen is not the village I was born in: brick houses, a higher dyke, a new mill, three years the tidiest village in the province. No thefts, no debts, no brawls: nobody goes to the inn. The choir is the best in the diocese.

VSG2Intro.5.full: Some families, over the years, have left: the Mulders, the De Graafs, the widow Brink, a dozen in all. They said they no longer felt at home here. Their houses have stayed empty, and nobody buys them; the roofs sag, the windows break, the grass grows on the doorsteps. In so tidy a village, those ruins jar. The mayor has promised to have them pulled down.
VSG2Intro.5.easy: Over the years some families have left: the Mulders, the De Graafs, the widow Brink, about twelve in all. They said they were not happy here any more. Their houses are still empty, and nobody buys them. The roofs are falling in, the windows are broken, and grass grows on the doorsteps. In such a tidy village, these ruins look wrong. The mayor has promised to knock them down.
VSG2Intro.5.short: A dozen families have left over the years, saying they no longer felt at home. Their empty houses are falling down, out of place in so tidy a village. The mayor will have them demolished.

VSG2Intro.6.full: The old man's grandchildren live at the estate now. The tower is open, the Machine is still there, under a sheet, and nobody knows how to make it work.
VSG2Intro.6.easy: Now the old man's grandchildren live at the estate. The tower is open. The Machine is still there, under a sheet, and nobody knows how to make it work.
VSG2Intro.6.short: The old man's grandchildren live at the estate now. The Machine waits under a sheet. Nobody can make it work.

G2Inizio.2.full: In the first week of the year a gentleman from the council comes to the estate, young, with a well-kept beard and his hands in his pockets: it is Bram Wessel, the mayor's son. He brings a proposal. The houses of the families who left are for sale, at a ridiculous price, and the council would rather the estate bought them, "people from here", than some outsider. The council, he adds, would gladly help to do them up.
G2Inizio.2.easy: In the first week of the year a young man from the council comes to the estate. He has a neat beard and his hands are in his pockets. It is Bram Wessel, the mayor's son. He has an offer. The houses of the families who left are for sale, very cheap. The council would like the estate to buy them, because they are "people from here", and not some stranger. He says the council would be happy to help repair them.
G2Inizio.2.short: Bram Wessel, the mayor's son, hands in pockets, offers the estate the empty houses for next to nothing: better "people from here" than outsiders. The council would gladly help do them up.

G2Inizio.3.full: While he talks, you ask after his mother, Mrs Wessel, who left for the city many years ago. Bram smiles: she is still at her sister's, she is very well, she writes every week. She has never come back. He does not seem to find it strange.
G2Inizio.3.easy: While he talks, you ask about his mother, Mrs Wessel, who went to the city many years ago. Bram smiles. She is still at her sister's, she is very well, and she writes every week. She has never come back. He does not think this is strange.
G2Inizio.3.short: You ask after his mother, gone to the city years ago. Still at her sister's, Bram smiles, writing every week. She has never come back. He finds nothing strange in it.

G2Inizio.6.full: You look for the families who left, first.

G2Inizio.7.full: You sign, pay very little, and the following week a team of workmen from the village is already at work: new roofs, new windows, white plaster. They work without pay, smiling. When you ask why, they answer that it is a pleasure to help one's neighbours.
G2Inizio.7.easy: You sign and pay very little. The next week a group of workers from the village is already working: new roofs, new windows, white walls. They work without pay, smiling. When you ask why, they say it is a pleasure to help their neighbours.
G2Inizio.7.short: You buy them cheaply, and the next week village workmen are rebuilding them, unpaid and smiling. "It is a pleasure to help one's neighbours."

G2Inizio.9.full: You write to all the families who left, at the addresses they left with the town hall. Three replies arrive. The Mulders are in Rotterdam, poor and happy; the De Graafs in America. The third is from a lodging-house keeper in the city: the widow Brink is dead, alone. Nobody wants to come back. The last letter, the Mulders', ends like this: *Life is too good there. We would rather be unhappy.*
G2Inizio.9.easy: You write to all the families who left, at the addresses they gave the town hall. Three answers come back. The Mulders are in Rotterdam, poor and happy. The De Graafs are in America.
