The third letter is from a woman who rents rooms in the city: the widow Brink has died, alone. Nobody wants to come back. The last letter, from the Mulders, ends like this: *Life there is too good. We would rather be unhappy.*
G2Inizio.9.short: Three replies come. The Mulders are poor and happy in Rotterdam, the De Graafs in America; the widow Brink has died alone in the city. Nobody will come back. *Life there is too good*, write the Mulders. *We would rather be unhappy.*

G2R1.2.full: Open the Village Chronicle to the **A Time of War** section ({icon:S3_ScenarioIcon}) and turn to **page 17**.

G2R1.3.full: *It is Lambert the master builder: he never gets a measurement wrong.*

G2R1.5.full: The stone {icon:S3_CrownToken} stays on the **Park**: it is in the bog.

G2R1.28.full: The village is celebrating the province's prize: bunting, a band, the mayor's speech on the platform in front of the Town Hall. Mayor Aldert Wessel is seventy and looks fifty. He speaks for an hour without once looking at his paper, and at the end everyone applauds at the same moment, and stops at the same moment.
G2R1.28.easy: The village is having a party for the province's prize. There are little flags, a band, and the mayor's speech on the stage in front of the Town Hall. Mayor Aldert Wessel is seventy but looks fifty. He talks for an hour and never looks at his notes. At the end everyone claps at the same moment, and stops at the same moment.
G2R1.28.short: The village celebrates its prize. Mayor Wessel, seventy and looking fifty, speaks for an hour without notes. Everyone claps at the same moment, and stops at the same moment.

G2R1.29.full: From the square you can see the tower of the estate, with the iron chains that Lambert the master builder put round it some years ago. It has not moved a finger's breadth. The children call it "the tower in prison".
G2R1.29.easy: From the square you can see the tower of the estate, with the iron chains that Lambert the master builder put around it some years ago. It has not moved at all. The children call it "the tower in prison".
G2R1.29.short: From the square you see the estate's tower in its iron chains. The children call it "the tower in prison".

G2R1.30.full: At the place of the light, in the bog, where the stone sleeps, ice never forms. In winter the skaters go round it without looking.
G2R1.30.easy: In the bog, at the place where the light was and the stone sleeps, the water never freezes. In winter the skaters go around it and do not look.
G2R1.30.short: Where the stone sleeps, the bog never freezes. The skaters go round it without looking.

round.G2R1.end.full: The Early Years of the Second Generation have ended.

VociRonda.2.full: Once this Generation, whoever has the Shield token {icon:S3_ShieldToken} (**{0}**) may remove a Neighbour {icon:S3_WoodenFigureToken} from the board without spending Evidence:

RondaNotte.2.full: They go out at midnight, six of them, with lanterns and sticks, and knock at a single door. The Neighbour opens in a nightshirt, awake, as if expecting them. It puts up no resistance. They take it to the dyke, sit it on the bank, and wait for dawn with it, in silence. At dawn, in its place, there is a heap of wet peat.
RondaNotte.2.easy: They go out at midnight, six of them, with lanterns and sticks, and knock at only one door. The Neighbour opens the door in a nightshirt. It is awake, as if it was waiting for them. It does not fight. They take it to the dyke, make it sit on the bank and wait with it until morning, in silence. At dawn, where it sat, there is a pile of wet peat.
RondaNotte.2.short: Six of them knock at one door at midnight. The Neighbour opens, awake, as if expecting them, and sits with them on the dyke till dawn. At dawn there is only wet peat.

RondaNotte.3.full: They go out at midnight, with electric lanterns and a hunting rifle, and knock at a single door. Hendrik Tammer, who has been to the war, goes in first. The Neighbour is sitting at the kitchen table, dressed, hands in its lap. It says only: "Quietly, the children are asleep." In the morning, on the chair, there is a heap of peat.
RondaNotte.3.easy: They go out at midnight with electric lamps and a hunting gun, and knock at only one door. Hendrik Tammer, who fought in the war, goes in first. The Neighbour is sitting at the kitchen table, dressed, with its hands in its lap. It says only: "Be quiet, the children are sleeping." In the morning there is a pile of peat on the chair.
RondaNotte.3.short: At midnight Hendrik Tammer, back from the war, goes in first. The Neighbour sits dressed at the kitchen table: "Quietly, the children are asleep." By morning, peat on the chair.

RondaNotte.4.full: *The house stays empty. The village asks nothing.*

RondaNotte.5.full: Return a Neighbour {icon:S3_WoodenFigureToken} of {0}'s choice to the supply. {1} gains 1VP and 1 {icon:Creepy_Icon}.

G2Scuola.2.full: The Brunveen school is held in the hall behind the church. The schoolmistress, Neeltje Borg, a young woman from the city with spectacles and a thin voice, stops you at the door with a folder under her arm. Every Monday, she says, she asks the children to draw their dream from Sunday night. It is an exercise they taught her at training college. Here, in Brunveen, half the children hand in a blank sheet. They do not dream, they say. The other half always draw the same thing: the bog, at night, with a light in the middle.
G2Scuola.2.easy: The Brunveen school is in the hall behind the church. The teacher, Neeltje Borg, is a young woman from the city with glasses and a soft voice. She stops you at the door with a folder under her arm. Every Monday, she says, she asks the children to draw their dream from Sunday night. She learned this exercise at teachers' college. Here in Brunveen, half the children give her an empty page. They say they do not dream. The other half always draw the same thing: the bog at night, with a light in the middle.
G2Scuola.2.short: Every Monday Miss Borg, the young teacher, has the children draw Sunday night's dream. Half hand in blank sheets: they do not dream. The other half always draw the bog at night, with a light in the middle.

G2Scuola.4.full: You take the drawings to Dr Maas.

G2Scuola.5.full: You tell the schoolmistress it is normal, at that age.

G2Scuola.6.full: You ask her which children hand in a blank sheet.

G2Scuola.7.full: Joost Maas leafs through the drawings in his surgery, one by one, in silence. Then he puts them in order, from the oldest to the newest, and shows you something you had not noticed: in each drawing, week after week, the light in the middle of the bog is a little bigger. Joost closes the folder and says it is collective suggestion. His hands are shaking.
G2Scuola.7.easy: In his surgery, Joost Maas looks at the drawings one by one, in silence. Then he puts them in order, from the oldest to the newest, and shows you something you did not see before. In every drawing, week after week, the light in the middle of the bog gets a little bigger. Joost closes the folder and says it is a case of mass suggestion. His hands are shaking.
G2Scuola.7.short: Dr Maas sorts the drawings by date and shows you: week by week, the light in the bog grows bigger. Mass suggestion, he says, closing the folder. His hands are shaking.

G2Scuola.9.full: The schoolmistress thanks you, relieved: she was afraid she was the strange one. She confesses that, since she came to Brunveen, she is the only person in the village who still dreams every night. Bad dreams, she says, but her own.
G2Scuola.9.easy: The teacher thanks you. She is relieved: she was afraid that she was the strange one. She tells you a secret: since she came to Brunveen, she is the only person in the village who still dreams every night. Bad dreams, she says, but they are hers.
G2Scuola.9.short: The teacher is relieved: she feared she was the strange one. She is the only one in Brunveen who still dreams every night. Bad dreams, but her own.

G2Scuola.11.full: The schoolmistress shows you the class register, with a little cross beside some names. The children of the blank sheets are the best in the class: punctual, tidy, polite. They do not quarrel, do not cry, never graze their knees. Beside some names there is a second, smaller cross: the parents, the schoolmistress says, signed the school reports in the same handwriting as the child.
G2Scuola.11.easy: The teacher shows you the class register. There is a small cross next to some names. The children with the empty pages are the best in the class. They are on time, tidy and polite. They do not fight, they do not cry, and they never hurt their knees. Next to some names there is a second, smaller cross. The teacher says that the parents signed the school reports with the same handwriting as the child.
G2Scuola.11.short: The blank-sheet children are the best in class: punctual, polite, never in tears, never a grazed knee. Some have a second cross: their parents signed the reports in the child's own handwriting.

G2Ronda.2.full: At the Town Hall, in the small room, a dozen citizens have gathered: peat-cutters, two shop girls, Siebe the gravedigger, old now, Miss Borg the schoolmistress. They want to keep a night watch, as Pastor Kalf once did. They have seen things, they say: people walking towards the bog in their nightshirts, barefoot, and coming back at dawn dry. The council has already said no: there is no crime in Brunveen, and a watch would frighten families. They need someone from the estate, they say, so that the council will not dare object.
G2Ronda.2.easy: At the Town Hall, in the small room, about ten people have come together: peat-cutters, two shop assistants, Siebe the gravedigger, who is old now, and Miss Borg the teacher. They want to keep watch at night, like Pastor Kalf once did. They say they have seen things: people walking to the bog at night in their nightshirts, with bare feet, and coming back dry in the morning. The council has already said no. There is no crime in Brunveen, they say, and a watch would frighten families. So they need someone from the estate, because the council will not dare to say no to the estate.
G2Ronda.2.short: A dozen villagers want to revive Pastor Kalf's night watch: they have seen barefoot sleepwalkers going to the bog and coming back dry. The council said no. With someone from the estate, it would not dare.

G2Ronda.3.full: On the table is the old lantern of the first watch, the pastor's. Someone has kept it.
G2Ronda.3.easy: On the table there is the old lantern of the first watch, the pastor's lantern. Someone kept it.
G2Ronda.3.short: On the table: the pastor's old lantern from the first watch. Someone kept it.

G2Ronda.6.full: You talk them out of it.

G2Ronda.7.full: You accept. They give you the biggest lantern, a whistle and the list of shifts. The first night nothing happens. The second, at one o'clock, on the dyke road, you meet a man in a nightshirt walking towards the bog with his eyes open. You call him by name. He stops, turns, greets you, and goes home.
G2Ronda.7.easy: You say yes. They give you the biggest lantern, a whistle and the list of who watches when. On the first night nothing happens. On the second night, at one o'clock, on the road along the dyke, you meet a man in a nightshirt. He is walking towards the bog with his eyes open. You call his name. He stops, turns, says hello, and goes home.
G2Ronda.7.short: You lead the Watch. On the second night, on the dyke, a man in a nightshirt walks open-eyed towards the bog. You call his name. He stops, greets you, and goes home.

G2Ronda.8.full: Take the **Shield token** {icon:S3_ShieldToken} from the **A Time of War** Box and keep it in front of you: you lead the Watch.

G2Ronda.9.full: You talk for a long time, calmly, and in the end you persuade them: a watch would divide the village, and the village is all they have. They leave one by one, disappointed. Miss Borg is the last. At the door she asks whether you, too, still dream at night.
G2Ronda.9.easy: You talk calmly for a long time, and in the end they agree: a watch would divide the village, and the village is all they have. They leave one by one, disappointed. Miss Borg is the last to go. At the door she asks if you also still dream at night.
G2Ronda.9.short: You persuade them a watch would divide the village. They leave disappointed. At the door, Miss Borg asks whether you still dream at night.

G2Vanga.2.full: At the cemetery on the dyke, sitting on a grave, is Gerrit Tammer, Fokke's son, a man of thirty-five with broad shoulders and the face of someone who does not sleep. He cuts peat like his father, but alone, with the old spade, the one from before. He comes here every Sunday, he says, to the grave of his mother, who died last year. She was the only one who understood him.
G2Vanga.2.easy: At the cemetery on the dyke, Gerrit Tammer, Fokke's son, is sitting on a grave. He is thirty-five, with wide shoulders and the face of a man who does not sleep. He cuts peat like his father, but alone, with the old spade, the one from before. He says he comes here every Sunday to visit his mother's grave. She died last year. She was the only person who understood him.
G2Vanga.2.short: Gerrit Tammer, Fokke's son, thirty-five and sleepless, sits on his mother's grave. He cuts peat alone, with the old spade. She was the only one who understood him.

G2Vanga.3.full: "My father is not my father," he says. "I have known it since I was ten. He raised me, he loved me, he never raised a hand to me. My real father did. He was a drunkard and a brute. But he was my father." He holds out the spade to you, its handle worn by the hands of two generations of Tammers. "Someone has to dig. I cannot do it alone."
G2Vanga.3.easy: "My father is not my father," he says. "I have known it since I was ten. He brought me up, he loved me, and he never hit me. My real father hit me. He was a drunk and a violent man. But he was my father." He gives you the spade. Its handle is worn by the hands of two generations of Tammers. "Someone must dig. I cannot do it alone."
G2Vanga.3.short: "My father is not my father. He loved me and never hit me. My real father was a violent drunk. But he was my father." He holds out the spade. "Someone has to dig. I cannot do it alone."

G2Vanga.6.full: You tell him to let the dead lie.

G2Vanga.7.full: You take the spade. Gerrit shakes your hand, for a long time, with his warm, rough hand. "We will dig together," he says. "At the place of the light. When the peat is dry, at the end of summer. The other peat-cutters do not go there: they say the peat down there is lukewarm."
G2Vanga.7.easy: You take the spade. Gerrit shakes your hand for a long time. His hand is warm and rough. "We will dig together," he says. "At the place where the light was. When the peat is dry, at the end of the summer. The other peat-cutters do not go there. They say the peat under there is warm."
G2Vanga.7.short: Gerrit shakes your hand with his warm, rough one. "We will dig together, at the place of the light, when the peat is dry. The others will not go there: they say it is warm down there."

G2Vanga.8.full: Take the **Sickle token** {icon:S3_SickleToken} from the **A Time of War** Box: it is the peat-cutter's spade. Also take the set-aside Compulsion **"Swing wide the iron gate!…"**. When one of your pieces visits the Park, you also gain 1 {icon:Bodies_Icon}.

G2Vanga.9.full: Gerrit listens, nods, and shoulders his spade again. He does not seem offended: he seems tired. He goes off along the dyke, towards the bog, alone. The next Sunday he does not come to the cemetery. Nor the one after.
G2Vanga.9.easy: Gerrit listens, nods and puts the spade back on his shoulder. He does not look offended. He looks tired. He walks away along the dyke, towards the bog, alone. The next Sunday he does not come to the cemetery. Or the Sunday after that.
G2Vanga.9.short: Gerrit nods and shoulders his spade, more tired than offended, and walks alone towards the bog. He does not come back the next Sunday, nor the one after.

G2Rovine.2.full: At the Builder's Office, Lambert the master builder, long past retirement age and still climbing on roofs, has received orders from the council to pull down the empty houses of the families who left. His bricklayers, though, will not go inside. It is not the unsafe walls, they say: it is that someone is inside. In the beds, under the mouldy blankets, there is always a shape, like a person asleep. When you uncover it, it is peat.
G2Rovine.2.easy: At the Builder's Office, Lambert the master builder is much older than the age to stop working, but he still climbs on roofs. The council has told him to knock down the empty houses of the families who left. But his builders do not want to go inside. They say it is not because the walls are unsafe. It is because someone is in there. In the beds, under the mouldy blankets, there is always a shape, like a sleeping person. When you lift the blanket, it is peat.
G2Rovine.2.short: The council has ordered Lambert to demolish the empty houses, but his men will not go in. In every bed, under the mouldy blankets, lies a shape like a sleeper. Underneath, it is peat.

G2Rovine.4.full: You go into the Mulders' house.

G2Rovine.5.full: You pay the bricklayers to pull them down at once.

G2Rovine.6.full: The Mulders' house is cold and dark. In the bedroom, under the blanket, there is a long, thin shape, with its head on the pillow. You lift the blanket: black peat, damp, moulded like a man asleep, hands folded on its chest. On the bedside table there is a pair of spectacles. Old Mulder's, which, they say, he still wears in Rotterdam.
G2Rovine.6.easy: The Mulders' house is cold and dark. In the bedroom, under the blanket, there is a long, thin shape with its head on the pillow. You lift the blanket. It is black, wet peat, shaped like a sleeping man, with its hands together on its chest. On the bedside table there is a pair of glasses. They belong to old Mulder, who, people say, still wears them in Rotterdam.
G2Rovine.6.short: In the Mulders' bedroom, under the blanket, lies a man of black peat, hands folded on his chest. On the bedside table: old Mulder's spectacles. The ones he still wears in Rotterdam, they say.

G2Rovine.8.full: You pay double, and the bricklayers work fast, without going in: ropes, horses, and the walls come down all together in a cloud of black dust. Lambert watches with his hands behind his back, without expression. All day long a smell of bog rises from the rubble.
G2Rovine.8.easy: You pay twice the price, and the builders work fast without going inside. With ropes and horses they pull the walls down, all together, in a cloud of black dust. Lambert watches with his hands behind his back and no expression on his face. All day long the ruins smell of the bog.
G2Rovine.8.short: You pay double, and ropes and horses bring the walls down in a cloud of black dust. Lambert watches without expression. All day the rubble smells of the bog.

G2Piet.2.full: At the Laborer's Union, now a clean office with white walls and a portrait of the queen, the council clerk hires labourers for the public works. It is Piet Brink, the widow's son: a young man of twenty-five, neat, courteous, with a prodigious memory. He knows the name of every labourer, every wife, every child. He has never taken a day off sick.
G2Piet.2.easy: The Laborer's Union is now a clean office with white walls and a picture of the queen. The council clerk hires workers there for the town's building work. He is Piet Brink, the widow's son. He is a young man of twenty-five, tidy and polite, with an amazing memory. He knows the name of every worker, every wife and every child. He has never missed a day of work because he was ill.
G2Piet.2.short: The council clerk at the Laborer's Union is Piet Brink, the widow's son: twenty-five, neat, polite, with a prodigious memory. He has never had a day off sick.

G2Piet.3.full: When he sees you, he recognises your family at once. "One of yours was there," he says, kindly, "that day at the bog, with my mother. She was calling me. I heard her, you know. But I was sleeping too well to answer."
G2Piet.3.easy: When he sees you, he knows your family at once. "One of your family was there," he says kindly, "that day at the bog, with my mother. She was calling me. I heard her, you know. But I was sleeping too well to answer."
G2Piet.3.short: He recognises your family at once. "One of yours was at the bog with my mother that day. She called me. I heard her. But I was sleeping too well to answer."

G2Piet.4.full: When he sees you, he recognises your family at once. "Midwife Maas examined me, when I was a boy, because one of yours asked her to," he says, kindly. "She wrote a sentence in her Register. I have always wondered which."
G2Piet.4.easy: When he sees you, he knows your family at once. "Midwife Maas examined me when I was a boy, because one of your family asked her to," he says kindly. "She wrote a sentence in her Register. I have always wondered what it said."
G2Piet.4.short: He recognises your family at once. "Midwife Maas examined me as a boy, because one of yours asked. She wrote a sentence in her Register. I have always wondered what."

G2Piet.5.full: When he sees you, he recognises your family at once, and thanks you: "One of yours told my mother I had grown up. They were right. She never believed it, poor woman. She died in the city, alone. I wrote to her every week."
G2Piet.5.easy: When he sees you, he knows your family at once, and he thanks you. "One of your family told my mother that I had grown up. They were right. She never believed it, poor woman. She died in the city, alone. I wrote to her every week."
G2Piet.5.short: He recognises your family and thanks you: "One of yours told my mother I had grown up. She never believed it. She died alone in the city. I wrote every week."

G2Piet.7.full: You ask him about his mother.

G2Piet.8.full: You ask him for work for the labourers of the Watch.

G2Piet.9.full: Piet speaks of the widow Brink with affection, at length, without hesitating once. He remembers everything: her recipes, her songs, her outbursts, the day she threw a clog at him. He remembers everything except one thing: he cannot say what he felt when she left. He thinks about it, sincerely, with his brow furrowed. Then he smiles: "Nothing bad, I think."
G2Piet.9.easy: Piet talks about the widow Brink with love, for a long time, and he never stops to think. He remembers everything: her recipes, her songs, her angry moments, the day she threw a wooden shoe at him. He remembers everything except one thing: he cannot say how he felt when she left. He really tries to remember, with a frown. Then he smiles: "Nothing bad, I think."
G2Piet.9.short: Piet remembers everything about his mother, even the clog she threw at him. Everything except what he felt when she left. He frowns, honestly trying. Then he smiles: "Nothing bad, I think."

G2Piet.11.full: Piet hires them all, at once, at full pay. He asks nothing in return. The next day the labourers of the Watch are working on the dyke, alongside the others, and in the evening they go home tired, and at night they sleep.
G2Piet.11.easy: Piet gives them all a job, immediately, with full pay. He asks for nothing in return. The next day the workers of the Watch are working on the dyke with the others. In the evening they go home tired, and at night they sleep.
G2Piet.11.short: Piet hires them all at full pay, asking nothing back. Now the Watch works on the dyke all day, and at night they sleep.

G2Mulder.2.full: At the Traveling Caravan, among the sellers' carts, there is a covered cart with a whole family sitting on it, in silence: the Mulders, back from Rotterdam for a week to collect their things from the empty house. Old Mulder has hands ruined by work at the docks and broken spectacles held together with wire. When he sees you he gets down from the cart and takes you aside, away from the others.
G2Mulder.2.easy: At the Traveling Caravan, among the sellers' carts, there is a covered cart with a whole family sitting on it in silence. It is the Mulders. They have come back from Rotterdam for a week to take their things from their empty house. Old Mulder's hands are damaged from work at the port, and his glasses are broken and held together with wire. When he sees you, he gets down from the cart and takes you away from the others.
G2Mulder.2.short: The Mulders are back from Rotterdam for a week, to fetch their things. Old Mulder, his hands ruined by the docks, his spectacles mended with wire, takes you aside.

G2Mulder.3.full: "Do not drink the water," he says. "And if you see someone with your face, do not look them in the eye. We left when my wife said goodnight to me in her usual voice, with cold hands. That evening I took the children and went away. She did not follow us. She writes to us. She says she is well."
G2Mulder.3.easy: "Do not drink the water," he says. "And if you see someone with your face, do not look into their eyes. We left when my wife said goodnight to me in her normal voice, but with cold hands. That evening I took the children and went away. She did not come with us. She writes to us. She says she is fine."
G2Mulder.3.short: "Do not drink the water. If you see someone with your face, do not look them in the eye. My wife said goodnight with cold hands, and I took the children and left. She writes. She says she is well."

G2Mulder.5.full: You offer them hospitality at the estate.

G2Mulder.7.full: The Mulders sleep at the estate for a week. They drink only beer. Old Mulder spends the evenings with you, by the fire, and tells you what Brunveen was like before the two lights: dirty, poor, quarrelsome, full of people who fought and sang. When he leaves, he gives you a list of names: those who, in his opinion, are still "real".
G2Mulder.7.easy: The Mulders sleep at the estate for a week. They drink only beer. In the evenings old Mulder sits with you by the fire and tells you what Brunveen was like before the two lights: dirty, poor, noisy, full of people who argued and sang. When he leaves, he gives you a list of names: the people he thinks are still "real".
G2Mulder.7.short: The Mulders stay a week, drinking only beer. By the fire old Mulder remembers Brunveen before the lights: dirty, poor, full of fights and songs. He leaves you a list of those still "real".

G2Mulder.9.full: Mrs Mulder, the old man tells you, still lives in the empty house. She has never left it. He has not gone in, these days: he sends the children to fetch their things. Tonight, though, he will go in. To say goodbye to her. The next day the Mulders' cart leaves at dawn. On the seat beside the old man there is a woman in a shawl, hands in her lap, smiling at everyone.
G2Mulder.9.easy: The old man tells you that Mrs Mulder still lives in the empty house. She has never left it. He has not gone inside these days: he sends the children to get their things. But tonight he will go in, to say goodbye to her. The next day the Mulders' cart leaves at dawn. On the seat next to the old man there is a woman in a shawl, with her hands in her lap, smiling at everyone.
G2Mulder.9.short: Mrs Mulder, the old man says, never left the empty house. Tonight he will go in to say goodbye. At dawn the cart leaves, and beside him sits a woman in a shawl, smiling at everyone.

G2Cronaca.3.full: I have measured the temperature of one hundred and sixty inhabitants of Brunveen, over six years, with a precision thermometer sent from Leiden. One hundred and twenty have an average temperature of thirty-four point eight degrees. According to my books, at thirty-four point eight a man shivers, raves and dies. These hundred and twenty are perfectly well. They do not shiver. They do not fall ill. They never come to me, except to bring someone who has a fever.
G2Cronaca.3.easy: In six years I have measured the temperature of one hundred and sixty people in Brunveen, with a very exact thermometer from Leiden. One hundred and twenty of them have an average temperature of thirty-four point eight degrees. My books say that at thirty-four point eight a person shivers, goes mad and dies. These hundred and twenty are very healthy. They do not shiver. They do not get ill. They never come to see me, except when they bring someone who has a fever.
G2Cronaca.3.short: In six years I have measured one hundred and sixty villagers. One hundred and twenty average thirty-four point eight degrees, a temperature that kills. They are perfectly well, and never ill.

G2Cronaca.4.full: I have begun to think my mother was right. I do not write it out in full: I just write it.
G2Cronaca.4.easy: I am starting to think that my mother was right. I do not write it all out. I just write it.
G2Cronaca.4.short: I begin to think my mother was right. I write only that.

G2Cronaca.5.full: In the drawer of the Register, under the broken watch she kept there, I found her loose notes: names, dates, temperatures, and beside some names a little cross. I checked the crosses one by one. They were all correct.
G2Cronaca.5.easy: In the drawer of the Register, under the broken watch that she kept there, I found her loose notes. There are names, dates and temperatures, and next to some names there is a small cross. I checked the crosses one by one. They were all right.
G2Cronaca.5.short: Under her broken watch in the drawer I found her notes, with crosses beside some names. I checked every one. All correct.

G2Cronaca.6.full: {0}'s Watch goes round at night, with lanterns. The council protests, very politely. In the village, by day, people greet {1} with the same courtesy as ever. At night, when the Watch goes by, the windows stay dark.
G2Cronaca.6.easy: {0}'s Watch walks around at night with lanterns. The council complains, very politely. In the village, during the day, people say hello to {1} as kindly as always. At night, when the Watch walks past, the windows stay dark.
G2Cronaca.6.short: {0}'s Watch walks the night with lanterns. By day the village greets {1} as politely as ever. By night the windows stay dark as the Watch goes by.

G2Cronaca.7.full: {0} digs with Gerrit Tammer at the place of the light, at the end of every summer. They say the peat down there is lukewarm, and that sometimes, if you put your ear to it, you can hear breathing. So they say.
G2Cronaca.7.easy: At the end of every summer, {0} digs with Gerrit Tammer at the place where the light was. People say the peat down there is warm, and sometimes, if you put your ear close, you can hear someone breathing. That is what people say.
G2Cronaca.7.short: Every late summer {0} digs with Gerrit Tammer at the place of the light. The peat there is warm, they say, and sometimes it breathes.

G2Cronaca.8.full: A colleague from the natural history museum writes to me from the city: Professor Ostrander has died, past ninety, without an illness, smiling. In his study they found a little velvet box standing in a glass of water, and on the armchair a little peat.
G2Cronaca.8.easy: A colleague from the natural history museum writes to me from the city. Professor Ostrander has died. He was over ninety, he was not ill, and he was smiling. In his study they found a little velvet box inside a glass of water, and some peat on the armchair.
G2Cronaca.8.short: Professor Ostrander has died past ninety, without illness, smiling. In his study: a velvet box in a glass of water, and peat on the armchair.

G2Cronaca.9.full: The grandchildren of Fokke Tammer's dog, the one the estate took in so many years ago, still bark at the same people. I have borrowed them for my rounds. They are never wrong.
G2Cronaca.9.easy: The grandchildren of Fokke Tammer's dog, the dog the estate took many years ago, still bark at the same people. I take them with me when I visit my patients. They are never wrong.
G2Cronaca.9.short: The grandchildren of Fokke's old dog still bark at the same people. I take them on my rounds. They are never wrong.

G2R2.3.full: *It is Jaap Mol the smith: he is seventy and strikes iron as he did at thirty.*

G2R2.4.full: Place a {icon:S3_ParadoxToken} token on the **Farmer's Market**.

G2R2.27.full: At night the bog smokes, even in summer: a white smoke, low, rising from the place of the light and spreading over the water without wind. Whoever watches it too long, they say, no longer wants to go to bed. They go and sit on the dyke, and wait.
G2R2.27.easy: At night the bog smokes, even in summer. It is a low, white smoke. It rises from the place where the light was and spreads over the water, with no wind. People say that if you watch it too long, you do not want to go to bed any more. You go and sit on the dyke, and wait.
G2R2.27.short: At night a low white smoke rises from the place of the light, even in summer. Watch it too long, they say, and you no longer want to sleep: you sit on the dyke, and wait.

G2R2.28.full: Invitations reach the estate for every party, every christening, every wedding. Everyone wants you. Everyone is waiting for you.
G2R2.28.easy: The estate gets invitations to every party, every christening and every wedding. Everyone wants you. Everyone is waiting for you.
G2R2.28.short: Invitations to everything reach the estate. Everyone wants you. Everyone is waiting for you.

G2R2.29.full: Nobody comes to the estate any more. They leave the post at the gate. The milkman rings and leaves before you open.
G2R2.29.easy: Nobody comes to the estate now. They leave the letters at the gate. The milkman rings the bell and goes away before you open the door.
G2R2.29.short: Nobody comes to the estate now. The post is left at the gate; the milkman rings and is gone.

round.G2R2.end.full: The Middle Years of the Second Generation have ended.

G2Coro.2.full: Trijntje Kalf, the old pastor's daughter, has played the church organ for twenty years. She is a small woman with long fingers and an unerring ear. She stops you after the service, under the porch. The choir, she says, sings too well. Thirty voices, and none goes out of tune any more, none coughs, none takes a breath out of time. They sing like a single man. At the end of the hymn, every Sunday, the silence lasts exactly four bars, then they all sit down together. She never taught them to do that.
G2Coro.2.easy: Trijntje Kalf, the old pastor's daughter, has played the church organ for twenty years. She is a small woman with long fingers and a perfect ear. She stops you after the service, under the porch. She says the choir sings too well. There are thirty voices, and none of them sings out of tune any more. Nobody coughs, nobody breathes at the wrong moment. They sing like one single person. Every Sunday, at the end of the hymn, the silence lasts exactly four bars. Then they all sit down at the same time. She never taught them to do that.
G2Coro.2.short: Trijntje Kalf, the organist, says the choir sings too well: thirty voices like one, never a cough, never a wrong breath. After every hymn, exactly four bars of silence, then they all sit at once. She never taught them that.

G2Coro.4.full: Next Sunday you sing with them.

G2Coro.6.full: You sing with them, and you have never sung so well. Your voice rests on the others like a boat on water, and for the whole hymn you need think of nothing. It is beautiful. When the hymn ends, you sit down together with all the others, exactly four bars later, and you notice only afterwards.
G2Coro.6.easy: You sing with them, and you have never sung so well. Your voice rests on the others like a boat on the water, and for the whole hymn you do not have to think about anything. It is beautiful. When the hymn ends, you sit down with all the others, exactly after four bars. You only notice it later.
G2Coro.6.short: You sing with them, better than ever, thinking of nothing. When the hymn ends you sit down with everyone, exactly four bars later. You notice only afterwards.

G2Coro.8.full: You sit at the back, eyes closed, and listen. Half the choir, between one verse and the next, takes no breath. It does not need to. Trijntje, at the organ, turns towards you, and for a moment plays a wrong note, on purpose, loudly. Nobody in the choir follows her into the mistake.
G2Coro.8.easy: You sit at the back with your eyes closed and listen. Between the verses, half of the choir does not breathe. They do not need to. At the organ, Trijntje turns towards you. For a moment she plays a wrong note, on purpose, loudly. Nobody in the choir follows her mistake.
G2Coro.8.short: Eyes closed at the back, you hear it: half the choir never takes a breath. Trijntje plays one loud wrong note on purpose. Nobody follows her.

G2Furto.2.full: At the Park, at night, by the pond, six of them are waiting for you. You know them all: Lambert the master builder, Piet Brink, Jaap Mol the smith, two shop girls, the miller. They are kind. They ask you for {0}'s stone. Not for themselves, they say: for the village. The stone suffers, far from water. And when it suffers, they feel it. They ask you to think about it. They have time.
G2Furto.2.easy: At night, in the Park, near the pond, six people are waiting for you. You know them all: Lambert the master builder, Piet Brink, Jaap Mol the smith, two shop assistants and the miller. They are kind. They ask you for {0}'s stone. Not for them, they say, but for the village. The stone suffers when it is far from water. And when it suffers, they feel it. They ask you to think about it. They have time.
G2Furto.2.short: Six villagers wait for you by the pond at night, all kind. They want {0}'s stone, for the village: it suffers far from water, and they feel it. Think about it. They have time.

G2Furto.3.full: You hand it over to them.

G2Furto.4.full: You hide it in the cellar.

G2Furto.5.full: At the Park, at night, the water of the pond glows with a low, greenish light, which comes from the bottom, from the canal that leads to the bog. Down there, at the place of the light, the stone sank. With tall boots and a rope, say the peat-cutters, it could be fished out.
G2Furto.5.easy: At night, in the Park, the water of the pond shines with a low, green light. It comes from the bottom, from the canal that goes to the bog. Down there, where the light was, the stone sank. The peat-cutters say that with tall boots and a rope you could pull it out.
G2Furto.5.short: At night the pond glows green from the canal that leads to the bog, where the stone sank. With tall boots and a rope, say the peat-cutters, it could be fished out.

G2Furto.7.full: You leave it where it is.

G2Furto.8.full: The next night you take it to the dyke, in its sack. A hundred of them are waiting for you, with lanterns, in silence. They take it carefully, pass it from hand to hand down to the bank, and carry it back into the bog in procession, singing the Sunday hymn in a single voice. When the stone sinks, they all stop singing together, and go home.
G2Furto.8.easy: The next night you take it to the dyke in its sack. A hundred people are waiting for you, with lanterns, in silence. They take it carefully and pass it from hand to hand down to the bank. Then they carry it back into the bog in a procession, singing the Sunday hymn with one voice. When the stone sinks, they all stop singing at the same moment and go home.
G2Furto.8.short: A hundred silent people take the stone from you at the dyke and carry it into the bog, singing the Sunday hymn in one voice. When it sinks, they all stop at once and go home.

G2Furto.9.full: {0} puts the Crown token {icon:S3_CrownToken} back on the **Park**. Gain $2: the council, grateful, sends you a gift.

G2Furto.10.full: You hide it in the cellar, behind the barrels, in an iron box shut with two padlocks. For a week, every night, someone knocks at the estate's door. Three knocks, softly. When you open there is nobody, but on the step there is always a pool of dark water, which is gone by morning.
G2Furto.10.easy: You hide it in the cellar, behind the barrels, in an iron box with two padlocks. For a week, every night, someone knocks at the door of the estate. Three soft knocks. When you open the door, nobody is there. But on the step there is always a pool of dark water, and in the morning it is gone.
G2Furto.10.short: You lock it in the cellar. For a week, every night, three soft knocks at the door. Nobody there, only a pool of dark water on the step, gone by morning.

G2Furto.12.full: You wade into the bog up to your chest, with a rope round your waist and a lantern. The water is icy, and for a moment you seem not to touch the bottom. Then you find it, in the soft peat: warm, smooth, alive under your fingers. When you pull it out, the whole bog sighs, softly, like a person turning over in their sleep.
G2Furto.12.easy: You walk into the bog up to your chest, with a rope around your waist and a lantern. The water is ice cold, and for a moment you think there is no bottom. Then you find it in the soft peat: warm, smooth, alive under your fingers. When you pull it out, the whole bog sighs softly, like a person turning over in their sleep.
G2Furto.12.short: Chest-deep in icy water, you find the stone in the soft peat, warm and alive. As you pull it out, the whole bog sighs like a sleeper turning over.

G2Furto.13.full: Take the Crown token {icon:S3_CrownToken} from the Park. Gain 1 {icon:Insanity_Icon}.

G2Furto.14.full: You go home with wet shoes and a thought you cannot shake off: that down there, at the bottom, something knew you were there, and let you go.
G2Furto.14.easy: You go home with wet shoes and a thought that will not go away: down there, at the bottom, something knew you were there, and it let you go.
G2Furto.14.short: You go home with wet shoes, sure that something down there knew you were there, and let you go.

G2Respiro.2.full: At the cemetery, Siebe the gravedigger, very old now, beckons you aside. For some nights, he says, when the bog smokes, he has heard breathing underground. Not in the graves: between the graves, where there is nobody. A very slow breath, one a minute, deep, like someone sound asleep. He takes you to the spot, near the new wall. You put your ear to the grass. Silence. Then, after a minute, under the earth, something breathes.
G2Respiro.2.easy: At the cemetery, Siebe the gravedigger, who is very old now, calls you over with his hand. For some nights, he says, when the bog smokes, he has heard breathing under the ground. Not in the graves, but between the graves, where nobody is buried. It is a very slow, deep breath, one each minute, like someone in a heavy sleep. He takes you to the place, near the new wall. You put your ear on the grass. Silence. Then, after a minute, something breathes under the ground.
G2Respiro.2.short: Old Siebe hears breathing underground between the graves, one slow breath a minute. You put your ear to the grass. Silence. Then, under the earth, something breathes.

G2Respiro.5.full: You call the Watch to keep vigil.

G2Respiro.6.full: You dig down a yard, by lantern light. You find water, dark and lukewarm, and nothing else. Siebe says it is the peat water, which rises and falls with the moon and makes that noise. He says it without looking at you. Then he fills in the hole in a hurry, and plants a cross without a name on it.
G2Respiro.6.easy: You dig down one metre, with the lantern. You find dark, warm water and nothing else. Siebe says it is the peat water, which goes up and down with the moon and makes that sound. He says it without looking at you. Then he fills the hole quickly and puts a cross with no name on top.
G2Respiro.6.short: A yard down you find only dark, lukewarm water. The peat water rising with the moon, says Siebe, not looking at you. He fills the hole fast and plants a nameless cross on it.

G2Respiro.8.full: The Watch keeps vigil all night in the cemetery, six people round a fire, in blankets. That night the breathing is silent. But at dawn, when they get up to leave, the grass around the fire is wet in a perfect circle, as if someone, below, had drawn near to warm themselves.
G2Respiro.8.easy: The Watch stays in the cemetery all night, six people around a fire, with blankets. That night the breathing is silent. But at dawn, when they stand up to leave, the grass around the fire is wet in a perfect circle, as if someone under the ground had come closer to get warm.
G2Respiro.8.short: The Watch keeps vigil all night by a fire. The breathing stays silent. But at dawn the grass round the fire is wet in a perfect circle, as if someone below had come closer to get warm.

G2Banco.2.full: At the Farmer's Market, the black peat stall is still there, and behind the stall is still Fokke Tammer. He is past seventy, white-haired, and still cuts his peat himself, every morning, at dawn. He no longer wears bandages: his hands are smooth, with no calluses, no lines. He recognises you at once, and asks after all your relatives, living and dead, one by one, by name. He does not get one wrong.
G2Banco.2.easy: At the Farmer's Market the black peat stall is still there, and Fokke Tammer is still behind it. He is over seventy, with white hair, and he still cuts the peat himself every morning at dawn. He does not wear bandages now. His hands are smooth, with no hard skin and no lines. He knows you at once, and asks about all your family, alive and dead, one by one, by name. He does not get one wrong.
G2Banco.2.short: Fokke Tammer, past seventy, still sells his black peat. His hands are smooth, without lines. He asks after all your family, living and dead, by name, and gets none wrong.

G2Banco.4.full: You ask him about his son Gerrit.

G2Banco.6.full: Fokke sighs. Gerrit is a good lad, he says, but he takes after his mother: he worries too much. He loves him all the same, as a father should. Then he asks you, kindly, to tell Gerrit to stop digging. "The peat belongs to everyone," he says. "But the bottom belongs to those who sleep there."
G2Banco.6.easy: Fokke sighs. Gerrit is a good boy, he says, but he is like his mother: he worries too much. Fokke loves him anyway, as a father must. Then he kindly asks you to tell Gerrit to stop digging. "The peat belongs to everyone," he says. "But the bottom belongs to the ones who sleep there."
G2Banco.6.short: Gerrit worries too much, like his mother, Fokke sighs, but he loves him. Tell him to stop digging. "The peat belongs to everyone. But the bottom belongs to those who sleep there."

G2Banco.8.full: Fokke thinks. He remembers the light, he says: white, without heat. And the stone in the water, hot as a stove, and the pain in his hands. Then he remembers bending down to look at the bottom, because under the stone someone was sleeping, with his face. "He looked so tired," says Fokke. "I told him: sleep, I will do it." Then he gives you your change, right to the penny.
G2Banco.8.easy: Fokke thinks. He says he remembers the light: white, with no heat. And the stone in the water, hot like a stove, and the pain in his hands. Then he remembers bending down to look at the bottom, because under the stone someone was sleeping, someone with his face. "He looked so tired," Fokke says. "I told him: sleep, I will do it." Then he gives you your change, exact to the penny.
G2Banco.8.short: Fokke remembers the light, the hot stone, the pain. And under the stone, someone asleep with his face. "He looked so tired. I told him: sleep, I will do it." He gives you your change, exact.

G2Apprendista.2.full: At the Blacksmith, Jaap Mol strikes the iron as hard as thirty years ago. His apprentice, a sixteen-year-old Van Dam boy with red ears, stops you at the door. He wants to leave, he says, but does not know where to go. The master never makes a mistake, never gets angry, never tires. He corrects him with infinite patience. Yesterday he told him that soon he too would learn not to make mistakes, and that one night's bathe in the canal would do it, as it did for him. The boy is afraid of water.
G2Apprendista.2.easy: At the Blacksmith, Jaap Mol hits the iron as hard as he did thirty years ago. His apprentice, a Van Dam boy of sixteen with red ears, stops you at the door. He wants to leave, he says, but he does not know where to go. His master never makes mistakes, never gets angry and never gets tired. He corrects the boy with endless patience. Yesterday he told the boy that soon he too will stop making mistakes: he only needs to go into the canal one night, like Jaap did. The boy is afraid of water.
G2Apprendista.2.short: Jaap Mol's apprentice, a red-eared Van Dam boy, wants to leave. His master never errs, never tires, and has told him one night's bathe in the canal will cure his mistakes too. The boy is afraid of water.

G2Apprendista.4.full: You take him on to work at the estate.

G2Apprendista.5.full: You tell him to do as his master says.

G2Apprendista.6.full: The Van Dam boy is called Kees. He works in the tower, cleans the ring, polishes the brass, and gets wrong everything that can be got wrong: he spills the oil, burns himself, breaks a pane. It is a joy to have him around. Jaap Mol does not come to fetch him back. He only sends, the week after, a present: a new hammer, perfect.
G2Apprendista.6.easy: The Van Dam boy's name is Kees. He works in the tower, cleans the ring and polishes the brass. He makes every mistake that can be made: he spills the oil, burns himself and breaks a piece of glass. It is wonderful to have him around. Jaap Mol does not come to take him back. The next week he only sends a present: a new hammer, perfect.
G2Apprendista.6.short: The boy is Kees. In the tower he spills oil, burns himself, breaks a pane: a joy to have around. Jaap Mol sends only a present: a perfect new hammer.

G2Apprendista.8.full: The boy lowers his eyes and goes back to the anvil. A week later you run into him at the market: upright, calm, his hands clean and his ears pale. He greets you by name. He thanks you for your advice.
G2Apprendista.8.easy: The boy looks down and goes back to the anvil. A week later you see him at the market. He stands straight and calm, his hands are clean and his ears are pale. He says hello to you by name. He thanks you for your advice.
G2Apprendista.8.short: The boy goes back to the anvil. A week later, at the market, he is calm, clean-handed, his ears pale. He greets you by name and thanks you for your advice.

G2Consiglio.2.full: **Letter from the Brunveen town council to the family of the estate – *1904.***

G2Consiglio.3.full: The council, unanimously, has the pleasure of conferring on the family of the estate the honorary citizenship of Brunveen, with an annual pension and a reserved seat in the front row at all ceremonies, in recognition of forty years of service to science and to the village.
G2Consiglio.3.easy: The whole council has voted, and is happy to make the family of the estate honorary citizens of Brunveen. The family will get money every year and a seat in the front row at all ceremonies. This is to thank them for forty years of service to science and to the village.
G2Consiglio.3.short: The council unanimously makes the family of the estate honorary citizens of Brunveen, with a yearly pension and front-row seats, for forty years of service.

G2Consiglio.4.full: The council trusts that the family will, in return, give up any activity that might disturb the peace of the citizens: night watches, digging in the bog, unrequested measurements. Peace, in Brunveen, is a common good.
G2Consiglio.4.easy: In return, the council hopes that the family will stop doing anything that could disturb the peace of the people: night watches, digging in the bog, measurements that nobody asked for. In Brunveen, peace belongs to everyone.
G2Consiglio.4.short: In return, the council trusts the family will give up night watches, digging and unrequested measurements. In Brunveen, peace is a common good.

G2Consiglio.5.full: Signed: the mayor, Aldert Wessel. The clerk, Piet Brink.

G2Consiglio.7.full: YAY: you accept the council's offer.

G2ConsiglioEsito.5.full: The ceremony is held at the Town Hall, with the band and flowers. The mayor pins on each heir's chest a silver medal with the village crest, and shakes their hands one by one, with his cold hand. The pension arrives punctually on the first of every month. The Watch's lanterns stay hanging in the cellar.
G2ConsiglioEsito.5.easy: The ceremony is at the Town Hall, with the band and flowers. The mayor pins a silver medal with the village crest on the chest of each heir, and shakes hands with each of them, with his cold hand. The money arrives on time on the first day of every month. The lanterns of the Watch stay hanging in the cellar.
G2ConsiglioEsito.5.short: At the Town Hall the mayor pins a silver medal on each heir and shakes their hands with his cold one. The pension comes every month. The Watch's lanterns stay in the cellar.

G2ConsiglioEsito.7.full: You reply with a short, courteous letter. The mayor is not offended: he thanks you for your frankness, assures you that the offer remains open "for ever", and the week after sends you a basket of fruit all the same. At the market, from that day on, the traders serve you last, always with a smile.
G2ConsiglioEsito.7.easy: You answer with a short, polite letter. The mayor is not offended. He thanks you for being honest, tells you the offer is open "for ever", and the next week he sends you a basket of fruit anyway. From that day, at the market, the sellers always serve you last, with a smile.
G2ConsiglioEsito.7.short: You decline politely. The mayor thanks you, keeps the offer open "for ever", and sends fruit. From then on the market serves you last, always smiling.

G2R3.3.full: *It is the star water seller, back for the fair, the same as forty years ago.*

G2R3.24.full: Gerrit Tammer digs every night at the place of the light, with a lantern and his father's spade. The council has twice sent a letter of warning, very courteous. In the tidy village of Brunveen, on the edge of the bog, a wound of black peat grows wider every week.
G2R3.24.easy: Every night Gerrit Tammer digs at the place where the light was, with a lantern and his father's spade. The council has sent him two very polite warning letters. In the tidy village of Brunveen, at the edge of the bog, a wound of black peat gets bigger every week.
G2R3.24.short: Every night Gerrit Tammer digs at the place of the light. Two polite warnings from the council. At the edge of tidy Brunveen, a wound of black peat widens every week.

round.G2R3.end.full: The Late Years of the Second Generation have ended.

G2Scavo.2.full: At the Park, where the pond opens into the bog canal, Gerrit Tammer has built a dam of sandbags and drained a stretch of water as big as a room. He works with three peat-cutters, the men of the Watch, stripped to the waist, in mud up to their knees. They have cut the peat into bricks, layer after layer, two metres down. Down there, Gerrit says, the peat is lukewarm. And soft, like a blanket.
G2Scavo.2.easy: At the Park, where the pond meets the canal of the bog, Gerrit Tammer has built a wall of sandbags and taken the water out of an area as big as a room. He works with three peat-cutters from the Watch. They have no shirts on, and they stand in mud up to their knees. They have cut the peat into bricks, layer after layer, two metres deep. Gerrit says the peat down there is warm. And soft, like a blanket.
G2Scavo.2.short: Behind a dam of sandbags, Gerrit Tammer and three men of the Watch have dug two metres into the peat. Down there, Gerrit says, it is warm, and soft as a blanket.

G2Scavo.3.full: {0} is with them, the old Tammer spade in hand. Each stroke is easier than the last.
G2Scavo.3.easy: {0} is with them, with the old Tammer spade. Every stroke is easier than the one before.
G2Scavo.3.short: {0} digs with them. Each stroke is easier than the last.

G2Scavo.5.full: You go down and dig with them.

G2Scavo.6.full: You bring food and drink, and keep watch.

G2Scavo.7.full: You go down into the pit. The peat gives under the spade like fresh bread. At a certain point the blade touches something soft and smooth that is not peat. Gerrit grips your wrist, white in the face. "Tomorrow," he says. "In daylight. And with everyone."
G2Scavo.7.easy: You go down into the hole. The peat is as soft as fresh bread under the spade. Then the blade touches something soft and smooth that is not peat. Gerrit grabs your wrist. His face is white. "Tomorrow," he says. "When it is light. And with everyone."
G2Scavo.7.short: The peat gives like fresh bread. Then the spade touches something smooth that is not peat. Gerrit grips your wrist, white-faced: "Tomorrow. In daylight. With everyone."

G2Scavo.9.full: You bring bread, herring, beer, and stay on the dyke with a lantern, keeping watch. Towards midnight you see coming from the village road a line of figures in silence, hands in their pockets. They stop fifty paces from the pit, and watch. At dawn they leave, all together.
G2Scavo.9.easy: You bring bread, herring and beer, and you stay on the dyke with a lantern to keep watch. Around midnight you see a line of people coming from the village road, in silence, with their hands in their pockets. They stop fifty steps from the hole and watch. At dawn they all leave together.
G2Scavo.9.short: Keeping watch on the dyke, at midnight you see a silent line of figures, hands in pockets, stop fifty paces from the pit and watch. At dawn they all leave together.

G2Gerrit.2.full: At the Farmer's Market, Fokke Tammer is selling his black peat, as every day, serene, courteous. On the other side of the square, leaning against the wall, is his son Gerrit, his hands dirty with peat and his shirt torn, watching him. They have not spoken for a year. Fokke smiles at him now and then. Gerrit does not smile back.
G2Gerrit.2.easy: At the Farmer's Market, Fokke Tammer sells his black peat, as he does every day, calm and polite. On the other side of the square his son Gerrit leans against the wall and watches him. His hands are dirty with peat and his shirt is torn. They have not spoken for a year. Sometimes Fokke smiles at him. Gerrit does not smile back.
G2Gerrit.2.short: Fokke sells his black peat, serene. Across the square his son Gerrit, peat-stained and torn, watches him. They have not spoken for a year. Fokke smiles. Gerrit does not.

G2Gerrit.6.full: Fokke asks you, gently, to talk to his son. He is afraid he will hurt himself, down there in the pit. He is afraid for him, he says, like any father. And he is afraid of what he will find: "Some things keep better if nobody pulls them out." He gives you a brick of black peat, for the stove.
G2Gerrit.6.easy: Fokke gently asks you to talk to his son. He is afraid Gerrit will get hurt down there in the hole. He is afraid for him, he says, like every father. And he is afraid of what Gerrit will find: "Some things keep better if nobody takes them out." He gives you a brick of black peat for your stove.
G2Gerrit.6.short: Fokke asks you to talk to his son: he fears for him, like any father, and fears what he will find. "Some things keep better if nobody pulls them out." He gives you a brick of black peat.

G2Gerrit.8.full: Gerrit does not look at you: he looks at his father. "My father snored," he says. "He snored so loud the neighbours heard him. This one sleeps like a stone, without a sound. For forty years." Then he pushes off from the wall and goes, towards the bog, his spade on his shoulder.
G2Gerrit.8.easy: Gerrit does not look at you. He looks at his father. "My father snored," he says. "He snored so loudly that the neighbours could hear him. This one sleeps like a stone and makes no sound. For forty years." Then he moves away from the wall and walks towards the bog with his spade on his shoulder.
G2Gerrit.8.short: Gerrit watches his father. "My father snored so loud the neighbours heard. This one has slept without a sound for forty years." He shoulders his spade and heads for the bog.

G2Joost.2.full: At the Town Hall, Dr Joost Maas has organised a vaccination campaign: smallpox has reached the neighbouring villages. Queuing in front of his table is half the village, orderly, patient, sleeves already rolled up. Joost vaccinates everyone, and from everyone, secretly, he takes a temperature. When your turn comes, he shows you the thermometer and asks, softly, for your permission.
G2Joost.2.easy: At the Town Hall, Dr Joost Maas has organised vaccinations: smallpox has arrived in the villages nearby. Half of the village is waiting in line in front of his table, calm and patient, with their sleeves already rolled up. Joost vaccinates everyone, and secretly he takes everyone's temperature too. When it is your turn, he shows you the thermometer and quietly asks if he may.
G2Joost.2.short: Dr Maas is vaccinating half the village against smallpox, and secretly taking every temperature. At your turn he shows you the thermometer and softly asks permission.

G2Joost.3.full: He thanks you, under his breath, for the schoolmistress's drawings: since that day, he says, he cannot stop counting.
G2Joost.3.easy: He quietly thanks you for the teacher's drawings. Since that day, he says, he cannot stop counting.
G2Joost.3.short: He thanks you quietly for the drawings: since then he cannot stop counting.

G2Joost.7.full: You ask him to take his own.

G2Joost.8.full: Thirty-six point eight. Joost looks at the thermometer, then at you, and sighs with relief, so loudly that those in the queue turn round. He shakes your hand: warm. Then he goes back to vaccinating, and all afternoon he hums.
G2Joost.8.easy: Thirty-six point eight. Joost looks at the thermometer, then at you, and gives a sigh of relief so loud that the people in the line turn around. He shakes your hand: it is warm. Then he goes back to his vaccinations, and he hums all afternoon.
G2Joost.8.short: Thirty-six point eight. Joost sighs so loudly with relief that the queue turns round. He shakes your warm hand, and hums all afternoon.

G2Joost.10.full: Joost does not insist. He notes the refusal in the Register, with the date and the time, and beside it a question mark. Those in the queue behind you smile at you, understanding.
G2Joost.10.easy: Joost does not insist. He writes in the Register that you said no, with the date and the time, and a question mark next to it. The people in the line behind you smile at you as if they understand.
G2Joost.10.short: Joost writes your refusal in the Register, with a question mark. The queue behind you smiles, understanding.

G2Joost.11.full: Move back 1 space on the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track.

G2Joost.12.full: Joost laughs, nervously. Then, in front of you, he puts the thermometer under his tongue. He waits. He looks at it. He shakes it, and puts it back. He looks at it again. Thirty-six point six. He sits down, hands on his knees, and stays like that for a while, like someone who has just learned he has won a bet he did not want to make.
G2Joost.12.easy: Joost laughs nervously. Then, in front of you, he puts the thermometer under his tongue. He waits. He looks at it. He shakes it and puts it back. He looks at it again. Thirty-six point six. He sits down with his hands on his knees and stays like that for a while, like a man who has just won a bet that he did not want to make.
G2Joost.12.short: Joost laughs nervously and takes his own, twice. Thirty-six point six. He sits down, hands on his knees, like a man who has won a bet he never wanted to make.

G2Pastore.2.full: Pastor Ewout Kalf is ninety and dying, in the parsonage behind the church, with his daughter Trijntje beside the bed. He has sent for you. His hands are warm and his voice is thin as paper. He wants to know only one thing before he goes: how many there are. He does not say who. There is no need.
G2Pastore.2.easy: Pastor Ewout Kalf is ninety and he is dying, in his house behind the church, with his daughter Trijntje next to the bed. He has asked for you. His hands are warm, and his voice is as thin as paper. Before he dies he wants to know only one thing: how many there are. He does not say who. He does not need to.
G2Pastore.2.short: Pastor Kalf, ninety and dying, has sent for you. His hands are warm, his voice thin as paper. He wants to know only one thing: how many there are. He need not say who.

G2Pastore.3.full: He recognises you, or recognises in you the parent who agreed with him on the church steps, so many years ago. He smiles.
G2Pastore.3.easy: He knows you, or he sees in you the parent who agreed with him on the church steps, many years ago. He smiles.
G2Pastore.3.short: He sees in you the parent who agreed with him on the church steps. He smiles.

G2Pastore.4.full: He recognises you, or recognises in you the parent who contradicted him on the church steps, so many years ago. He holds out his hand to you all the same.
G2Pastore.4.easy: He knows you, or he sees in you the parent who argued with him on the church steps, many years ago. He reaches out his hand to you anyway.
G2Pastore.4.short: He sees in you the parent who argued with him on the church steps. He holds out his hand anyway.

G2Pastore.7.full: You tell him they are few.

G2Pastore.8.full: You tell him Joost Maas's figure: more than half. The pastor closes his eyes. Then he tells Trijntje to go on playing the organ, always, every Sunday, and to play one wrong note, just one, every time: "So they will know you are still there." He dies at dawn. At the funeral the choir sings perfectly.
G2Pastore.8.easy: You tell him Joost Maas's number: more than half. The pastor closes his eyes. Then he tells Trijntje to keep playing the organ, always, every Sunday, and to play one wrong note, only one, every time. "Then they will know you are still there." He dies at dawn. At the funeral the choir sings perfectly.
G2Pastore.8.short: More than half, you tell him. He closes his eyes, and asks Trijntje to play one wrong note every Sunday: "So they will know you are still there." He dies at dawn. At the funeral the choir sings perfectly.

G2Pastore.10.full: You tell him they are few, and growing fewer. The pastor looks at you for a long time, his eyes wet, and thanks you for the lie: "It was kind," he says. "That is how they are recognised, these days: by their kindness." He dies at dawn. Trijntje does not greet you at the funeral.
G2Pastore.10.easy: You tell him there are only a few, and fewer every year. The pastor looks at you for a long time, with tears in his eyes, and thanks you for the lie. "It was kind," he says. "That is how you know them now: they are kind." He dies at dawn. At the funeral Trijntje does not say hello to you.
G2Pastore.10.short: Few, you tell him. He thanks you for the lie, tearful: "It was kind. That is how you know them now: by their kindness." He dies at dawn. Trijntje ignores you at the funeral.

G2Macerie.2.full: At the Builder's Office, Lambert the master builder has hung a map of the village on the wall, with red crosses on it. They are the sinking houses: three in a year, all near the bog, all in the same direction, towards Gerrit Tammer's dig. The walls crack, the floors tilt, and in the end the house gives way, slowly, as if the ground beneath had been hollowed out. Lambert says it is the dig. He asks the family of the estate, "who have so much influence", to have it closed.
G2Macerie.2.easy: At the Builder's Office, Lambert the master builder has put a map of the village on the wall, with red crosses on it. They show the houses that are sinking: three in one year, all near the bog, all in the same direction, towards Gerrit Tammer's dig. The walls crack, the floors lean, and in the end the house falls in, slowly, as if the ground under it were empty. Lambert says it is because of the dig. He asks the family of the estate, "who have so much influence", to close it.
G2Macerie.2.short: Lambert's map shows three sinking houses, all in a line towards Gerrit Tammer's dig, as if hollowed out from below. He asks the family of the estate, "who have such influence", to have the dig closed.

G2Macerie.4.full: You agree with him and have the dig closed for a month.

G2Macerie.5.full: You go and look at the collapsed houses.

G2Macerie.6.full: Gerrit obeys, through gritted teeth. For a month the pit fills with water, and the peat closes over again, soft, above what lay beneath. Lambert thanks you and gives you the map, with its crosses. That month, the houses stop sinking.
G2Macerie.6.easy: Gerrit obeys, but he is angry. For a month the hole fills with water, and the soft peat closes again over what was under it. Lambert thanks you and gives you the map with the crosses. That month the houses stop sinking.
G2Macerie.6.short: Gerrit obeys, furious. The pit fills with water and the peat closes over what lay below. That month, the houses stop sinking.

G2Macerie.8.full: In the cellars of the collapsed houses, among the rubble, the floor has caved in, and beneath it a hollow opens in the peat, long and narrow, like a bed. There is nobody inside. But at the bottom the print of a body is still lukewarm, and leading towards the bog is a trail as wide as a man, which someone, or something, has dragged.
G2Macerie.8.easy: In the cellars of the fallen houses, among the broken bricks, the floor has broken open. Under it there is a hole in the peat, long and narrow, like a bed. Nobody is inside. But at the bottom the shape of a body is still warm. And from there a track as wide as a man goes towards the bog, as if someone, or something, was dragged along it.
G2Macerie.8.short: Under each collapsed cellar lies a hollow in the peat shaped like a bed. Empty, but the print of a body is still warm, and a trail as wide as a man leads off towards the bog.

G2Dormienti.3.full: Called at dawn to Gerrit Tammer's dig, at the Park. Present: Gerrit, the peat-cutters of the Watch, some members of the family of the estate, and myself.
G2Dormienti.3.easy: They called me at dawn to Gerrit Tammer's dig, at the Park. There were Gerrit, the peat-cutters of the Watch, some members of the family of the estate, and me.
G2Dormienti.3.short: Called at dawn to Gerrit Tammer's dig. Present: Gerrit, the Watch, some of the estate family, and myself.

G2Dormienti.4.full: Under two metres of peat, in a hollow as soft as a bed, lies a man. White skin, black hair, the clothes of a peat-cutter of fifty years ago, hands folded on his chest. The hands have recent burns on the palms, not yet healed. Body temperature: thirty-one degrees. Pulse: four beats a minute. Breathing: once a minute, deep, regular. The man is asleep.
G2Dormienti.4.easy: Under two metres of peat, in a hollow as soft as a bed, there is a man. He has white skin and black hair, and he wears the clothes of a peat-cutter from fifty years ago. His hands are together on his chest. There are new burns on his palms, not yet healed. His body temperature is thirty-one degrees. His heart beats four times a minute. He breathes once a minute, deeply and regularly. The man is asleep.
G2Dormienti.4.short: Two metres down, in a hollow soft as a bed, lies a man in the clothes of fifty years ago, fresh burns on his palms. Thirty-one degrees, four heartbeats a minute, one breath. He is asleep.

G2Dormienti.5.full: The man is Fokke Tammer, at about forty years of age. His son Gerrit recognises him; he has knelt in the mud and cannot get up. I recognise him too, by the burns: my mother dressed them. Fokke Tammer, the one who is eighty-eight, is at this moment at the Farmer's Market, behind his stall, serving customers.
G2Dormienti.5.easy: The man is Fokke Tammer, at about forty years old. His son Gerrit knows him. Gerrit has fallen on his knees in the mud and cannot stand up. I know him too, from the burns: my mother put bandages on them. The other Fokke Tammer, who is eighty-eight, is at the Farmer's Market right now, behind his stall, serving his customers.
G2Dormienti.5.short: It is Fokke Tammer, aged about forty. Gerrit kneels in the mud and cannot rise. I know the burns: my mother dressed them. The eighty-eight-year-old Fokke is at his market stall right now.

G2Dormienti.6.full: **The originals are not dead. They sleep in the peat, preserved as on the day they were taken. Those who walk about Brunveen are something else.**
G2Dormienti.6.easy: **The real people are not dead. They are sleeping in the peat, kept just as they were on the day they were taken. The ones who walk around Brunveen are something else.**
G2Dormienti.6.short: **The originals are not dead: they sleep in the peat. Those who walk Brunveen are something else.**

G2Dormienti.7.full: I checked my pulse three times while I was writing. It was normal.

G2FokkeVoto.2.full: Gerrit wants to wake him. Joost Maas says he does not know what would happen: a man who has slept almost fifty years in the peat might not survive waking, or might survive in a worse way. And the other Fokke, the one at the market, what would he do? Meanwhile, on the dyke, the people of the village have begun to arrive. They do not come closer. They wait.
G2FokkeVoto.2.easy: Gerrit wants to wake him. Joost Maas says he does not know what would happen. A man who has slept in the peat for almost fifty years might die when he wakes up, or he might live in a worse way. And what would the other Fokke, the one at the market, do? Meanwhile, on the dyke, the people of the village are starting to arrive. They do not come closer. They wait.
G2FokkeVoto.2.short: Gerrit wants to wake him. Joost does not know what would happen, to this Fokke or to the other. On the dyke the villagers have begun to gather. They come no closer. They wait.

G2FokkeVoto.5.full: NAY: you cover him with peat again, and let him sleep.

G2FokkeEsito.5.full: Six of them lift him out, wrapped in blankets, and carry him to Joost Maas's surgery, by the stove. It takes three days. On the third day Fokke Tammer opens his eyes, looks at the ceiling, then at Gerrit, who is almost sixty with a grey beard, and asks who he is. Then he asks what year it is. Then he asks for gin.
G2FokkeEsito.5.easy: Six people lift him out, wrapped in blankets, and carry him to Joost Maas's surgery, next to the stove. It takes three days. On the third day Fokke Tammer opens his eyes. He looks at the ceiling, then at Gerrit, who is almost sixty and has a grey beard, and asks who he is. Then he asks what year it is. Then he asks for gin.
G2FokkeEsito.5.short: They carry him to Joost's stove. On the third day Fokke opens his eyes, looks at grey-bearded Gerrit and asks who he is. Then what year it is. Then for gin.

G2FokkeEsito.6.full: At the Farmer's Market, that morning, the other Fokke stops serving in the middle of a sentence, leaves his stall, and walks straight towards the bog. Nobody follows him. In the evening he comes back, and reopens the stall the next day as if nothing had happened. But he no longer greets anyone by name.
G2FokkeEsito.6.easy: That morning, at the Farmer's Market, the other Fokke stops serving in the middle of a sentence. He leaves his stall and walks straight to the bog. Nobody follows him. In the evening he comes back, and the next day he opens his stall again as if nothing has happened. But he does not say hello to anyone by name any more.
G2FokkeEsito.6.short: That morning the other Fokke stops mid-sentence and walks straight to the bog. He is back by evening, and opens his stall next day as usual. But he no longer greets anyone by name.

G2FokkeEsito.8.full: Gerrit covers his father with his own hands, weeping, brick by brick, the way one tucks in a blanket. Then he opens the dam and lets the water come back. On the dyke the people of the village wait until the water has covered everything, then go home, in silence, all together. At the Farmer's Market, the next day, Fokke gives Gerrit a brick of black peat. Gerrit accepts it.
G2FokkeEsito.8.easy: Crying, Gerrit covers his father with his own hands, brick by brick, like someone tucking in a blanket. Then he opens the wall of sandbags and lets the water come back. On the dyke the village people wait until the water covers everything. Then they all go home together, in silence. The next day, at the Farmer's Market, Fokke gives Gerrit a brick of black peat. Gerrit takes it.
G2FokkeEsito.8.short: Weeping, Gerrit covers his father brick by brick and lets the water back in. The villagers wait until it is all covered, then leave together. Next day Fokke gives Gerrit a brick of black peat. Gerrit takes it.

G2Chiusura.3.full: I write the last page of my part of the Register. The war broke out last year, and even though our country is not in it, half of Europe is burning, and the young people of Brunveen leave as volunteers, for the ambulances, for the factories, for the front. The children of the estate leave. My daughter Wilhelmina leaves; she has just qualified in medicine and says doctors are needed at the front more than here. She is right. I gave her my mother's watch, the broken one: it will bring her luck, or at least tell her what time it was when it stopped working.
G2Chiusura.3.easy: I am writing the last page of my part of the Register. The war started last year. Our country is not fighting, but half of Europe is on fire, and the young people of Brunveen are leaving as volunteers: for the ambulances, for the factories, for the front. The children of the estate are leaving. My daughter Wilhelmina is leaving too. She has just become a doctor, and she says the front needs doctors more than we do here. She is right. I gave her my mother's watch, the broken one. It will bring her luck, or at least it will tell her the time when it stopped.
G2Chiusura.3.short: My last page. The war has come; our country is not in it, but Brunveen's young volunteer for the front, the children of the estate among them. My daughter Wilhelmina, a doctor now, goes too. I gave her my mother's broken watch, for luck.

G2Chiusura.4.full: Those leaving all drank the water from the fountain, on the morning of departure, as the village's new custom has it: "so as to come back". Not Wil. Wil drank beer.
G2Chiusura.4.easy: On the morning they left, everyone who was leaving drank the water from the fountain. It is the village's new custom: "so you will come back". But not Wil. Wil drank beer.
G2Chiusura.4.short: Everyone leaving drank the fountain water, "so as to come back". Not Wil. Wil drank beer.

G2Chiusura.5.full: The council's medal hangs in the entrance hall of the estate, beside the grandfather clock. It gleams. Nobody touches it.
G2Chiusura.5.easy: The council's medal hangs in the hall of the estate, next to the big clock. It shines. Nobody touches it.
G2Chiusura.5.short: The council's medal gleams in the hall. Nobody touches it.

G2Chiusura.6.full: The council still sends the basket of fruit, every month. The fruit is perfect. At the estate they give it to the pigs.
G2Chiusura.6.easy: The council still sends the basket of fruit every month. The fruit is perfect. At the estate they give it to the pigs.
G2Chiusura.6.short: The council's perfect fruit still comes every month. The estate feeds it to the pigs.

G2Chiusura.7.full: Fokke Tammer, the real one, lives with his son Gerrit in a house on the dyke. He drinks, swears, snores, and recognises nobody in the village. He says they are all too kind. The other Fokke still sells his peat at the market, on the other side of the square. They never look at each other.
G2Chiusura.7.easy: The real Fokke Tammer lives with his son Gerrit in a house on the dyke. He drinks, swears and snores, and he does not know anyone in the village. He says they are all too kind. The other Fokke still sells his peat at the market, on the other side of the square. They never look at each other.
