G2Chiusura.7.short: The real Fokke lives with Gerrit on the dyke, drinking, swearing, snoring. Everyone is too kind, he says. Across the square the other Fokke sells his peat. They never look at each other.

G2Chiusura.8.full: Under the peat, at the place of the dig, Fokke Tammer is still asleep. Gerrit takes flowers there on Sundays, instead of to his mother's grave.
G2Chiusura.8.easy: Under the peat, at the place of the dig, Fokke Tammer is still sleeping. On Sundays Gerrit takes flowers there, instead of to his mother's grave.
G2Chiusura.8.short: Fokke Tammer still sleeps under the dig. On Sundays Gerrit brings flowers there, not to his mother's grave.

G2Wessel.2.full: At the Town Hall they are celebrating Aldert Wessel's forty years as mayor of Brunveen. Garlands, a new portrait in oils, a children's choir in a row. The mayor is eighty and walks as straight as a soldier. The committee asks someone from the estate, "the oldest family in the village", to say a few words of tribute from the platform. The sheet with the speech is already prepared: the clerk, Piet Brink, wrote it.
G2Wessel.2.easy: At the Town Hall there is a party for Aldert Wessel's forty years as mayor of Brunveen. There are flowers, a new oil painting of him, and a choir of children in a line. The mayor is eighty and walks as straight as a soldier. The committee asks someone from the estate, "the oldest family in the village", to say a few kind words from the stage. The speech is already written on a sheet of paper. The clerk, Piet Brink, wrote it.
G2Wessel.2.short: Brunveen celebrates forty years of Mayor Wessel, eighty and straight as a soldier. Someone from the estate, "the oldest family", is asked to speak. The clerk, Piet Brink, has already written the speech.

G2Wessel.3.full: At the table of honour, beside the cake, there is a place laid and empty, with a card: *Mrs Wessel*. The mayor explains that his wife is still at her sister's, in the city, and has written to apologise. The letter is on the plate. The handwriting is the mayor's.
G2Wessel.3.easy: At the table of honour, next to the cake, there is an empty place with a card: *Mrs Wessel*. The mayor explains that his wife is still at her sister's in the city, and she has written to say sorry. The letter is on the plate. It is in the mayor's handwriting.
G2Wessel.3.short: Beside the cake an empty place is laid for *Mrs Wessel*, still at her sister's. Her letter of apology lies on the plate, in the mayor's handwriting.

G2Wessel.6.full: You improvise, and speak of Mrs Wessel.

G2Wessel.8.full: You read the speech: it is perfect, warm, without a word out of place. As you read, you notice the hall moving its lips along with you. They know it by heart. At the end they applaud, all at the same instant, and the mayor embraces you, cold and moved.
G2Wessel.8.easy: You read the speech. It is perfect and warm, and every word is right. While you read, you notice that the people in the hall are moving their lips with you. They know it by heart. At the end they all clap at the same moment, and the mayor hugs you, cold and full of emotion.
G2Wessel.8.short: You read the perfect speech, and the whole hall mouths it with you: they know it by heart. They clap as one, and the mayor embraces you, cold and moved.

G2Wessel.10.full: You put the sheet aside and speak of Mrs Wessel: of her cackling laugh, her dreadful hats, the quarrels with her husband that could be heard as far as the square. You tell them what Brunveen was like when people quarrelled. The hall listens to you in perfect silence. The mayor smiles the whole time. When you have finished, an old woman at the back of the hall is crying. She is the only one.
G2Wessel.10.easy: You put the paper away and talk about Mrs Wessel: her laugh like a hen's, her terrible hats, and her fights with her husband, which people could hear from the square. You tell them what Brunveen was like when people argued. The hall listens to you in perfect silence. The mayor smiles the whole time. When you finish, an old woman at the back of the hall is crying. She is the only one.
G2Wessel.10.short: You speak instead of Mrs Wessel: her cackle, her awful hats, the rows heard across the square. The hall listens in perfect silence; the mayor smiles throughout. At the back, one old woman cries. Only one.

G2Wessel.12.full: You decline gracefully: the family of the estate is no good at speeches. The committee does not insist. In your place the clerk Piet Brink speaks, without notes, without hesitation, for exactly twenty minutes. At the end the mayor embraces him like a son.
G2Wessel.12.easy: You say no politely: the family of the estate is not good at speeches. The committee does not insist. Instead, the clerk Piet Brink speaks, with no paper and no pauses, for exactly twenty minutes. At the end the mayor hugs him like a son.
G2Wessel.12.short: You decline. Piet Brink speaks instead, without notes, for exactly twenty minutes. The mayor embraces him like a son.

G2Siebe.2.full: At the cemetery, in the tool shed beside the gate, Siebe the gravedigger is dying, at ninety-one, on a camp bed, his short leg wrapped in a blanket. He has sent for someone from the estate. From the mattress he pulls out a school exercise book, greasy and crumpled, and puts it in your hand. In fifty years, he says, every time he dug a grave and found water, he looked down. And every time he saw a face down there, in the peat, he wrote it down. Name, date, depth.
G2Siebe.2.easy: At the cemetery, in the tool shed next to the gate, Siebe the gravedigger is dying. He is ninety-one. He lies on a small bed, with his short leg wrapped in a blanket. He has asked for someone from the estate. From under the mattress he takes out an old school notebook, dirty and creased, and puts it in your hand. For fifty years, he says, every time he dug a grave and found water, he looked down. And every time he saw a face down there in the peat, he wrote it down. Name, date, depth.
G2Siebe.2.short: Siebe, ninety-one and dying in the tool shed, gives you a greasy exercise book. For fifty years, whenever he saw a face in the water of a fresh grave, he wrote it down: name, date, depth.

G2Siebe.3.full: The first page is from 1868: *the miller's wife, third grave, under the coffin*. Your family was there.
G2Siebe.3.easy: The first page is from 1868: *the miller's wife, third grave, under the coffin*. Your family was there.
G2Siebe.3.short: The first page, 1868: *the miller's wife, third grave, under the coffin*. Your family was there.

G2Siebe.4.full: There are forty pages. The names are in their hundreds. "I never told anyone," says Siebe. "They would not have believed me. And those who would have believed me were written in here."
G2Siebe.4.easy: There are forty pages, and hundreds of names. "I never told anyone," says Siebe. "They would not believe me. And the people who would believe me were written in here."
G2Siebe.4.short: Forty pages, hundreds of names. "I told nobody. Those who would have believed me were written in here."

G2Siebe.7.full: You burn it, as he asks you to.

G2Siebe.8.full: Siebe squeezes your hand with the last of his strength, warm and bony, and closes his eyes. He dies that night, in his sleep, at the right temperature: Joost Maas takes it in the morning and writes it in the Register, underlined. You take the notebook to the estate and put it beside the Register. Read together, the names answer each other.
G2Siebe.8.easy: Siebe holds your hand with the last of his strength. His hand is warm and bony. He closes his eyes. He dies that night, in his sleep, with a normal temperature: Joost Maas measures it in the morning and writes it in the Register, underlined. You take the notebook to the estate and put it next to the Register. When you read them together, the names answer each other.
G2Siebe.8.short: Siebe grips your hand, warm, and dies that night at a normal temperature: Joost underlines it in the Register. You keep the notebook beside the Register. Read together, the names answer each other.

G2Siebe.10.full: Siebe asks you to burn it: he does not want "them" to find it when he is dead. You burn it in the shed's stove, page by page, in front of him. He watches the pages blacken and smiles, relieved. "Now they sleep in peace," he says. "All of them. Me too."
G2Siebe.10.easy: Siebe asks you to burn it. He does not want "them" to find it after he dies. You burn it in the stove of the shed, page by page, in front of him. He watches the pages turn black and smiles. He is relieved. "Now they sleep in peace," he says. "All of them. And me too."

G2Trijntje.2.full: **Letter from Trijntje Kalf to her brother Willem, a missionary in Batavia – *1908.***

G2Trijntje.3.full: Dear Willem, our father is dying, if you still care to know. Ninety years old, his mind clear, his hands warm: I check them every morning. Every evening he asks me to play him something on the parsonage harmonium, and to play one wrong note, just one, so that he can hear it. On Sundays, in church, the choir sings perfectly. It makes me want to scream.
G2Trijntje.3.easy: Dear Willem, our father is dying, if you still want to know. He is ninety, his mind is clear and his hands are warm: I check them every morning. Every evening he asks me to play something for him on the little organ in the house, and to play one wrong note, only one, so that he can hear it. On Sundays, in church, the choir sings perfectly. It makes me want to scream.
G2Trijntje.3.short: Dear Willem, our father is dying: ninety, clear-headed, warm hands. Each evening I play him one wrong note, so he can hear it. On Sundays the choir is perfect. I want to scream.

G2Trijntje.4.full: The family of the estate accepted the council's medal. I do not blame them: they are tired, like all of us. But since that day the lanterns of the Watch no longer go out, and at night, from the bell tower, I see the dyke road full of people walking towards the bog in their nightshirts.
G2Trijntje.4.easy: The family of the estate accepted the council's medal. I do not blame them: they are tired, like all of us. But since that day the lanterns of the Watch have stayed at home. At night, from the bell tower, I see the road on the dyke full of people in nightshirts, walking towards the bog.
G2Trijntje.4.short: The estate family took the council's medal. I do not blame them. But the Watch no longer goes out, and at night I see the dyke road full of people in nightshirts, walking to the bog.

G2Trijntje.5.full: The family of the estate refused the council's medal. Our father is proud of it. In the village they treat them with a kindness so perfect that it hurts to watch. At the market they serve them last, smiling.
G2Trijntje.5.easy: The family of the estate said no to the council's medal. Our father is proud of them. In the village people are so perfectly kind to them that it hurts to watch. At the market they serve them last, with a smile.
G2Trijntje.5.short: The estate family refused the medal. Father is proud. The village is so perfectly kind to them it hurts to watch.

G2Trijntje.6.full: {0}'s Watch still goes out, two nights a week. I bring hot tea. There are few of us left, but we all sing out of tune beautifully.
G2Trijntje.6.easy: {0}'s Watch still goes out two nights a week. I bring hot tea. There are not many of us now, but we all sing out of tune beautifully.
G2Trijntje.6.short: {0}'s Watch still goes out twice a week. I bring tea. We are few, but we all sing beautifully out of tune.

G2Trijntje.7.full: Gerrit Tammer, the peat-cutter's son, is still digging, at the Park, at the place of the light. He says he is close. To what, he does not say. Please, Willem, do not come back to Brunveen. Stay where it is hot, where people sweat and complain and die of fever. Here nobody dies any more, and I am afraid that I will not manage to die either. Your Trijntje.
G2Trijntje.7.easy: Gerrit Tammer, the peat-cutter's son, is still digging at the Park, at the place where the light was. He says he is close. Close to what, he does not say. Please, Willem, do not come back to Brunveen. Stay where it is hot, where people sweat and complain and die of fever. Here nobody dies any more, and I am afraid that I will not be able to die either. Your Trijntje.
G2Trijntje.7.short: Gerrit Tammer still digs at the place of the light. He says he is close. Willem, do not come back. Stay where people sweat and complain and die of fever. Here nobody dies, and I fear I will not manage to either. Trijntje.

G2SognoA.3.full: You dream of the dyke, at night, and your bare feet on the wet grass. You walk towards the bog without wanting to, and you are not cold. At the place of the light, with the water up to their chest, someone is waiting for you: they have your face, your hair, your clothes. They hold out a hand to you, with a smile so serene that it makes you want to cry. Further off, under the water, your parents are sleeping.
G2SognoA.3.easy: You dream of the dyke at night, and of your bare feet on the wet grass. You walk towards the bog, but you do not want to, and you are not cold. At the place where the light was, someone is standing in the water up to the chest, waiting for you. They have your face, your hair, your clothes. They reach out a hand to you, with a smile so peaceful that you want to cry. Further away, under the water, your parents are sleeping.
G2SognoA.3.short: You dream of walking barefoot to the bog. Waiting chest-deep at the place of the light is someone with your face, smiling so serenely you want to weep. Beyond, under the water, your parents sleep.

G2SognoA.4.full: You dream of the estate as it was in your childhood, with your parents at the kitchen table. The one who raised you pours you a glass of water, dark, from the jug, and tells you to drink, it is good for you: they drank it only once, and it was the most peaceful evening of their life. The hands on the jug are white. Outside the window, the bog is smoking.
G2SognoA.4.easy: You dream of the estate as it was when you were a child, with your parents at the kitchen table. The person who brought you up pours you a glass of dark water from the jug. They tell you to drink it, because it is good for you. They drank it only once, and it was the calmest evening of their life. The hands on the jug are white. Outside the window, the bog is smoking.
G2SognoA.4.short: You dream of your childhood kitchen. The one who raised you pours you dark water: drink, it is good for you. Their hands on the jug are white. Outside, the bog smokes.

G2SognoA.5.full: You dream of the tower, with its welded door and dark windows. You climb the spiral stair and never reach the top: the steps go on, one after another, while up above something hums, softly, like bees in a wall. Halfway up you find a silver watch on a step, its glass cracked. It says a quarter past eleven. You pick it up, and it is warm.
G2SognoA.5.easy: You dream of the tower, with its welded door and its dark windows. You climb the spiral stairs and never get to the top. The steps go on and on, and above you something hums softly, like bees in a wall. Halfway up you find a silver watch on a step. Its glass is cracked. It says a quarter past eleven. You pick it up, and it is warm.
G2SognoA.5.short: You dream of climbing the tower's endless stair towards a humming like bees. On a step lies a silver watch, cracked, at a quarter past eleven. It is warm.

G2SognoA.6.full: What do you do, in the dream?

G2SognoA.9.full: You go on, and the dream turns sweet, very slow, without fear. You wake at dawn with cold hands and a peace that does not belong to you. It takes an hour to pass.
G2SognoA.9.easy: You go on, and the dream becomes sweet and very slow, with no fear. You wake up at dawn with cold hands and a peace that is not yours. It takes an hour to go away.
G2SognoA.9.short: You go on, and the dream turns sweet. You wake with cold hands and a peace not your own. It takes an hour to fade.

G2SognoA.10.full: You go on, and the stair suddenly ends: before you is the brass ring, lit, white. You wake at dawn with the watch in your hand. No: with your hand clenched on nothing, as if you were really holding it.
G2SognoA.10.easy: You go on, and suddenly the stairs end. In front of you is the brass ring, lit up, white. You wake up at dawn with the watch in your hand. No: your hand is closed tight around nothing, as if you were really holding it.
G2SognoA.10.short: The stair ends at the brass ring, lit white. You wake at dawn clutching the watch. No: clutching nothing, as if it were there.

G2SognoA.12.full: You wake with a start, in your bed, your heart pounding. You touch your hands: they are warm. You do not get back to sleep until dawn, and you listen to the silence of Brunveen, which is deeper than you remembered.
G2SognoA.12.easy: You wake up suddenly in your bed, with your heart beating hard. You touch your hands: they are warm. You cannot sleep again until dawn. You listen to the silence of Brunveen. It is deeper than you remember.
G2SognoA.12.short: You wake with a start. Your hands are warm. Until dawn you lie listening to Brunveen's silence, deeper than you remembered.

G2SognoFine.2.full: The next morning, at breakfast, nobody tells their dream. You look at your hands, secretly, over your cups. From the window you can see the bog, flat and grey, and the tower, straight against the sky. Someone at the gate is already ringing the bell: it is a gentleman from the council.
G2SognoFine.2.easy: The next morning, at breakfast, nobody talks about their dream. You all look at your hands secretly, over your cups. From the window you can see the bog, flat and grey, and the tower, straight against the sky. Someone at the gate is already ringing the bell. It is a man from the council.
G2SognoFine.2.short: At breakfast nobody tells their dream. You all check your hands, over your cups. At the gate, a gentleman from the council is already ringing.

G2Ghiaccio.2.full: At the Park, in winter, the pond freezes, and the children of Brunveen skate on it, all together, in a circle, never colliding. All except one: the youngest in Miss Borg's class, eight years old, who skates badly, falls, laughs, cries, and gets up again. Today he fell where the ice is thin, near the canal that leads to the bog, and the ice broke open. The other children stopped on the bank, in a row, and are watching. Nobody shouts. The boy clings to the edge, and the dark water reaches his chin.
G2Ghiaccio.2.easy: In winter the pond in the Park freezes, and the children of Brunveen skate on it, all together, in a circle. They never bump into each other. All except one: the youngest child in Miss Borg's class. He is eight, and he skates badly. He falls, laughs, cries and gets up again. Today he fell where the ice is thin, near the canal to the bog, and the ice broke. The other children stopped on the bank, in a line, and they are watching. Nobody shouts. The boy holds on to the edge, and the dark water is up to his chin.
G2Ghiaccio.2.short: The children skate in a perfect circle, except the youngest in Miss Borg's class, who falls, laughs and cries. Today the thin ice by the canal broke under him. The others watch from the bank in a row. Nobody shouts. The dark water is at his chin.

G2Ghiaccio.3.full: The estate's dog, a grandson of Bruin, dashes onto the ice barking, before anyone else.
G2Ghiaccio.3.easy: The estate's dog, one of Bruin's grandchildren, runs onto the ice barking, before anyone else moves.
G2Ghiaccio.3.short: Bruin's grandson is first onto the ice, barking.

G2Ghiaccio.5.full: You throw yourself into the water to get him.

G2Ghiaccio.6.full: You pull him out with a stick, lying flat on the ice.

G2Ghiaccio.7.full: The water is so cold that for an instant you feel nothing: not your hands, not your heart, not your fear. It is a wonderful feeling. Then the child clings to your neck, crying, and the cold comes back, terrible, human. You carry him to the bank. Miss Borg, arriving at a run, wraps you both in her shawl. The child shivers and screams for an hour. It is the most beautiful thing you have ever heard.
G2Ghiaccio.7.easy: The water is so cold that for a moment you feel nothing: not your hands, not your heart, not your fear. It is a wonderful feeling. Then the child holds on to your neck, crying, and the cold comes back, terrible and human. You carry him to the bank. Miss Borg runs up and wraps you both in her shawl. The child shakes and screams for an hour. It is the most beautiful sound you have ever heard.
G2Ghiaccio.7.short: The cold is so deep that for an instant you feel nothing, and it is wonderful. Then the child clings to you, sobbing, and the cold returns, terrible and human. He screams for an hour. The most beautiful sound you have ever heard.

G2Ghiaccio.9.full: You lie flat on the ice, stretch out a branch, and the child grabs it at the second try. You pull him out soaked, blue, his teeth chattering. He is fine. As you carry him back to the bank, the children lined up on the shore look at you without expression, then go back to skating, in a circle, all together, as if nothing had happened.
G2Ghiaccio.9.easy: You lie on the ice and reach out with a branch. The child grabs it the second time. You pull him out, wet through, blue with cold, his teeth chattering. He is all right. While you carry him back to the bank, the children standing in a line look at you with empty faces. Then they go back to skating, in a circle, all together, as if nothing has happened.
G2Ghiaccio.9.short: Flat on the ice, you reach him with a branch and pull him out, blue and chattering, but well. The children on the bank watch blankly, then go back to their perfect circle.

G2Cassa.2.full: At the Laborer's Union, the old head of the labourers' union, Teun Bos, is closing the office for good. There is no more need for a union, he says: nobody asks for a rise, nobody complains about shifts, nobody gets hurt. The mutual aid fund, the one for widows and the sick, is full: in twenty years it has not been needed by anyone. Teun would like to give it to the estate, "who still fall ill", or else to the council, which has asked for it to build a new fountain in the square.
G2Cassa.2.easy: At the Laborer's Union, Teun Bos, the old head of the workers' union, is closing the office for ever. Nobody needs a union now, he says. Nobody asks for more pay, nobody complains about working hours, nobody gets hurt. The help fund for widows and sick people is full: in twenty years nobody has needed it. Teun would like to give it to the estate, "because you still get ill". Or he could give it to the council, which wants it to build a new fountain in the square.
G2Cassa.2.short: Teun Bos is closing the union for good: nobody complains, nobody gets hurt. The fund for widows and the sick is untouched after twenty years. He would give it to the estate, "who still fall ill", or to the council, for a new fountain.

G2Cassa.4.full: You accept the fund for the family.

G2Cassa.5.full: You tell him to give it to the council.

G2Cassa.6.full: You tell him to keep it, for when it is needed.

G2Cassa.7.full: Teun hands you the tin box with the coins and the register of dues, and shakes your hand, warm, calloused. "Use it for those who are still unwell," he says. The council, hearing of it, sends you a letter of congratulations. Most kind.
G2Cassa.7.easy: Teun gives you the tin box with the coins and the book of payments, and shakes your hand. His hand is warm and rough. "Use it for the people who are still ill," he says. When the council hears about it, they send you a letter of congratulations. It is very kind.
G2Cassa.7.short: Teun gives you the tin box: "Use it for those still unwell." The council sends a most kind letter of congratulations.

G2Cassa.9.full: The new fountain is unveiled in the spring: bronze, marble, three spouts pouring dark water straight from the bog canal. The children drink from it on their way out of school. Teun Bos, on the day of the unveiling, drinks too, and stops coughing.
G2Cassa.9.easy: The new fountain opens in the spring. It is made of bronze and marble, with three mouths that pour dark water straight from the bog canal. The children drink from it when they come out of school. On the opening day Teun Bos drinks from it too, and stops coughing.
G2Cassa.9.short: The new bronze fountain pours dark water straight from the bog. The children drink there after school. On the opening day Teun Bos drinks too, and stops coughing.

G2Cassa.11.full: Teun nods, slowly, and puts the box back under the floor, where he has always kept it. He gives you the key to the office, "just in case", and leaves. In the register of dues, the last page is blank, with a date at the top. Teun has left it that way for whoever comes after.
G2Cassa.11.easy: Teun nods slowly and puts the box back under the floor, where he always kept it. He gives you the key to the office, "just in case", and leaves. In the book of payments the last page is empty, with a date at the top. Teun has left it like that for the next person.
G2Cassa.11.short: Teun hides the box under the floor again and gives you the key, "just in case". The last page of the register is blank but for a date, left for whoever comes after.

VSG3Intro.3.full: I came back to Brunveen in June, after four years in the field hospitals of Flanders, with a suitcase, a medal I did not ask for and grandmother Hester's broken watch in my pocket. My father Joost died last winter, of influenza, with a fever of thirty-nine: they wrote it to me in the telegram, and I was glad of it. He left me his surgery and this Register.
VSG3Intro.3.easy: I came back to Brunveen in June, after four years in the field hospitals of Flanders. I brought a suitcase, a medal I did not ask for, and grandmother Hester's broken watch in my pocket. My father Joost died last winter of influenza, with a fever of thirty-nine degrees. The telegram told me so, and I was glad. He left me his surgery and this Register.
VSG3Intro.3.short: Back in Brunveen after four years in the field hospitals of Flanders, with grandmother Hester's broken watch. My father died last winter with a fever of thirty-nine: I was glad. He left me this Register.

VSG3Intro.4.full: Brunveen has become a small town: electric light, the telephone at the Town Hall, a University with three faculties, two newspapers, a cooperative bank. The streets are clean. The inhabitants are kind, healthy, hard-working. It is the quietest place I have ever been, and I have come from the war.
VSG3Intro.4.easy: Brunveen is a small town now. It has electric light, a telephone at the Town Hall, a University with three departments, two newspapers and a cooperative bank. The streets are clean. The people are kind, healthy and hard-working. It is the quietest place I have ever been to, and I have just come back from the war.
VSG3Intro.4.short: Brunveen is a town now: electric light, a University, two newspapers. Clean streets, kind and healthy people. The quietest place I have ever known, and I have come from the war.

VSG3Intro.5.full: The boys who volunteered have almost all come back. That is what worries me. At the front they died in their millions, and forty left Brunveen and thirty-eight came back, healthy, without a scar, without a nightmare. At the station the band was waiting for them, and at the fountain in the square a glass of dark water for each of them, "for welcome home".
VSG3Intro.5.easy: Almost all the young men who went as volunteers have come back. That is what worries me. At the front millions died. Forty left Brunveen, and thirty-eight came back, healthy, with no scars and no bad dreams. The band was waiting for them at the station, and at the fountain in the square there was a glass of dark water for each of them, "to say welcome home".
VSG3Intro.5.short: Forty left for the war and thirty-eight came back, without a scar or a nightmare. Millions died out there. At the station, the band; at the fountain, a glass of dark water each, "for welcome home".

VSG3Intro.6.full: The heirs of the estate have come back too. Tomorrow I will call on them, one by one, and sign a certificate of good health for each. The council requires it for all returning soldiers. I will sign it only after I have measured.
VSG3Intro.6.easy: The heirs of the estate have come back too. Tomorrow I will visit them, one by one, and sign a certificate of good health for each of them. The council asks for one for everyone back from the war. I will only sign it after I have taken their temperature.
VSG3Intro.6.short: The heirs of the estate are back too. Tomorrow I will sign their certificates of good health, as the council requires. But only after I have measured.

VSG3Intro.8.full: Each player takes a **Separatist/Monarchist token** from the **A Time of War** Box: it is their **doctor's certificate**. They put it under their Player Aid, without showing it, with the **Monarchist** side (the crown) face up: healthy. They do not touch it until the Storybook says so.

G3R1.2.full: Open the Village Chronicle to the **A Time of War** section ({icon:S3_ScenarioIcon}) and turn to **page 16**.

G3R1.3.full: *It is the cashier of the cooperative bank: he has never got a sum wrong.*

G3R1.4.full: Place a {icon:S3_ParadoxToken} token on the **Park** and one on the **General Store**.

G3R1.5.full: The **Technician** on this page uses the **Circuitry**, **Gasoline** and **Vitamin** tokens: take them from the **A Time of War** Box and place them next to the board.

G3R1.10.full: The first player who sends one of their pieces to the Credit Union

G3R1.16.full: The first player who sends one of their pieces to the University

G3R1.25.full: The first player who sends one of their pieces to the Technician

G3R1.28.full: Flags at every window, the band in the square, the returned soldiers in the front row before the Town Hall with their medals pinned to their chests. The dark water is everywhere: in the fountains, in the café carafes, in the glasses for the toast. In Brunveen, by now, they just call it "the water".
G3R1.28.easy: There are flags at every window, the band is in the square, and the soldiers who came back stand in the front row in front of the Town Hall, with medals on their chests. The dark water is everywhere: in the fountains, in the jugs at the cafés, in the glasses for the toast. In Brunveen they now just call it "the water".
G3R1.28.short: Flags, a band, the returned soldiers in the front row with their medals. Dark water everywhere: fountains, carafes, toasting glasses. In Brunveen they just call it "the water" now.

G3R1.29.full: The family of the estate sits in the front row, in the place of honour the council gave it years ago, with the silver medal pinned to their chests. Behind, three hundred people are looking at the backs of your heads.
G3R1.29.easy: The family of the estate sits in the front row, in the place of honour that the council gave it years ago, with the silver medals on their chests. Behind you, three hundred people are looking at the backs of your heads.
G3R1.29.short: The estate family sits in the place of honour, silver medals on. Behind you, three hundred people watch the backs of your heads.

G3R1.30.full: No place has been provided for the family of the estate. You stand at the back of the square, beside Trijntje Kalf and Miss Borg. Nobody asks you to leave.
G3R1.30.easy: There is no seat for the family of the estate. You stand at the back of the square, next to Trijntje Kalf and Miss Borg. Nobody asks you to go away.
G3R1.30.short: No seats for the estate family. You stand at the back with Trijntje Kalf and Miss Borg. Nobody asks you to leave.

round.G3R1.end.full: The Early Years of the Third Generation have ended.

G3Festa.2.full: At the Town Hall, in the ceremonial hall, the returned soldiers are being celebrated. Mayor Bram Wessel, old Aldert's son, gives a short, perfect speech on sacrifice and peace. Then the waiters go round the guests with trays: crystal glasses full of dark water, "the best in the province". The mayor raises his. Three hundred people raise theirs, at the same moment. Everyone is looking at you.
G3Festa.2.easy: At the Town Hall, in the big hall, there is a party for the soldiers who came back. Mayor Bram Wessel, old Aldert's son, gives a short, perfect speech about sacrifice and peace. Then the waiters walk among the guests with trays of crystal glasses full of dark water, "the best in the province". The mayor raises his glass. Three hundred people raise theirs at the same moment. Everyone is looking at you.
G3Festa.2.short: After Mayor Bram Wessel's perfect speech, waiters bring crystal glasses of dark water. The mayor raises his; three hundred people raise theirs at the same moment. Everyone is looking at you.

G3Festa.4.full: You drink the toast with them.

G3Festa.5.full: You pour your glass into the flower vase.

G3Festa.6.full: You toast with the wine you brought.

G3Festa.7.full: You drink. The hall applauds, and you feel the applause like an embrace. For the rest of the evening everything is easy: the words, the smiles, the cold handshakes. You walk home, humming the Sunday hymn under your breath, and you do not know that you know it by heart.
G3Festa.7.easy: You drink. The hall claps, and the applause feels like a hug. For the rest of the evening everything is easy: the words, the smiles, the cold handshakes. You walk home, softly singing the Sunday hymn, and you do not know that you know it by heart.
G3Festa.7.short: You drink, and the applause feels like an embrace. All evening everything is easy. You walk home humming the Sunday hymn, not knowing you know it by heart.

G3Festa.9.full: With a small movement, while everyone drinks, you pour the water into the vase of lilies. Nobody notices, or so it seems. The next day the lilies in that vase are perfect: open, white, fragrant. The others, in the other vases, have wilted.
G3Festa.9.easy: While everyone drinks, you quietly pour the water into the vase of lilies. Nobody notices, or it seems that way. The next day the lilies in that vase are perfect: open, white and sweet-smelling. The lilies in the other vases are dead.
G3Festa.9.short: While everyone drinks, you tip the water into the lilies. Nobody seems to notice. Next day those lilies are perfect. All the others have wilted.

G3Festa.11.full: You take a flask of wine out of your jacket and toast with that, smiling. The silence lasts an instant too long. Then the mayor laughs, courteously, and everyone laughs with him. At the table, for the rest of the evening, nobody pours you anything again.
G3Festa.11.easy: You take a little bottle of wine out of your jacket and make the toast with that, smiling. The silence lasts a moment too long. Then the mayor laughs politely, and everyone laughs with him. For the rest of the evening, at the table, nobody pours you anything.
G3Festa.11.short: You toast with wine from your own flask. The silence lasts a moment too long; then the mayor laughs, and everyone with him. Nobody pours you anything else all evening.

G3Bram.2.full: At the Credit Union, the cooperative bank the council founded after the war, Mayor Bram Wessel receives you in the manager's office. He is fifty-four, his grey hair carefully combed, with his father's prodigious memory. Old Aldert died ten years ago, he says, of old age, in his sleep: a happy man. The council has taken many decisions since the war, and one concerns your family.
G3Bram.2.easy: At the Credit Union, the cooperative bank that the council started after the war, Mayor Bram Wessel meets you in the manager's office. He is fifty-four. His grey hair is carefully combed, and he has his father's amazing memory. Old Aldert died ten years ago, he says, of old age, in his sleep. He was a happy man. The council has made many decisions since the war, and one of them is about your family.
G3Bram.2.short: At the Credit Union, Mayor Bram Wessel, fifty-four, grey and precise as his father, says old Aldert died happy in his sleep. The council has made a decision about your family.

G3Bram.3.full: He would like to buy {0}'s stone. Not for himself: for the village. He would put it in the bog, in its place, "where it does everyone good". He offers a sum that makes your head spin. He has already drawn up the contract.
G3Bram.3.easy: He wants to buy {0}'s stone. Not for himself, but for the village. He would put it in the bog, where it belongs, "where it is good for everyone". He offers so much money that your head spins. The contract is already written.
G3Bram.3.short: He wants to buy {0}'s stone for the village, to put it in the bog "where it does everyone good". The sum is dizzying. The contract is ready.

G3Bram.6.full: He would like the stone to stay where it is, in the bog, for ever. The council has voted to protect the place of the light as a civic monument, with a fence and a keeper. He asks the family not to fish it out, "for the good of all".
G3Bram.6.easy: He wants the stone to stay where it is, in the bog, for ever. The council has voted to protect the place where the light was, like a town monument, with a fence and a guard. He asks the family not to take it out, "for the good of everyone".
G3Bram.6.short: He wants the stone left in the bog for ever: the council will make the place of the light a monument, with a fence and a keeper. Do not fish it out, "for the good of all".

G3Bram.8.full: You tell him you can promise nothing.

G3Bram.9.full: You sign. The mayor pays you in cash, new notes smelling of the press, and that same evening takes the stone to the dyke with the whole council. He throws it into the bog in front of everyone. When it sinks, the people on the dyke sigh, all together, like someone setting down a weight.
G3Bram.9.easy: You sign. The mayor pays you in cash, with new banknotes that still smell of ink. That same evening he takes the stone to the dyke with the whole council and throws it into the bog in front of everyone. When it sinks, all the people on the dyke sigh at the same time, like someone putting down something heavy.
G3Bram.9.short: You sign, and are paid in crisp new notes. That evening the mayor throws the stone into the bog before the whole council. As it sinks, the crowd sighs as one, as if setting down a weight.

G3Bram.10.full: {0} gains $5 and puts the Crown token {icon:S3_CrownToken} back on the **Park**.

G3Bram.11.full: You give him your word, and he shakes your hand for a long time. It is cold, but the grip is sincere. "I knew I could trust you," he says. "You are people from here."
G3Bram.11.easy: You give him your word, and he shakes your hand for a long time. His hand is cold, but he means it. "I knew I could trust you," he says. "You are people from here."
G3Bram.11.short: You give your word. His handshake is cold, but sincere. "I knew I could trust you. You are people from here."

G3Bram.13.full: The mayor is not offended. Nobody is ever offended in Brunveen. He puts the contract back in the drawer, carefully, and sees you to the door. "The council has time," he says. "Much more than you."
G3Bram.13.easy: The mayor is not offended. In Brunveen nobody is ever offended. He carefully puts the contract back in the drawer and walks with you to the door. "The council has time," he says. "Much more time than you."
G3Bram.13.short: The mayor is not offended; nobody in Brunveen ever is. He puts the contract away. "The council has time. Much more than you."

G3Lavori.2.full: At the Blacksmith, now an engineering workshop with an electric lathe, Jaap Mol's grandson is keeping a crate aside for the family of the estate: brass parts, copper wire, panes of black glass. Old Jaap ordered them, he says, before he died, "for when the Machine is needed". In the workshop there is also a gentleman from the council, who offers to buy the whole crate, at any price. For the museum, he says.
G3Lavori.2.easy: The Blacksmith is now a workshop for machines, with an electric lathe. Jaap Mol's grandson is keeping a box for the family of the estate. Inside are brass parts, copper wire and pieces of black glass. He says old Jaap ordered them before he died, "for when the Machine is needed". A man from the council is in the workshop too. He wants to buy the whole box, for any price. For the museum, he says.
G3Lavori.2.short: Jaap Mol's grandson has a crate for the estate: brass, copper wire, black glass, ordered by old Jaap "for when the Machine is needed". A council gentleman offers any price for it. For the museum, he says.

G3Lavori.3.full: With these parts, and the spare segment your family has kept in the cellar since it paid for it at the foundry, the ring would be complete.
G3Lavori.3.easy: With these parts, and with the spare part that your family has kept in the cellar since it paid for it at the foundry, the ring would be complete.
G3Lavori.3.short: With these and the spare segment in your cellar, the ring would be complete.

G3Lavori.4.full: The council gentleman turns to you, with a smile: he knows the Machine is yours. He offers you double, if you let it go.
G3Lavori.4.easy: The man from the council turns to you with a smile. He knows the Machine is yours. He offers you twice as much if you forget about it.
G3Lavori.4.short: The council gentleman knows the Machine is yours. He offers double if you let it go.

G3Lavori.9.full: You leave them to the council gentleman.

G3Lavori.10.full: The council gentleman pays and has the crate loaded onto a cart. The cart takes the dyke road, not the road to the museum. In the evening, from the tower, you see the crate float for a moment on the bog, then sink, slowly.
G3Lavori.10.easy: The man from the council pays and has the box put on a cart. The cart goes along the dyke, not towards the museum. In the evening, from the tower, you see the box float on the bog for a moment, and then slowly sink.
G3Lavori.10.short: The cart with the crate takes the dyke road, not the museum's. That evening, from the tower, you watch the crate float a moment on the bog, then sink.

G3Lavori.12.full: You take the crate into the tower and work all night. Every part fits, as if it had been made yesterday. Towards dawn the ring, for an instant, hums: a low hum, like bees inside a wall. Then it falls silent.
G3Lavori.12.easy: You take the box to the tower and work all night. Every part fits, as if it was made yesterday. Near dawn, for a moment, the ring hums: a low sound, like bees inside a wall. Then it is quiet.
G3Lavori.12.short: You work all night in the tower. Every part fits. Towards dawn the ring hums for an instant, like bees in a wall. Then silence.

G3Lavori.14.full: You load the crate onto your cart under the eyes of the council gentleman, who says nothing. {0} is waiting for you at the tower, hands black with grease, and embraces you.
G3Lavori.14.easy: You put the box on your cart while the man from the council watches. He says nothing. {0} is waiting for you at the tower, with hands dirty with grease, and hugs you.
G3Lavori.14.short: You load the crate as the council gentleman watches in silence. At the tower {0}, hands black with grease, embraces you.

G3Wil.2.full: At the University, in the physiology laboratory they have lent her, Wil Maas is measuring temperatures. She is thirty-three, with short hair, hands ruined by disinfectant, and she smokes English cigarettes one after another. At the front, she says, she saw men come back from no man's land after three days in the mud, with cold hands and a calm smile, and queue for their rations as if nothing had happened. The doctors called them "the lucky ones". She called them something else, and did not write it down.
G3Wil.2.easy: At the University, in a laboratory they have lent her, Wil Maas is measuring temperatures. She is thirty-three, with short hair and hands damaged by disinfectant. She smokes English cigarettes, one after the other. At the front, she says, she saw men come back from no man's land after three days in the mud, with cold hands and a calm smile. They stood in line for their food as if nothing had happened. The doctors called them "the lucky ones". She had a different name for them, and she did not write it down.
G3Wil.2.short: At the University Wil Maas, thirty-three, chain-smoking, measures temperatures. At the front she saw men come back from three days in the mud with cold hands and calm smiles. "The lucky ones," said the doctors. She called them something else.

G3Wil.4.full: You help her with the measurements.

G3Wil.5.full: You ask her about her grandmother's Register.

G3Wil.6.full: You spend the afternoon with her: a name, a thermometer, a number, the next one. Three cold hands in four hours, all returned soldiers, all smiling. At the end Wil lights her last cigarette and asks whether you dream, at night. You say yes. She nods, and writes the number on your wrist, in pen, "so that you remember it".
G3Wil.6.easy: You spend the afternoon with her: a name, a thermometer, a number, the next person. In four hours there are three cold hands, all soldiers back from the war, all smiling. At the end Wil lights her last cigarette and asks if you dream at night. You say yes. She nods and writes the number on your wrist with her pen, "so you will remember it".
G3Wil.6.short: An afternoon of names and thermometers: three cold hands in four hours, all smiling soldiers. Wil asks if you still dream. You say yes. She writes your temperature on your wrist, "so you remember".

G3Wil.8.full: Wil takes grandmother Hester's watch out of her pocket: old, worn, its glass cracked, your family's crest on the lid. It has stopped at a quarter past eleven since before she was born. "Grandmother said it was yours," she says. "That your great-grandfather found it on the floor of the tower. My father said it was one of her stories." She puts it back in her pocket. "I believe it."
G3Wil.8.easy: Wil takes grandmother Hester's watch out of her pocket. It is old and worn, its glass is cracked, and your family's crest is on the lid. It has been stopped at a quarter past eleven since before she was born. "Grandmother said it was yours," she says. "She said your great-grandfather found it on the floor of the tower. My father said it was just one of her stories." She puts it back in her pocket. "I believe it."
G3Wil.8.short: Wil shows you Hester's cracked watch, your crest on the lid, stopped at a quarter past eleven. "Grandmother said your great-grandfather found it in the tower. My father called it one of her stories. I believe it."

G3Monumento.2.full: At the cemetery on the dyke they are putting up the war memorial: a granite obelisk with an angel on top. There are two names carved on it: the two Brunveen boys who did not come back. But the stonemason has a problem, and he shows it to you: in March the council sent him a list of five names. Then, in June, a new list, with only two names. The other three have come back, says the council. The stonemason saw them at the party. He has also seen the ministry telegrams that reported them dead.
G3Monumento.2.easy: At the cemetery on the dyke they are building the war memorial: a tall granite stone with an angel on top. Two names are carved on it: the two Brunveen boys who did not come back. But the stonemason has a problem, and he shows you. In March the council sent him a list of five names. Then, in June, it sent a new list with only two names. The council says the other three have come back. The stonemason saw them at the party. But he has also seen the telegrams from the ministry that said they were dead.
G3Monumento.2.short: The war memorial bears two names. But the council's list in March had five. The other three came back, says the council. The stonemason saw them at the party. He has also seen the telegrams reporting them dead.

G3Monumento.3.full: Beside the memorial is your great-grandfather's grave, covered with Fokke Tammer's black peat: in fifty years not a blade of grass has grown on it.
G3Monumento.3.easy: Next to the memorial is your great-grandfather's grave, covered with Fokke Tammer's black peat. In fifty years not one blade of grass has grown on it.
G3Monumento.3.short: Beside it, your great-grandfather's grave under Fokke's black peat: not a blade of grass in fifty years.

G3Monumento.4.full: Beside the memorial is your great-grandfather's grave, its granite slab tilted, as if something underneath had pushed for half a century without ever managing to get out.
G3Monumento.4.easy: Next to the memorial is your great-grandfather's grave. Its granite stone is leaning, as if something under it had pushed for fifty years and never got out.
G3Monumento.4.short: Beside it, your great-grandfather's tilted slab, as if something below had pushed for half a century.

G3Monumento.6.full: You ask for the names of the three.

G3Monumento.7.full: You tell the stonemason to carve all five names.

G3Monumento.8.full: The stonemason gives you the sheet. Three names of Brunveen boys, missing in the mud of Flanders in 1917, and back home in 1919, healthy, without papers, with dry clothes. One of the three is Jan Hoek, Hendrik Tammer's cousin. Hendrik, Fokke's grandson, came back with his papers in order and a wound in his shoulder.
G3Monumento.8.easy: The stonemason gives you the paper. It has the names of three Brunveen boys. They went missing in the mud of Flanders in 1917, and they came home in 1919, healthy, without papers, with dry clothes. One of the three is Jan Hoek, Hendrik Tammer's cousin. Hendrik, Fokke's grandson, came back with the right papers and a wound in his shoulder.
G3Monumento.8.short: Three boys missing in Flanders in 1917, home in 1919: healthy, no papers, dry clothes. One is Jan Hoek, Hendrik Tammer's cousin. Hendrik came back with papers in order and a wounded shoulder.

G3Monumento.10.full: The stonemason carves the five names, and on the day of the unveiling the mayor reads them all, without hesitating, in the same voice. The three "returned" are in the front row, with their medals. They hear their own names on the monument to the dead without batting an eyelid. Then they applaud, along with the others.
G3Monumento.10.easy: The stonemason carves the five names. On the day of the ceremony the mayor reads them all, without stopping, in the same voice. The three who "came back" are in the front row with their medals. They hear their own names on the memorial to the dead, and they do not move. Then they clap with everyone else.
G3Monumento.10.short: The stonemason carves all five. The mayor reads them out unhesitating. The three "returned", front row, hear their names among the dead without blinking, then applaud with the rest.

G3Tecnico.2.full: At the Technician, the workshop where dynamos are repaired and electrical goods are sold, the light company's engineer, a city man in a boater and bow tie, is drawing up the plan for the new dyke line. He has a problem: the tower of the estate is the highest point in the area, and the company would like to put an insulator on top of it. He has seen the brass ring from the road, and asked what it is. Nobody in the village could answer him. Nobody, he says, wanted to.
G3Tecnico.2.easy: The Technician is the workshop where they repair dynamos and sell electrical things. The engineer from the electric company, a man from the city with a straw hat and a bow tie, is planning the new power line along the dyke. He has a problem. The tower of the estate is the highest point in the area, and the company wants to put an insulator on top. He has seen the brass ring from the road and asked what it is. Nobody in the village could tell him. He says nobody wanted to.
G3Tecnico.2.short: The light company's engineer wants an insulator on the estate's tower, the highest point around. He saw the brass ring from the road and asked what it was. Nobody would tell him.

G3Tecnico.4.full: You give him permission, in exchange for a line to the tower.

G3Tecnico.5.full: You tell him to keep well away from the tower.

G3Tecnico.6.full: The engineer accepts with enthusiasm. In a week the tower has an insulator, a cable, a meter and a light bulb hanging above the brass ring. The first evening you switch it on, all the panes of black glass light up by reflection, for an instant, like an eye opening and closing again.
G3Tecnico.6.easy: The engineer is happy to agree. In one week the tower has an insulator, a cable, a meter and a light bulb hanging over the brass ring. The first evening you turn it on, all the pieces of black glass shine for a moment, like an eye that opens and closes.
G3Tecnico.6.short: Within a week a bulb hangs over the brass ring. The first evening you switch it on, the black glass lights up for an instant, like an eye opening and closing.

G3Tecnico.8.full: The engineer shrugs and moves the line three hundred metres, towards the bog. They plant the new pole at the point nearest the light. Two weeks later, the pole is leaning. After a month, it is gone, swallowed by the peat up to the insulator.
G3Tecnico.8.easy: The engineer shrugs and moves the line three hundred metres towards the bog. They put the new pole at the point closest to the light. Two weeks later the pole is leaning. After a month it is gone: the peat has swallowed it up to the top.
G3Tecnico.8.short: The line moves towards the bog, its pole planted near the place of the light. In two weeks it leans. In a month the peat has swallowed it whole.

G3NotteA.3.full: You wake in the water of the bog, standing, the water up to your waist. It is dawn. You are not cold. You remember everything: your childhood, the war, the party, the name of every person you love. You are still you. Only, for the first time in your life, you are at peace. Your hands are cold. Beneath you, in the peat, someone with your face is sleeping deeply. You do not wake that sleeping body: it looks so tired.
G3NotteA.3.easy: You wake up standing in the water of the bog, with the water up to your waist. It is dawn. You are not cold. You remember everything: your childhood, the war, the party, the name of every person you love. You are still you. But for the first time in your life, you feel at peace. Your hands are cold. Under you, in the peat, someone with your face is in a deep sleep. You do not wake that sleeping body. It looks so tired.
G3NotteA.3.short: You wake at dawn waist-deep in the bog, not cold, remembering everything. You are still you, only at peace for the first time. Your hands are cold. Below you in the peat, someone with your face sleeps. You let them sleep.

G3NotteA.4.full: **You are the Copy.** Tell no one. Turn your certificate under your Player Aid to the **Separatist** side. At the end of the game you gain 1VP for each Neighbour {icon:S3_WoodenFigureToken} on the board and 3VP if the stone {icon:S3_CrownToken} is in the bog.

G3NotteA.5.full: You dream of the bog at dawn, standing waist-deep, still as a mirror. Someone with your face comes out of the water, dry, and walks towards the village without turning round. You wake with a start, in your bed, sweat on your forehead and your heart in your mouth. It was only a dream. Perhaps the last you will ever have.
G3NotteA.5.easy: You dream that you are in the bog at dawn, with the water up to your waist. The water is as still as a mirror. Someone with your face comes out of the water, dry, and walks towards the village without looking back. You wake up suddenly in your bed, with sweat on your forehead and your heart beating fast. It was only a dream. Maybe the last dream you will ever have.
G3NotteA.5.short: You dream that someone with your face climbs dry out of the bog and walks to the village without looking back. You wake sweating. Only a dream. Perhaps your last.

G3NotteA.6.full: You are not the Copy. One of you might be, or perhaps none: watch who drinks, and who is no longer afraid. Do not touch your certificate.

G3NotteA.8.full: You get up and look outside.

G3NotteA.10.full: From the window you can see the bog, flat and grey under the dawn sky. At the place of the light, for a moment, the water ripples.
G3NotteA.10.easy: From the window you can see the bog, flat and grey under the morning sky. At the place where the light was, for a moment, the water moves.
G3NotteA.10.short: At the place of the light, under the grey dawn, the water ripples for a moment.

G3NotteA.12.full: Sleep comes at once, deep and dreamless, and on waking you feel stronger than you have in years.
G3NotteA.12.easy: You fall asleep at once, deeply, with no dreams. When you wake up, you feel stronger than you have felt for years.
G3NotteA.12.short: You sleep at once, deep and dreamless, and wake stronger than in years.

G3NotteFine.2.full: The morning after the party, Brunveen is quieter than usual. At the market people speak softly, at the café nobody reads the paper aloud, the children go to school in a line without running. At the estate breakfast is served at eight, as always. You all sit down at table together, and look at one another, for a long time, without saying anything. Then someone asks for the salt, and someone passes it.
G3NotteFine.2.easy: The morning after the party, Brunveen is quieter than usual. At the market people talk softly. At the café nobody reads the newspaper out loud. The children walk to school in a line and do not run. At the estate breakfast is at eight, as always. You all sit down at the table together and look at each other for a long time, without speaking. Then someone asks for the salt, and someone passes it.
G3NotteFine.2.short: The morning after, Brunveen is quieter than ever. At the estate's breakfast you all look at one another a long time in silence. Then someone asks for the salt, and someone passes it.

G3NotteFine.3.full: What do you do, at breakfast? *(Decide together.)*

G3NotteFine.4.full: You tell each other the night's dreams.

G3NotteFine.5.full: You touch hands, in turn, over the tablecloth.

G3NotteFine.7.full: You tell them, one after another: the dyke, the water up to the waist, someone with your face. The dreams are almost the same. Almost. One of you, when their turn comes, tells a beautiful dream, peaceful, full of light; and all of you at the table stop eating.
G3NotteFine.7.easy: You tell your dreams, one after the other: the dyke, the water up to the waist, someone with your face. The dreams are almost the same. Almost. When it is their turn, one of you tells a beautiful, peaceful dream, full of light. And everyone at the table stops eating.
G3NotteFine.7.short: You tell your dreams in turn: the dyke, the water, someone with your face. Almost the same. Then one of you tells a dream full of peace and light, and everyone stops eating.

G3NotteFine.9.full: You take hands over the tablecloth, in a chain, as at a séance. Nobody speaks. Some hands are warm, some lukewarm: it is November, the stove is not drawing, the coffee has gone cold. None of you lets go first. When at last you break apart, nobody has understood anything, and everyone is afraid.
G3NotteFine.9.easy: You hold hands over the tablecloth in a circle, like people calling spirits. Nobody speaks. Some hands are warm, some are only a little warm: it is November, the stove is not working well, the coffee is cold. Nobody wants to let go first. When you finally let go, nobody has understood anything, and everyone is afraid.
G3NotteFine.9.short: You join hands round the table like a séance. Some warm, some lukewarm: it is November, the coffee is cold. When you let go, nobody knows anything, and everyone is afraid.

G3NotteFine.11.full: You pretend nothing is wrong. You talk about the weather, the party, the mayor's speech. It is a perfect breakfast, courteous, calm, like the ones every family in Brunveen has. At a certain point you all notice it, at the same moment.
G3NotteFine.11.easy: You act as if nothing has happened. You talk about the weather, the party and the mayor's speech. It is a perfect breakfast, polite and calm, like the breakfasts of every family in Brunveen. At some point you all notice it, at the same moment.
G3NotteFine.11.short: You talk about the weather and the party: a perfect, calm breakfast, like every family's in Brunveen. You all notice it at the same moment.

G3Orologio.3.full: Called to the tower of the estate at half past eleven at night, by {0}, who had the voice of someone who does not know whether to laugh or cry.
G3Orologio.3.easy: At half past eleven at night {0} called me to the tower of the estate. They sounded like someone who did not know whether to laugh or cry.
G3Orologio.3.short: Called to the estate's tower at half past eleven at night by {0}, torn between laughing and crying.

G3Orologio.4.full: I record what I was told, and what I saw. {0} has been working for months on great-grandfather's Machine, the brass ring at the top of the tower. This evening, to test it, half repaired, they put on the platform the first thing in their pocket: great-grandfather's silver pocket watch, the one with the family crest, which in the family passes to whoever keeps the Machine. Its glass had cracked in the war, in a trench in Flanders. At a quarter past eleven the Machine came on: white light, no heat, a hum of bees. The watch vanished. It has not reappeared anywhere: not on the bog, not in the garden, not in the village.
G3Orologio.4.easy: I write what I was told, and what I saw. For months {0} has been working on the great-grandfather's Machine, the brass ring at the top of the tower. This evening, to test it when it was only half repaired, they put on the platform the first thing in their pocket. It was the great-grandfather's silver pocket watch, the one with the family crest. At a quarter past eleven the Machine turned on: white light, no heat, a hum like bees. The watch disappeared. It did not appear anywhere else: not on the bog, not in the garden, not in the village.
G3Orologio.4.short: Testing the half-repaired Machine tonight, {0} put great-grandfather's watch on the platform, its glass cracked in a Flanders trench. At a quarter past eleven: white light, a hum of bees. The watch vanished, and appeared nowhere.

G3Orologio.5.full: I took grandmother Hester's watch out of my pocket. We put it on the table, beside the empty platform. Same crest. Same scratch on the lid, shaped like a hook. Same crack in the glass, with the same chip missing at the top left. Mine is only older: the silver worn down to the copper, the initials inside the lid erased by the years. Stopped at a quarter past eleven.
G3Orologio.5.easy: I took grandmother Hester's watch out of my pocket. We put it on the table, next to the empty platform. The same crest. The same scratch on the lid, shaped like a hook. The same crack in the glass, with the same small piece missing at the top left. Mine is just older: the silver is worn down to the copper, and the letters inside the lid are gone with the years. It has stopped at a quarter past eleven.
G3Orologio.5.short: I put grandmother Hester's watch beside the empty platform. Same crest, same hook-shaped scratch, same crack, same missing chip. Mine is only older, worn to the copper. Stopped at a quarter past eleven.

G3Orologio.6.full: It is the same watch. Great-grandfather found it on the floor of the tower on the night of the two lights, in 1865, and gave it to grandmother as payment. It is the same watch that {0} sent away this evening.
G3Orologio.6.easy: It is the same watch. The great-grandfather found it on the floor of the tower on the night of the two lights, in 1865, and gave it to my grandmother to pay her. It is the same watch that {0} sent away this evening.
G3Orologio.6.short: It is the same watch. Great-grandfather found it in the tower on the night of the two lights, in 1865. {0} sent it away this evening.

G3Orologio.7.full: **The Machine does not move things only from one place to another. It moves them in time as well. And the other end of the thread is the night of the two lights. That night the Machine did not turn on by itself: someone, from here, was using it. The stone came from the future.**
G3Orologio.7.easy: **The Machine does not only move things from one place to another. It also moves them in time. And the other end of the line is the night of the two lights. That night the Machine did not turn on by itself: someone here, now, was using it. The stone came from the future.**
G3Orologio.7.short: **The Machine moves things in time as well. Its other end is the night of the two lights: that night someone, from here, was using it. The stone came from the future.**

G3Orologio.8.full: I checked my pulse three times, like my father. It was normal. It was the only normal thing in the room.
G3Orologio.8.easy: I checked my pulse three times, like my father did. It was normal. It was the only normal thing in the room.
G3Orologio.8.short: I checked my pulse three times, like my father. Normal. The only normal thing in the room.

G3Orologio.9.full: Tomorrow the journalists will climb up to the tower. What do you tell the village? *(Decide together.)*

G3Orologio.12.full: You decide to tell everything. Wil Maas looks at you for a long time, then nods: "At least it will be written down somewhere, besides here." That night, for the first time in years, nobody at the estate can sleep. Outside, on the road, people pass, slowly, and stop to look at the tower.
G3Orologio.12.easy: You decide to tell everything. Wil Maas looks at you for a long time, then nods. "At least it will be written somewhere else, not only here." That night, for the first time in years, nobody at the estate can sleep. Outside, on the road, people walk past slowly and stop to look at the tower.
G3Orologio.12.short: You will tell everything. "At least it will be written somewhere besides here," says Wil. That night nobody at the estate sleeps. People pass slowly on the road, stopping to look at the tower.

G3Orologio.13.full: {0} gains 1 Occult Knowledge. Every other player gains 1 Evidence {icon:S3_WeaponToken}.

G3Orologio.14.full: You decide to keep quiet. Wil Maas closes the Register without comment, puts grandmother's watch back in her pocket, and asks you only not to use the Machine until you are sure you know what you are doing. None of you tells her that, by now, it is too late to be sure.
G3Orologio.14.easy: You decide to say nothing. Wil Maas closes the Register without a word, puts her grandmother's watch back in her pocket, and asks you only one thing: do not use the Machine until you are sure what you are doing. Nobody tells her that now it is too late to be sure.
G3Orologio.14.short: You keep quiet. Wil asks only that you not use the Machine until you are sure what you are doing. Nobody tells her it is too late to be sure.

G3Orologio.15.full: {0} gains 1 Occult Knowledge. Every other player gains 1 Evidence {icon:S3_WeaponToken} and 1VP.

G3R2.27.full: The papers are talking about the Machine. Someone in the village saw the light on the tower on 11 November, a year to the day after the armistice, and wrote about it. The Morning Liberal calls it "the beacon of science"; the Conservative Report "a provocation". Neither paper mentions the bog.

round.G3R2.end.full: The Middle Years of the Third Generation have ended.

G3Giornali.2.full: In the offices of the Morning Liberal, two rooms above a printing works, the editor Siemens, a young man with his sleeves rolled up and ink on his fingers, wants an interview. About the Machine, naturally: the science that is carrying Brunveen into the future. But he also has another idea, and he lowers his voice to say it: an investigation into "the water", into the perfect health of the citizens, into the soldiers who came back without a scratch. He lacks someone who will talk.
G3Giornali.2.easy: The Morning Liberal has two rooms above a printing shop. The editor, Siemens, is a young man with his sleeves rolled up and ink on his fingers. He wants an interview about the Machine, of course: the science that takes Brunveen into the future. But he has another idea too, and he says it quietly: a story about "the water", about the perfect health of the people, about the soldiers who came back without a scratch. He needs someone who will talk.
G3Giornali.2.short: Siemens, the young editor of the Morning Liberal, wants an interview about the Machine. And, more quietly, an investigation into "the water" and the soldiers back without a scratch. He needs someone who will talk.

G3Giornali.4.full: You tell him about the Machine.

G3Giornali.5.full: You tell him about the Neighbours.

G3Giornali.6.full: You talk about the Machine for an hour, and the editor fills a notebook. The article comes out on Sunday, on the front page, with a drawing of the tower. Nobody believes it. Everybody reads it. In the evening the curious gather under the tower, and look up, waiting for the light.
G3Giornali.6.easy: You talk about the Machine for an hour, and the editor fills a notebook. The article comes out on Sunday, on the front page, with a drawing of the tower. Nobody believes it. Everyone reads it. In the evening curious people gather under the tower and look up, waiting for the light.
G3Giornali.6.short: The article runs on Sunday's front page. Nobody believes it; everybody reads it. In the evening a crowd gathers under the tower, waiting for the light.

G3Giornali.8.full: You tell him everything: the temperatures, the names, Gerrit's dig, the three boys on the memorial. The editor writes without looking up. The investigation comes out in three instalments, and at the third the printing works closes with a breakdown. The next day editor Siemens greets you in the street, cordially, hands in his pockets. He does not remember interviewing you.
G3Giornali.8.easy: You tell him everything: the temperatures, the names, Gerrit's dig, the three boys on the memorial. The editor writes without looking up. The story comes out in three parts. He does not remember that he interviewed you.
G3Giornali.8.short: You tell him everything. The investigation runs in three parts, and then the press "breaks down". Next day Siemens greets you warmly in the street, hands in his pockets. He does not remember interviewing you.

G3Report.2.full: The Conservative Report has its offices in a brick building with shining windows, and a grey-haired editor, Piet Brink, who left the council to devote himself "to the news". He welcomes you with tea and a proposal: a special issue devoted to your family, "who have given so much to Brunveen". A portrait of each of you, a biography, a page on the tower. He asks only that you tell the right version: the tower is a tower, the bog is a bog, and Brunveen is a happy village.
G3Report.2.easy: The Conservative Report is in a brick building with shiny windows. Its editor is Piet Brink, a grey-haired man who left the council to work "for the news". He welcomes you with tea and an offer: a special issue about your family, "who have given so much to Brunveen". A picture of each of you, the story of your lives, a page about the tower.
