G3Report.2.short: Piet Brink, grey-haired editor of the Conservative Report, offers a special issue on your family. He asks only the right version: the tower is a tower, the bog is a bog, Brunveen is happy.

G3Report.5.full: You ask him about his mother, the widow Brink.

G3Report.6.full: The special issue comes out with your faces on the front page, retouched by the photographer until they look healthier than you are. In the village everyone has you sign it. They keep it on the parlour table, beside the water jug.
G3Report.6.easy: The special issue comes out with your faces on the front page. The photographer has changed the pictures so you look healthier than you are. In the village everyone asks you to sign a copy. They keep it on the table in the sitting room, next to the jug of water.
G3Report.6.short: The issue prints your faces retouched to look healthier than you are. Everyone has you sign it, and keeps it beside the water jug.

G3Report.8.full: Piet Brink smiles, kindly, as always. His mother died in the city, alone, many years ago. He wrote to her every week. "I do not think she ever forgave me for growing up," he says. Then he is silent for a moment, and adds, softly, in a voice you do not know: "Sometimes, at night, I hear her calling. From down there."
G3Report.8.easy: Piet Brink smiles kindly, as always. His mother died alone in the city, many years ago. He wrote to her every week. "I think she never forgave me for growing up," he says. Then he is quiet for a moment, and he adds softly, in a voice you have never heard before: "Sometimes, at night, I hear her calling. From down there."
G3Report.8.short: His mother died alone in the city, Piet smiles. "She never forgave me for growing up." Then, in a voice you do not know: "Sometimes, at night, I hear her calling. From down there."

G3Pietra.2.full: At the General Store, among the jars and the shovels, they sell rubber boots up to the chest, for peat-cutters. The shop assistant watches you take a pair and says nothing. The stone is in the bog, at the place of the light, half a mile from here. There is no fence, no keeper.
G3Pietra.2.easy: At the General Store, among the jars and the shovels, they sell rubber boots that come up to your chest, for the peat-cutters. The shop assistant watches you take a pair and says nothing. The stone is in the bog, at the place where the light was, half a mile away. There is no fence and no guard.
G3Pietra.2.short: At the General Store you buy chest-high rubber boots. The assistant says nothing. The stone lies half a mile away in the bog. No fence, no keeper.

G3Pietra.3.full: You go and fish it out.

G3Pietra.5.full: At the General Store the shop assistant, a young man with clean hands, asks you, kindly, as he wraps your parcel, where you keep the stone, at the estate. Out of curiosity, he says. Everyone in the village wonders.
G3Pietra.5.easy: At the General Store the shop assistant, a young man with clean hands, wraps your parcel. While he does it, he kindly asks where you keep the stone at the estate. He says he is just curious. Everyone in the village wants to know.
G3Pietra.5.short: Wrapping your parcel, the clean-handed assistant asks kindly where the estate keeps the stone. Just curious. Everyone wonders.

G3Pietra.8.full: You wade into the bog at dawn, with the boots and a rope, as far as the place of the light. The water is icy. The stone is down there, at the bottom, where they left it: warm, smooth, alive under your fingers. When you pull it out, on the dyke, a hundred paces away, there are already ten people from the village, in silence, watching you come back to the bank.
G3Pietra.8.easy: At dawn you walk into the bog with the boots and a rope, to the place where the light was. The water is ice cold. The stone is down there, at the bottom, where they left it: warm, smooth, alive under your fingers. When you pull it out, ten people from the village are already standing on the dyke, a hundred steps away. They watch you come back to the bank in silence.
G3Pietra.8.short: At dawn you wade out and find the stone, warm and alive. As you pull it out, ten villagers are already on the dyke, silently watching you come back.

G3Pietra.10.full: You tell him: in the iron box, in the laboratory. The shop assistant thanks you. The next night nobody hears anything, nobody forces a lock. In the morning the box is open and empty, and the bog, from the window, is smoking.
G3Pietra.10.easy: You tell him: in the iron box, in the laboratory. The shop assistant thanks you. The next night nobody hears anything, and nobody breaks a lock. In the morning the box is open and empty, and from the window you see the bog smoking.
G3Pietra.10.short: You tell him: the iron box in the laboratory. That night nobody hears a thing. By morning the box is open and empty, and the bog is smoking.

G3Pietra.11.full: {0} puts the Crown token {icon:S3_CrownToken} back on the **Park**.

G3Pietra.12.full: You leave with the parcel under your arm and the feeling that someone, the whole time, was watching you already knowing the answer.
G3Pietra.12.easy: You leave with the parcel under your arm. You feel that someone was watching you the whole time, and already knew the answer.
G3Pietra.12.short: You leave feeling that someone watched you all along, already knowing the answer.

G3Hendrik.2.full: At the Laborer's Union, where returned soldiers are hired for the work on the dyke, there is Hendrik Tammer, Fokke's grandson, Gerrit's son. He is thirty, with a wounded shoulder and the eyes of someone who has not slept for months. He is the only returned soldier who did not drink at the fountain. He does not sleep, he says, because he is afraid of falling asleep near the water. In the trenches he slept in the mud. In Brunveen he cannot any more.
G3Hendrik.2.easy: At the Laborer's Union, where soldiers back from the war are hired to work on the dyke, there is Hendrik Tammer, Fokke's grandson and Gerrit's son. He is thirty. He has a wound in his shoulder and the eyes of a man who has not slept for months. He is the only soldier who did not drink at the fountain. He says he does not sleep because he is afraid to fall asleep near the water. In the trenches he slept in the mud. In Brunveen he cannot sleep any more.
G3Hendrik.2.short: Hendrik Tammer, Gerrit's son, thirty, wounded, sleepless, is the only soldier who did not drink at the fountain. He slept in the mud of the trenches. In Brunveen he is afraid to fall asleep near the water.

G3Hendrik.3.full: His grandfather Fokke, the real one, the one woken from the peat, died two years ago, drunk and happy, cursing the neighbours. Hendrik loved him.
G3Hendrik.3.easy: His grandfather Fokke, the real one, the one they woke up from the peat, died two years ago. He was drunk and happy, and he was shouting at the neighbours. Hendrik loved him.
G3Hendrik.3.short: His real grandfather Fokke, woken from the peat, died two years ago, drunk, happy, cursing the neighbours. Hendrik loved him.

G3Hendrik.4.full: His grandfather Fokke, the real one, still sleeps under the peat of the Park. Gerrit, his father, made him promise never to let them pull him out without him.
G3Hendrik.4.easy: His grandfather Fokke, the real one, is still sleeping under the peat in the Park. His father Gerrit made him promise never to let anyone take Fokke out unless Gerrit is there.
G3Hendrik.4.short: His real grandfather still sleeps under the Park. Gerrit made him promise never to let them dig Fokke out without him.

G3Hendrik.6.full: You take him to the Watch.

G3Hendrik.7.full: You take him to Wil Maas.

G3Hendrik.8.full: Hendrik joins the Watch the way one goes into a trench: without speaking, checking his rifle. From that night the Watch has a man who does not sleep and who can shoot. The first night, on the dyke, he stays motionless for six hours, watching the bog. At dawn he says only: "They are moving."
G3Hendrik.8.easy: Hendrik joins the Watch like a soldier going into a trench: without talking, checking his gun. From that night the Watch has a man who does not sleep and who can shoot. On the first night, on the dyke, he does not move for six hours. He watches the bog. At dawn he says only: "They are moving."
G3Hendrik.8.short: Hendrik joins the Watch like a man entering a trench. The first night he watches the bog for six hours without moving. At dawn he says only: "They are moving."

G3Hendrik.10.full: Wil Maas gives him some drops to help him sleep and a piece of advice: sleep away from water, upstairs, with the window shut. Hendrik thanks her. He sleeps, for the first time in months, fourteen hours straight. When he wakes his hands are warm. He checks them for an hour.
G3Hendrik.10.easy: Wil Maas gives him some drops to help him sleep, and some advice: sleep far from the water, upstairs, with the window closed. Hendrik thanks her. For the first time in months he sleeps for fourteen hours. When he wakes up, his hands are warm. He checks them for an hour.
G3Hendrik.10.short: Wil gives him sleeping drops: sleep upstairs, far from water. He sleeps fourteen hours. When he wakes his hands are warm. He checks them for an hour.

G3Neeltje.2.full: At the Library, at the lending desk, is the new librarian, perfect, who greets you by name. At the back of the room, in the armchair by the stove, is Miss Neeltje Borg, who left the school last year, with a bundle of exercise books on her knees. They are her pupils' dream diaries, from 1891 to 1918: almost thirty years of Mondays. She has kept them all. She wants to leave them to someone, before the new librarian puts them "in order".
G3Neeltje.2.easy: At the Library, at the desk, the new librarian, who is perfect, says hello to you by name. At the back of the room, in the armchair by the stove, sits Miss Neeltje Borg. She stopped teaching last year. She has a pile of notebooks on her knees. They are her pupils' dream diaries, from 1891 to 1918: almost thirty years of Mondays. She has kept them all. She wants to give them to someone before the new librarian puts them "in order".
G3Neeltje.2.short: By the Library stove sits Miss Borg, retired, with her pupils' dream diaries from 1891 to 1918. She wants to give them to someone before the perfect new librarian puts them "in order".

G3Neeltje.5.full: You ask her whether she still dreams.

G3Neeltje.6.full: You take them to the estate and leaf through them in the evening, one by one. Year after year the blank sheets increase. In the last book, the one from 1918, there is only one drawing: a child who has drawn himself, twice, side by side, one in colour and one in black. Underneath, in the crooked hand of a six-year-old: *me and me*.
G3Neeltje.6.easy: You take them to the estate and look through them in the evening, one by one. Every year there are more empty pages. In the last notebook, from 1918, there is only one drawing. A child has drawn himself twice, side by side: one in colour and one in black. Under it, in the crooked writing of a six-year-old: *me and me*.
G3Neeltje.6.short: Year by year the blank sheets multiply. In the 1918 book there is one drawing: a child drawn twice, side by side, once in colour, once in black. Below: *me and me*.

G3Neeltje.8.full: Neeltje laughs, softly. She dreams every night, she says: bad dreams, confused, full of people who are no longer there. She wakes tired, with a headache. She is the happiest person in Brunveen. "The day I stop dreaming," she says, "come and check my hands."
G3Neeltje.8.easy: Neeltje laughs softly. She says she dreams every night: bad, confused dreams, full of people who are gone. She wakes up tired, with a headache. She is the happiest person in Brunveen. "The day I stop dreaming," she says, "come and check my hands."
G3Neeltje.8.short: Neeltje laughs. She has bad dreams every night and wakes with a headache: the happiest woman in Brunveen. "The day I stop dreaming, come and check my hands."

G3Neeltje.9.full: Move back 1 space on the {icon:Insanity_Icon} track and gain 1VP.

G3Notte2A.3.full: The village sleeps. You do not: you no longer need to. You walk the dark streets with your hands in your pockets, and from every window someone greets you, softly. There are many of them, but not enough. Choose a house, tonight. Tomorrow someone happier will live in it.
G3Notte2A.3.easy: The village is sleeping. You are not: you do not need to sleep any more. You walk through the dark streets with your hands in your pockets, and from every window someone softly says hello. There are many of them, but not enough. Choose a house tonight. Tomorrow someone happier will live there.
G3Notte2A.3.short: The village sleeps; you no longer need to. From every dark window someone greets you softly. Many, but not enough. Choose a house tonight. Tomorrow someone happier will live there.

G3Notte2A.4.full: Where do you place a Neighbour, tonight?

G3Notte2A.5.full: The village sleeps. You almost do. Outside, on the road, someone is walking, slowly, with an easy step, and stops in front of a house. Then moves on, and stops in front of another. Before you fall asleep you try to work out where.
G3Notte2A.5.easy: The village is sleeping. You are almost asleep. Outside on the road someone is walking slowly and calmly. They stop in front of a house. Then they walk on and stop in front of another one. Before you fall asleep, you try to understand where.
G3Notte2A.5.short: Half asleep, you hear slow, calm steps outside stop at one house, then another. Before sleep takes you, you try to tell where.

G3Notte2A.6.full: Where do you look, before you sleep?

G3Notte2Fine.2.full: In the morning, in a house in the village, someone wakes up more serene than usual, has breakfast in silence and leaves the house at an easy pace, hands in their pockets. Nobody notices. Almost nobody.
G3Notte2Fine.2.easy: In the morning, in a house in the village, someone wakes up calmer than usual. They eat breakfast in silence and walk out of the house slowly, with their hands in their pockets. Nobody notices. Almost nobody.
G3Notte2Fine.2.short: In the morning, somewhere in the village, someone wakes more serene than usual and walks out, hands in pockets. Almost nobody notices.

G3Fokke.3.full: Called to the Farmer's Market at nine in the morning. Fokke Tammer, ninety-three according to the register, was serving a customer when he stopped talking in the middle of a sentence. He stood motionless, the change in his hand. Then the skin of his face dried, like paper in the sun, and cracked. In less than an hour, in front of a hundred people, Fokke Tammer crumbled into peat, from head to foot, like a brick left too long on the stove. On the cobbles, when I arrived, there were a heap of black peat, an apron, and the coins of the change.
G3Fokke.3.easy: They called me to the Farmer's Market at nine in the morning. Fokke Tammer, ninety-three years old on paper, was serving a customer when he stopped talking in the middle of a sentence. He stood still, with the change in his hand. Then the skin on his face became dry, like paper in the sun, and it cracked. In less than an hour, in front of a hundred people, Fokke Tammer fell apart into peat, from his head to his feet, like a brick left too long on the stove. When I arrived, on the stones of the street there was a pile of black peat, an apron and the coins of the change.
G3Fokke.3.short: Called to the market at nine. Fokke Tammer, ninety-three, stopped mid-sentence, the change in his hand. His face dried and cracked like paper, and within an hour he crumbled into peat before a hundred people. I found black peat, an apron, and the coins.

G3Fokke.4.full: Nobody screamed. People watched. Then, one after another, they looked at their hands.
G3Fokke.4.easy: Nobody screamed. People watched. Then, one after the other, they looked at their own hands.
G3Fokke.4.short: Nobody screamed. Then, one by one, they looked at their hands.

G3Fokke.5.full: **After fifty-four years the body of peat no longer holds. The Neighbours do not last for ever, and they know it. The oldest are in a hurry to renew themselves.**
G3Fokke.5.easy: **After fifty-four years the peat body cannot last any longer. The Neighbours do not live for ever, and they know it. The oldest ones are in a hurry to find new bodies.**
G3Fokke.5.short: **After fifty-four years the peat body gives out. The Neighbours do not last for ever, and the oldest are in a hurry.**

G3Fokke.6.full: Gerrit Tammer, old now, came to the market with his stick. He looked at the peat for a long time, then took off his hat. It was the man who had raised him.
G3Fokke.6.easy: Gerrit Tammer, who is old now, came to the market with his walking stick. He looked at the peat for a long time, then took off his hat. It was the man who brought him up.
G3Fokke.6.short: Old Gerrit Tammer came with his stick, looked long at the peat, and took off his hat. It was the man who raised him.

G3Fokke.7.full: Gerrit Tammer, old now, came to the market with his stick, gathered a handful of peat in a handkerchief and went to the Park, to the dig, where his father still sleeps. He scattered it over him.
G3Fokke.7.easy: Gerrit Tammer, who is old now, came to the market with his walking stick. He picked up a handful of peat in a handkerchief and went to the Park, to the dig, where his real father is still sleeping. He put the peat on top of him.
G3Fokke.7.short: Old Gerrit gathered a handful of the peat and scattered it over the dig in the Park, where his father still sleeps.

G3R3.2.full: Open the Village Chronicle to the **Fear of the Unknown** section ({icon:S2_ScenarioIcon}) and turn to **page 21**.

G3R3.5.full: When one of your pieces visits the Town Hall, you may spend 3 Evidence {icon:S3_WeaponToken} and have Wil Maas examine another player:

G3R3.13.full: {icon:Storybook} **The last crate of water – General Store**

G3R3.23.full: The council has decreed a curfew, "as a precaution", after the death of Fokke Tammer. Nobody goes out after ten. At night, in the streets of Brunveen, only those who have no need of sleep walk about, and there are many of them.
G3R3.23.easy: After Fokke Tammer's death the council has ordered a curfew, "to be careful". Nobody may go out after ten o'clock. At night, in the streets of Brunveen, the only people walking are the ones who do not need to sleep. And there are many of them.
G3R3.23.short: After Fokke's death the council imposes a curfew. At night only those who need no sleep walk Brunveen's streets. There are many.

G3R3.24.full: After Wil Maas's test, the word went round the village in an hour. Nobody, though, talks about it. At the estate, in the morning, the milkman leaves an extra bottle.
G3R3.24.easy: After Wil Maas's test, the news went around the village in one hour. But nobody talks about it. In the morning, at the estate, the milkman leaves one more bottle than usual.
G3R3.24.short: News of Wil's test went round the village in an hour. Nobody mentions it. The milkman leaves the estate an extra bottle.

G3R3.25.full: After the Morning Liberal's article, the curious gather under the tower every evening, and more every evening. They look up, in silence, and wait for the light.
G3R3.25.easy: Since the article in the Morning Liberal, curious people come under the tower every evening, and every evening there are more. They look up, in silence, and wait for the light.
G3R3.25.short: Every evening, more of the curious gather under the tower, silently waiting for the light.

round.G3R3.end.full: The Late Years of the Third Generation have ended.

G3Coprifuoco.2.full: At the cemetery, at night, during the curfew, the Watch found the grave of Jaap Mol, the smith, open. Not desecrated: opened from the inside, the earth pushed up and to the side, the way one throws back a blanket. The coffin is empty, apart from a little peat. Jaap Mol died, according to the register, in 1915. But in 1915, Hendrik reminds you, the village's Jaap already had almost fifty years of peat in him. Then who was the one buried?
G3Coprifuoco.2.easy: At night, during the curfew, the Watch found the grave of Jaap Mol, the smith, open. Nobody broke into it. It was opened from the inside. The earth is pushed up and to one side, like a blanket pushed away. The coffin is empty, except for a little peat. On paper, Jaap Mol died in 1915. But in 1915, Hendrik reminds you, the Jaap of the village was already almost fifty years old in peat. So who was buried here?
G3Coprifuoco.2.short: The Watch found Jaap Mol's grave opened from inside, the earth thrown back like a blanket, the coffin empty but for peat. Jaap was buried in 1915. But by then the village's Jaap was nearly fifty years of peat. Who was buried, then?

G3Coprifuoco.5.full: You close the grave, before word gets out.

G3Coprifuoco.6.full: Wil examines the peat in the coffin with her lens, kneeling on the loose earth. It has the shape of a man, she says, but not of a dead man: of a man who got up. The Jaap buried in 1915 was the real one, fished out of the canal by someone and put to sleep here. And tonight, on his own, he woke up.
G3Coprifuoco.6.easy: Wil kneels on the loose earth and looks at the peat in the coffin with her lens. She says it has the shape of a man, but not of a dead man. It is the shape of a man who stood up. The Jaap buried in 1915 was the real one. Someone took him out of the canal and put him here to sleep. And tonight he woke up by himself.
G3Coprifuoco.6.short: The peat holds the shape of a man, says Wil, not dead but risen. The Jaap buried in 1915 was the real one, taken from the canal and laid here. Tonight he woke on his own.

G3Coprifuoco.8.full: You close the grave with the Watch's spades, in silence, and put the flowers back on it. Nobody in the village will ever call you to account. But the next morning, on the dyke, the footprints of a barefoot man lead from the cemetery to the bog, and do not come back.
G3Coprifuoco.8.easy: In silence you close the grave with the spades of the Watch and put the flowers back on top. Nobody in the village will ever ask you about it. But the next morning, on the dyke, there are the footprints of a man with bare feet. They go from the cemetery to the bog, and they do not come back.
G3Coprifuoco.8.short: You close the grave in silence. Nobody will ever ask. But next morning a barefoot man's prints lead from the cemetery to the bog, and do not come back.

G3Ultimi.2.full: In church, on Sunday, Trijntje Kalf plays the organ for a few: twenty or so people in the front pews, old folk, children, a few returned soldiers. The choir is gone. The others, she tells you, go to the bog on Sunday mornings, in a line, and stand on the dyke with the water round their ankles, in silence, for an hour. It is their Mass. Halfway through the hymn, as her father asked her on his deathbed, Trijntje plays a wrong note, loudly. In the front pews, someone smiles.
G3Ultimi.2.easy: In church on Sunday, Trijntje Kalf plays the organ for only a few people: about twenty, in the front benches, old people, children and a few soldiers back from the war. There is no choir now. She tells you the others go to the bog on Sunday mornings, in a line. They stand on the dyke with water up to their ankles, in silence, for an hour. It is their church service. In the middle of the hymn, as her father asked before he died, Trijntje plays a wrong note, loudly. In the front benches someone smiles.
G3Ultimi.2.short: On Sunday Trijntje plays for twenty people. The rest stand in silence at the bog, ankle-deep: their Mass. Mid-hymn she plays her loud wrong note. Someone in the front pews smiles.

G3Ultimi.4.full: You stay until the end of the hymn.

G3Ultimi.5.full: You go to the bog to watch their Mass.

G3Ultimi.6.full: You stay. You sing badly, out of time, your voice cracking. Next to you an old peat-cutter sings worse than you, and nudges you, laughing. Trijntje plays another wrong note, and another. At the end nobody sits down at the same moment.
G3Ultimi.6.easy: You stay. You sing badly, at the wrong speed, and your voice breaks. Next to you an old peat-cutter sings even worse, and pushes you with his elbow, laughing. Trijntje plays another wrong note, and another. At the end, nobody sits down at the same moment.
G3Ultimi.6.short: You stay and sing badly. An old peat-cutter sings worse and nudges you, laughing. Trijntje plays wrong note after wrong note. At the end nobody sits down at the same moment.

G3Ultimi.8.full: At the dyke there are three hundred people, in a line, with the water round their ankles, hands at their sides, eyes closed. Nobody speaks. Nobody moves. The silence is so deep that you hear, beneath the peat, in their hundreds, the sleepers breathing. For a moment you want to take off your shoes and get in line too.
G3Ultimi.8.easy: At the dyke there are three hundred people in a line, with water up to their ankles, hands by their sides and eyes closed. Nobody speaks. Nobody moves. It is so quiet that you can hear the sleepers breathing under the peat, hundreds of them. For a moment you want to take off your shoes and stand in the line too.
G3Ultimi.8.short: Three hundred people stand ankle-deep at the dyke, eyes closed. In the silence you hear hundreds of sleepers breathing beneath the peat. For a moment you want to take off your shoes and join them.

G3Emporio.2.full: At the General Store, out the back, is the warehouse for the bottles of "Brunveen Water", the labelled kind, which the village has sold all over the province for thirty years. The owner, a calm man in a white apron, shows you the latest order: a city in the south wants ten thousand bottles. For the soldiers' hospitals, he says. Against nightmares. The council has already approved it. Only the crates are missing, and the estate's carts are the biggest in the village.
G3Emporio.2.easy: At the back of the General Store there is the storeroom for the bottles of "Brunveen Water", with the label. The village has sold it all over the province for thirty years. The owner, a calm man with a white apron, shows you the latest order. A city in the south wants ten thousand bottles, for the hospitals for soldiers. Against bad dreams, he says. The council has already said yes. They only need transport, and the estate's carts are the biggest in the village.
G3Emporio.2.short: A southern city has ordered ten thousand bottles of Brunveen Water, for the soldiers' hospitals, against nightmares. The council has approved. They need only carts, and the estate's are the biggest.

G3Emporio.6.full: The carts leave at dawn, loaded to the brim, for the station. The owner pays you well and thanks you on behalf of the village. The next month, in the paper, you read that in the soldiers' hospitals in the south the nightmares have vanished, and with them the screams in the night, the fits, the escapes. The doctors speak of a miracle. The patients do not speak much any more.
G3Emporio.6.easy: The carts leave at dawn for the station, full to the top. The owner pays you well and thanks you for the village. The next month you read in the newspaper that in the southern hospitals the soldiers' bad dreams have gone. No more screaming at night, no more attacks, no more running away. The doctors call it a miracle. The patients do not talk much any more.
G3Emporio.6.short: The carts leave at dawn. A month later the paper reports the southern hospitals' nightmares gone: no screams, no fits. The doctors speak of a miracle. The patients hardly speak at all.

G3Emporio.8.full: You go into the warehouse with a stick and smash everything you can before they stop you. Nobody stops you. The owner watches, hands in his pockets, as the dark water spreads over the floor and runs under the door, towards the road, towards the dyke. When you have finished, he offers you a towel.
G3Emporio.8.easy: You go into the storeroom with a stick and break everything you can before someone stops you. Nobody stops you. The owner watches with his hands in his pockets, while the dark water spreads over the floor and runs under the door, towards the road and towards the dyke. When you finish, he gives you a towel.
G3Emporio.8.short: You smash every bottle you can. Nobody stops you. The owner watches, hands in pockets, as the water runs under the door towards the dyke. Then he offers you a towel.

G3Mercato.2.full: At the Farmer's Market, the black peat stall is empty, covered with a sheet. Fokke's heap of peat was swept away the same day. But on the cobbles, where he fell, the stone has stayed darker, in the shape of a man, and nobody walks on it. In front of the stall there are flowers. And there is a line of people, in silence, waiting. They explain that they are waiting for the new peat-cutter. One will come, they say. One always comes.
G3Mercato.2.easy: At the Farmer's Market the black peat stall is empty, under a sheet. Fokke's pile of peat was swept away the same day. But on the stones where he fell there is a darker shape, like a man, and nobody walks on it. There are flowers in front of the stall. And there is a line of people, waiting in silence. They tell you they are waiting for the new peat-cutter. One will come, they say. One always comes.
G3Mercato.2.short: Fokke's stall stands empty under a sheet. A man-shaped stain darkens the cobbles. A silent queue waits in front: for the new peat-cutter. One always comes, they say.

G3Mercato.4.full: You ask who it will be.

G3Mercato.5.full: You take off the sheet and stand behind the stall.

G3Mercato.6.full: They answer you gently, one after another, the way one answers a child: someone who loves the peat, who is good with their hands, who works hard. Someone from Fokke's family, perhaps. Hendrik, for instance, who never sleeps. They say it with affection, and with a patient expectancy that chills you.
G3Mercato.6.easy: They answer you kindly, one after the other, the way you answer a child. Someone who loves peat, who is good with their hands, who works hard. Someone from Fokke's family, maybe. Hendrik, for example, who never sleeps. They say it with love, and with a patient waiting that makes you go cold.
G3Mercato.6.short: Someone who loves the peat and works hard, they answer gently. From Fokke's family, perhaps. Hendrik, who never sleeps. Their patient affection chills you.

G3Mercato.8.full: You take off the sheet and stand behind the stall, your hands on Fokke's black peat. The queue moves, and the first customer asks you for two bricks, with a smile. You serve all day. In the evening your hands are black to the wrists, with a smell of bog that will not wash off with soap. But they are warm.
G3Mercato.8.easy: You take off the sheet and stand behind the stall, with your hands on Fokke's black peat. The line moves, and the first customer asks you for two bricks, with a smile. You sell all day. In the evening your hands are black up to the wrists, and the smell of the bog does not go away with soap. But your hands are warm.
G3Mercato.8.short: You stand behind the stall and sell Fokke's peat all day. By evening your hands are black to the wrists and smell of the bog. But they are warm.

G3Test.2.full: In the surgery at the Town Hall, Wil Maas prepares the thermometer, a lens, a needle sterilised in the lamp flame. "Red blood, healthy," she says. "Dark water, not. I am not wrong. I have not been wrong for four years." She asks whom she is to examine.
G3Test.2.easy: In her room at the Town Hall, Wil Maas gets ready a thermometer, a lens and a needle that she cleans in the flame of the lamp. "Red blood: healthy," she says. "Dark water: not. I do not make mistakes. I have not made a mistake for four years." She asks who she must examine.
G3Test.2.short: Wil Maas readies a thermometer, a lens and a flame-sterilised needle. "Red blood, healthy. Dark water, not. I have not been wrong in four years." Whom is she to examine?

G3Test.3.full: *Whoever has another player examined spends 3 Evidence {icon:S3_WeaponToken}.* Who is examined?

G3Test.10.full: The needle enters the fingertip, without pain. Out comes a black drop, thick, smelling of smoke. Wil Maas says nothing. She looks at the drop, then at {0}, for a long time, without fear and without hatred. Then, gently, she takes {1}'s hand in hers and holds it, as one does at a sickbed. It is cold.
G3Test.10.easy: The needle goes into the fingertip, without pain. A thick black drop comes out. It smells of smoke. Wil Maas says nothing. She looks at the drop, then at {0}, for a long time, with no fear and no hate. Then, gently, she takes {1}'s hand in hers and holds it, like you hold the hand of a sick person in bed. It is cold.
G3Test.10.short: A thick black drop, smelling of smoke. Wil looks long at {0}, without fear or hatred, then holds {1}'s hand as at a sickbed. It is cold.

G3Test.11.full: {0} spends 3 Evidence {icon:S3_WeaponToken}. **{1} is the Copy**: they turn their certificate to the Separatist side and place it in front of them, visible to all. They lose 5VP and take the set-aside Maladjustment **Must Be Loved**. They go on playing and voting.

G3Test.12.full: The needle enters the fingertip, and {0} flinches. Out comes a red drop, alive. Wil Maas looks at it, dabs it with cotton wool, and smiles for the first time since she came back. "Thirty-six point eight," she says. "A living person's blood."
G3Test.12.easy: The needle goes into the fingertip, and {0} jumps. A red drop comes out, alive. Wil Maas looks at it, cleans it with cotton, and smiles for the first time since she came back. "Thirty-six point eight," she says. "The blood of a living person."
G3Test.12.short: {0} flinches at the needle. A red, living drop. Wil smiles for the first time since she came back. "Thirty-six point eight. Living blood."

G3Test.13.full: {0} spends 3 Evidence {icon:S3_WeaponToken}. **{1} is not the Copy**: they place their certificate in front of them, Monarchist side up, and gain 2VP.

G3Reduce.3.full: Everyone knows what you are. Nobody has thrown it in your face: in the family they treat you with a kindness you did not know, the way one treats an invalid. But at night, from the window, you hear the bog calling you, softly, in your own voice. Down there, under the peat, someone with your face has been sleeping for weeks, in the cold. You could go back, and let them wake. You could stay, and live in their place, for fifty years, in peace.
G3Reduce.3.easy: Everyone knows what you are. Nobody has blamed you for it. The family treats you with a kindness you never knew before, like a sick person. But at night, from the window, you hear the bog calling you softly, with your own voice. Down there, under the peat, someone with your face has been sleeping in the cold for weeks. You could go back and let them wake up. Or you could stay, and live in their place for fifty years, in peace.
G3Reduce.3.short: Everyone knows what you are, and treats you kindly, like an invalid. At night the bog calls you in your own voice. Under the peat someone with your face sleeps in the cold. Go back and let them wake, or stay and live fifty peaceful years in their place.

G3Reduce.4.full: You go back to the bog.

G3UltimaNotte.2.full: On 31 December 1919, at eleven at night, the family is gathered at the top of the tower, around the brass ring. Outside it is snowing on the bog, but at the place of the light the snow does not settle. Wil Maas has come up with the Register under her arm and grandmother's watch in her pocket. She lays it on the table, open, stopped at a quarter past eleven. From the windows you can see the village, all dark. Nobody in Brunveen is asleep tonight.
G3UltimaNotte.2.easy: On 31 December 1919, at eleven at night, the family is together at the top of the tower, around the brass ring. Outside it is snowing on the bog, but at the place where the light was the snow does not stay. Wil Maas has come up with the Register under her arm and her grandmother's watch in her pocket. She puts the watch on the table, open. It has stopped at a quarter past eleven. From the windows you can see the village, completely dark. Nobody in Brunveen is sleeping tonight.
G3UltimaNotte.2.short: 31 December 1919, eleven at night. The family gathers round the brass ring. Snow falls on the bog, but not on the place of the light. Wil lays Hester's watch on the table, at a quarter past eleven. The village is dark. Nobody in Brunveen sleeps tonight.

G3UltimaNotte.3.full: Turn over your certificates, all together.

G3UltimaNotte.4.full: One of the certificates on the table shows the side without the crown. The silence lasts a long time. Then whoever turned it smiles, calmly, and holds their hands out to the fire, without any need to warm them.
G3UltimaNotte.4.easy: One of the certificates on the table shows the side with no crown. There is a long silence. Then the person who turned it smiles calmly and holds out their hands to the fire, though they do not need to warm them.
G3UltimaNotte.4.short: One certificate shows no crown. A long silence. Then its owner smiles calmly and holds their hands to the fire, with no need of the warmth.

G3UltimaNotte.5.full: **{0} is the Copy.** Their vote, tonight, counts double.

G3UltimaNotte.6.easy: All the certificates show the crown. None of you has changed. You look at each other, and someone laughs with relief, too loudly. "For now," says Wil Maas.
G3UltimaNotte.6.short: Every certificate shows the crown. Someone laughs with relief, too loudly. "For now," says Wil.

G3ReduceFine.2.easy: Before the vote starts, {0} stands up, puts on a coat and goes down the stairs of the tower without looking back. Nobody tries to stop them. G3VotoCerchio.2.full: The Machine is on. The stone is on the table, warm, beside Wil's watch. Great-grandfather wrote it: *it must go back where it came from*. Now you know where it came from: from the opposite end of the thread, from the night of the two lights. You need only put it on the platform. Or there is Jaap Mol's hammer, on the workbench. With a single precise blow, it can be broken.
G3VotoCerchio.2.easy: The Machine is on. The stone is on the table, warm, next to Wil's watch. The great-grandfather wrote it: *it must go back where it came from*. Now you know where it came from: from the other end of the line, from the night of the two lights. You only need to put it on the platform. Or there is Jaap Mol's hammer on the workbench. With one exact blow, you can break the stone.
G3VotoCerchio.2.short: The Machine is on, the warm stone beside Wil's watch. *It must go back where it came from*: to the night of the two lights. Put it on the platform. Or take Jaap Mol's hammer, and break it with one precise blow.

G3VotoCerchio.4.full: YAY: you send the stone back where it came from, with the Machine.

G3VotoPietra.2.full: The Machine is silent. The stone is on the table, warm, beside Wil's watch. Two roads remain, and neither sends it back where it came from. Jaap Mol's hammer, on the workbench, with a single precise blow. Or the dyke, the bog, the place of the light, where the whole village has been waiting for it for fifty years.
G3VotoPietra.2.easy: The Machine is quiet. The stone is on the table, warm, next to Wil's watch. There are two ways left, and neither of them sends it back where it came from. Jaap Mol's hammer on the workbench, with one exact blow. Or the dyke, the bog, the place where the light was, where the whole village has waited for it for fifty years.
G3VotoPietra.2.short: The Machine is silent. Two roads remain, neither of them home for the stone: Jaap Mol's hammer, or the place of the light, where the whole village has waited fifty years.

G3VotoPietra.5.full: NAY: you take it back to the bog.

G3EsitoPietra.4.full: Take it back to the bog. (NAY)

G3VotoDormienti.2.full: The stone is in the bog, far away, under the snow that does not settle. You will not reach it tonight. But under the peat, in their hundreds, the originals sleep: Fokke, the miller's wife, Mrs Mulder, the boys on the memorial. Gerrit Tammer has left the spades from the dig at the estate, with a note: *If you want, it can be done.* Wake them all, tonight. Or let them sleep, and close the Register.
G3VotoDormienti.2.easy: The stone is in the bog, far away, under the snow that does not stay. You will not get to it tonight. But under the peat, hundreds of the real people are sleeping: Fokke, the miller's wife, Mrs Mulder, the boys on the memorial. Gerrit Tammer has left the spades from the dig at the estate, with a note: *If you want, it can be done.* You can wake them all tonight. Or you can let them sleep, and close the Register.
G3VotoDormienti.2.short: The stone is out of reach tonight. But hundreds of originals sleep under the peat. Gerrit has left his spades with a note: *If you want, it can be done.* Wake them all, or let them sleep and close the Register.

G3VotoDormienti.5.full: NAY: you stay silent, and close the Register.

G3Giornale.3.full: **A LIGHT ON THE TOWER.** The day before yesterday, at a quarter past eleven at night, a year to the day after the armistice, many citizens saw an intensely bright white light flare for an instant at the top of the tower of the estate. No noise, no smoke. The family of the estate, questioned by this paper, spoke of "scientific experiments".
G3Giornale.3.easy: **A LIGHT ON THE TOWER.** Two days ago, at a quarter past eleven at night, exactly one year after the armistice, many people saw a very bright white light for a moment at the top of the tower of the estate. There was no noise and no smoke. This newspaper asked the family of the estate about it. They said it was "scientific experiments".
G3Giornale.3.short: **A LIGHT ON THE TOWER.** On the armistice's anniversary, at a quarter past eleven at night, many saw a blinding white light flash atop the estate's tower. The family speaks of "scientific experiments".

G3Giornale.4.full: One of the heirs added, to our surprise, a statement that we report in full, leaving judgement to our readers: "Our great-grandfather's machine moves things in time. The stone from the bog comes from the future. Stop drinking that water." The editors merely observe that in Brunveen, for fifty years, nobody has fallen ill.
G3Giornale.4.easy: To our surprise, one of the heirs added something more. We print it all here, and our readers can judge: "Our great-grandfather's machine moves things in time. The stone from the bog comes from the future. Stop drinking that water." We only point out that in Brunveen nobody has been ill for fifty years.
G3Giornale.4.short: One heir added: "Our great-grandfather's machine moves things in time. The stone comes from the future. Stop drinking that water." We note only that nobody in Brunveen has been ill for fifty years.

G3Giornale.5.full: The heirs would add nothing more. Dr Maas, present at the tower, merely said that "everyone is well", in a tone that seemed to this writer anything but reassuring.
G3Giornale.5.easy: The heirs did not want to say more. Dr Maas, who was at the tower, only said that "everyone is well". To the writer of this article, her voice did not sound reassuring at all.
G3Giornale.5.short: The heirs would say no more. Dr Maas said only that "everyone is well", in a tone far from reassuring.

G3Giornale.7.full: **BRUNVEEN HAS NO NEED OF SPECTACLES.** Our village is the healthiest, the tidiest, the quietest in the province. It has no need of lights on towers nor of outlandish theories. We invite the family of the estate to remember that peace is a common good, and that the council has already offered, in the past, every help to preserve it.
G3Giornale.7.easy: **BRUNVEEN DOES NOT NEED A SHOW.** Our village is the healthiest, the tidiest and the quietest in the province. It does not need lights on towers or strange ideas. We ask the family of the estate to remember that peace belongs to everyone, and that the council has already offered every kind of help to keep it.
G3Giornale.7.short: **BRUNVEEN HAS NO NEED OF SPECTACLES.** The healthiest, quietest village in the province needs no lights on towers. Peace is a common good: the family of the estate would do well to remember it.

G3Mostra.2.full: At the Traveling Caravan, among the carts of the autumn fair, there is a canvas pavilion with a painted sign: WONDERS OF SCIENCE – TRAVELLING EXHIBITION OF THE NATURAL HISTORY MUSEUM. Inside, under the glass cases, a mammoth's tooth, a two-headed calf foetus, a piece of meteorite. And, at the back, in a case of its own, a little velvet box, open.
G3Mostra.2.easy: At the Traveling Caravan, among the carts of the autumn fair, there is a tent with a painted sign: WONDERS OF SCIENCE – TRAVELLING SHOW OF THE NATURAL HISTORY MUSEUM. Inside, in glass cases, there is a mammoth's tooth, a calf with two heads that was never born, and a piece of a meteorite. At the back, in a case by itself, there is a little velvet box, open.
G3Mostra.2.short: At the autumn fair, the city museum's travelling exhibition: a mammoth's tooth, a two-headed calf, a meteorite. At the back, alone in its case, an open velvet box.

G3Mostra.3.full: In the little box is the chip of the stone that your family sold to Professor Ostrander, many years ago. It sits in a glass of water, because "if it stays dry it gets too hot", the attendant explains. The attendant is an elderly man, serene, with cold hands. He is the same man who worked at the museum in Ostrander's day. He has not aged much.
G3Mostra.3.easy: In the little box there is the chip of the stone that your family sold to Professor Ostrander many years ago. It is in a glass of water, because "if it stays dry it gets too hot", the attendant explains. The attendant is an old, calm man with cold hands. He is the same man who worked at the museum when Ostrander was there. He has not got much older.
G3Mostra.3.short: In it, in a glass of water, lies the chip your family sold to Ostrander: "dry, it gets too hot". The attendant, calm, cold-handed, worked at the museum in Ostrander's day. He has hardly aged.

G3Mostra.6.full: There is nothing in the little box. The label says: *Stone of the light, Brunveen. Not acquired.* Beside it, in a frame, is a page from the diary of Professor Ostrander, dead for years: *I asked the family for a chip and they refused me. Bless them. The city is ill enough already.*
G3Mostra.6.easy: The little box is empty. The label says: *Stone of the light, Brunveen. Not acquired.* Next to it, in a frame, there is a page from the diary of Professor Ostrander, who died years ago: *I asked the family for a chip and they said no. Bless them. The city has enough troubles already.*
G3Mostra.6.short: The box is empty: *Stone of the light, Brunveen. Not acquired.* Beside it, a page of Ostrander's diary: *The family refused me a chip. Bless them. The city is ill enough already.*

G3Mostra.9.full: The attendant accepts the money without argument, as if he had been expecting you. He hands you the little box, with the glass, and urges you never to leave it dry. At home, the chip moves by itself to the edge of the glass, on the side facing the tower. When you take it into the tower, beside the ring, it stops moving.
G3Mostra.9.easy: The attendant takes the money without arguing, as if he was waiting for you. He gives you the little box with the glass, and tells you never to let it get dry. At home the chip moves by itself to the edge of the glass, on the side towards the tower. When you take it into the tower, next to the ring, it stops moving.
G3Mostra.9.short: The attendant sells it as if he expected you. At home the chip creeps to the side of the glass facing the tower. Beside the ring, it lies still.

G3Mostra.10.full: Pay $3. Gain 1 Engineering Knowledge and 1 Occult Knowledge.

G3Mostra.11.full: You break the case with your elbow. The water spills, and the chip, on the wooden floor of the pavilion, begins to smoke. In a few seconds it burns a hole in the floor and disappears into the earth. The attendant does not shout. He looks at the hole, then at you, with clear, patient eyes. "It will go home," he says. "They all go home."
G3Mostra.11.easy: You break the glass with your elbow. The water spills, and on the wooden floor of the tent the chip starts to smoke. In a few seconds it burns a hole in the floor and disappears into the ground. The attendant does not shout. He looks at the hole, then at you, with pale, patient eyes. "It will go home," he says. "They all go home."
G3Mostra.11.short: You smash the case. Out of the water the chip smokes, burns through the floor and vanishes into the earth. The attendant looks at you patiently. "It will go home. They all go home."

G3Mostra.13.full: The diary is open at another page, further on, written in a trembling hand: *I brought a phial of Brunveen water to the museum, for analysis. The attendant drank a sip of it, for a bet. The attendant is cured. The attendant's wife is cured. We never analysed it: we finished it, and ordered more. I have sold my beer and drink water. I have never been so serene. The only thing that frightens me is the thought that soon it will no longer frighten me.*
G3Mostra.13.easy: The diary is open at another page, later on, written by a shaking hand: *I brought a little bottle of Brunveen water to the museum, to study it. The attendant drank a sip, for a bet. The attendant got better. The attendant's wife got better. We never studied it: we drank it all and ordered more. I have sold my beer and I drink water. I have never felt so calm. The only thing that frightens me is the idea that soon it will not frighten me any more.*
G3Mostra.13.short: A later page, in a shaking hand: *I brought Brunveen water to the museum. The attendant drank some for a bet, and was cured. We never analysed it: we drank it and ordered more. I have never been so serene. I fear only that soon I will not fear it.*

G3Mostra.15.full: You leave the pavilion. Outside, the fair is full of people laughing. You notice, counting them, that they all laugh at the same moment.
G3Mostra.15.easy: You leave the tent. Outside, the fair is full of people who are laughing. You count them, and you notice that they all laugh at the same moment.
G3Mostra.15.short: Outside, the fair is full of laughter. Counting, you notice they all laugh at the same moment.

G3Carovana.2.full: At the Traveling Caravan, during the curfew, there is a single cart, painted blue, with faded gold letters: STAR WATER – FROM BRUNVEEN. The seller is a little man without a top hat, with the face of fifty years ago: identical. He is selling the last green glass phials. He says it is his last fair. His hands are cracking, like Fokke's.
G3Carovana.2.easy: At the Traveling Caravan, during the curfew, there is only one cart. It is painted blue, with old gold letters: STAR WATER – FROM BRUNVEEN. The seller is a small man with no top hat. His face is the same as fifty years ago, exactly the same. He is selling the last little bottles of green glass. He says it is his last fair. His hands are cracking, like Fokke's.
G3Carovana.2.short: One blue cart remains: STAR WATER – FROM BRUNVEEN. The seller has the very face of fifty years ago. It is his last fair, he says. His hands are cracking, like Fokke's.

G3Carovana.3.full: When he sees you he recognises you, or recognises your family. "You followed me, that night," he says. "I was in the water up to my knees. You saw me go in. You did not see me come out, though: the one who came out was already me."
G3Carovana.3.easy: When he sees you, he knows you, or he knows your family. "You followed me that night," he says. "I was in the water up to my knees. You saw me go in. But you did not see me come out: the one who came out was already me."
G3Carovana.3.short: He knows your family. "You followed me that night. You saw me go into the water. But the one who came out was already me."

G3Carovana.4.full: When he sees you he recognises you, or recognises your family. "Mayor Wessel told me who had reported me," he says, kindly. "I was grateful to him. That evening, at the inn, I left behind everything I no longer needed."
G3Carovana.4.easy: When he sees you, he knows you, or he knows your family. "Mayor Wessel told me who reported me," he says kindly. "I was grateful to him. That evening, at the inn, I left behind everything I did not need any more."
G3Carovana.4.short: He knows your family. "Mayor Wessel told me who reported me. I was grateful. At the inn I left behind everything I no longer needed."

G3Carovana.7.full: You ask him where he really comes from.

G3Carovana.8.full: The phial is cold as ice. The seller thanks you, shuts up the cart and goes off towards the dyke, on foot, leaving the horse tethered. The next morning, on the road, there is a heap of peat and a hand-drawn label: a star falling on a meadow.
G3Carovana.8.easy: The little bottle is as cold as ice. The seller thanks you, closes his cart and walks away towards the dyke, leaving his horse tied up. The next morning, on the road, there is a pile of peat and a label drawn by hand: a star falling on a field.
G3Carovana.8.short: The phial is ice cold. The seller walks off towards the dyke, leaving his horse. Next morning on the road: a heap of peat, and a label with a falling star.

G3Carovana.10.full: The seller thinks about it, frowning. He comes from here, he says. Always has. Before, he was from another village, with another name, another wife, a top hat. Then he went into the water and woke up from here. "We are all from here," he says. "You too, by now. You will see."
G3Carovana.10.easy: The seller thinks, with a frown. He says he comes from here. He always has. Before, he was from another village, with another name, another wife and a top hat. Then he went into the water and woke up belonging here. "We are all from here," he says. "You too, now. You will see."
G3Carovana.10.short: He comes from here, he says, frowning. Before, he had another village, another name, a top hat. Then he went into the water. "We are all from here. You too, by now. You will see."

G3Nozze.2.full: In the church the wedding is being celebrated of Jan Hoek, one of the three boys from the memorial, and Marieke, the girl who waited four years for him. Jan came back in June, healthy, smiling, without papers. Marieke stops you on the church steps, before the ceremony, her veil in her hand. She received the ministry telegram in 1917: *missing*. Then Jan came back. He is kind, he is patient, he has no nightmares. He does not remember the song he used to sing to her under her window. He asks her to marry him every day, with the same words.
G3Nozze.2.easy: In the church Jan Hoek, one of the three boys from the memorial, is marrying Marieke, the girl who waited four years for him. Jan came back in June, healthy and smiling, without papers. Before the ceremony Marieke stops you on the church steps, with her veil in her hand. In 1917 she got the telegram from the ministry: *missing*. Then Jan came back. He is kind and patient, and he has no bad dreams. He does not remember the song he used to sing to her under her window. Every day he asks her to marry him, with the same words.
G3Nozze.2.short: Jan Hoek, back from Flanders without papers, is marrying Marieke. On the church steps she tells you: he is kind, patient, without nightmares. He has forgotten the song he sang under her window. He proposes every day, in the same words.

G3Nozze.3.full: "You at the estate know things," she says. "Should I marry him?"

G3Nozze.5.full: You tell her to marry him: he came back, and he is good.

G3Nozze.7.full: You ask her to have him sing the song, at the altar.

G3Nozze.8.full: Marieke lowers her veil and goes into the church. The wedding is perfect: nobody cries, nobody laughs, nobody gets a response wrong. On the way out, under the shower of rice, Jan squeezes his bride's hand with his cold hand, and she smiles. A month later you run into her at the market: serene, calm, hands in her pockets.
G3Nozze.8.easy: Marieke pulls down her veil and goes into the church. The wedding is perfect: nobody cries, nobody laughs, nobody says the wrong words. Outside, under the rice, Jan holds his wife's hand with his cold hand, and she smiles. A month later you see her at the market. She is calm and peaceful, with her hands in her pockets.
G3Nozze.8.short: Marieke lowers her veil and goes in. A perfect wedding. A month later you see her at the market: serene, hands in her pockets.

G3Nozze.10.full: Marieke looks at you for a long time, then takes off her veil and goes home. The wedding is postponed "for reasons of the bride's health". Jan takes no offence. He brings her flowers every morning, punctually, and waits. He has all the time he wants.
G3Nozze.10.easy: Marieke looks at you for a long time. Then she takes off her veil and goes home. The wedding is moved to a later date "because the bride is not well". Jan is not offended. Every morning, always on time, he brings her flowers, and he waits. He has all the time he wants.
G3Nozze.10.short: Marieke takes off her veil and goes home. The wedding is postponed. Jan brings her flowers every morning, and waits. He has all the time in the world.

G3Nozze.12.full: At the altar, in front of everyone, Marieke asks Jan to sing her the window song. Jan smiles, kindly, and sings. Some ordinary song, perfectly in tune, that nobody has ever heard. Marieke listens to the end. Then she says no, in front of the pastor, and runs out of the church with her veil in her hand. Jan stays at the altar, serene, and thanks everyone for coming.
G3Nozze.12.easy: At the altar, in front of everyone, Marieke asks Jan to sing her the song from the window. Jan smiles kindly and sings. It is just a song, perfectly in tune, that nobody has ever heard. Marieke listens until the end. Then she says no, in front of the pastor, and runs out of the church with her veil in her hand. Jan stays at the altar, calm, and thanks everyone for coming.
G3Nozze.12.short: At the altar Marieke asks for the window song. Jan sings, perfectly, a song nobody has ever heard. She says no and runs out. Jan stays, serene, and thanks everyone for coming.

G3Pastore.2.full: In church, at the Thursday service, the new pastor is preaching, who arrived after old Kalf's death: a young man, fair-haired, with a warm, calm voice. His sermons are short, beautiful, without threats. They speak of peace, of quiet, of the sleep of the just. The church is full. Trijntje Kalf, at the organ, plays her usual wrong note, and looks at him with hatred. After the service the pastor approaches you on the church steps. He has heard about the light on the tower. He would like to bless the Machine.
G3Pastore.2.easy: At the Thursday service the new pastor is preaching. He came after old Kalf died. He is a young man with fair hair and a warm, calm voice. His sermons are short and beautiful, with no threats. They talk about peace, about quiet, about the sleep of good people. The church is full. At the organ Trijntje Kalf plays her usual wrong note, and looks at him with hate. After the service the pastor comes up to you on the church steps. He has heard about the light on the tower. He would like to bless the Machine.
G3Pastore.2.short: The fair-haired new pastor preaches peace, quiet and the sleep of the just to a full church. Trijntje plays her wrong note and glares at him. Afterwards he asks to bless the Machine.

G3Pastore.5.full: You ask him where he comes from.

G3Pastore.6.full: The pastor climbs the tower with holy water and a book. Before the brass ring he recites a prayer you do not know, long, sweet, repetitive. Then he sprinkles the ring. The holy water, when it touches the black glass, sizzles, as on a stove. The pastor smiles, satisfied, and leaves without turning round.
G3Pastore.6.easy: The pastor climbs the tower with holy water and a book. In front of the brass ring he says a prayer you do not know. It is long and sweet, and it repeats itself. Then he throws drops of water on the ring. When the holy water touches the black glass, it hisses, like water on a hot stove. The pastor smiles, pleased, and leaves without looking back.
G3Pastore.6.short: Before the ring the pastor recites a long, sweet prayer you do not know. The holy water sizzles on the black glass like a stove. He smiles, satisfied, and leaves.

G3Pastore.8.full: The pastor laughs: from the seminary in the city, of course. But when you ask him the name of the seminary he hesitates, for an instant only, and then says it. Trijntje, who has been listening behind the door, takes you aside: she wrote to that seminary. They replied that the pastor drowned, two years ago, skating on a bog near Brunveen.
G3Pastore.8.easy: The pastor laughs: from the seminary in the city, of course. But when you ask the name of the seminary, he stops for just a moment before he says it. Trijntje was listening behind the door, and she takes you to one side. She wrote to that seminary. They answered that the pastor drowned two years ago, while he was skating on a bog near Brunveen.
G3Pastore.8.short: From the city seminary, he laughs, after the briefest pause over its name. Trijntje takes you aside: she wrote to them. The pastor drowned two years ago, skating on a bog near Brunveen.

Epilogo.2.full: Trijntje Kalf played the organ of the Brunveen church until she was eighty-five, every Sunday, and every Sunday she played one wrong note, just one, loudly, halfway through the hymn. When she died, at the funeral, the new organist played everything perfectly. At the back of the church, someone stood up and left.
Epilogo.2.easy: Trijntje Kalf played the organ in the Brunveen church every Sunday until she was eighty-five. Every Sunday, in the middle of the hymn, she played one wrong note, only one, loudly. When she died, the new organist played everything perfectly at her funeral. At the back of the church, someone stood up and walked out.
Epilogo.2.short: Trijntje Kalf played one loud wrong note every Sunday until she was eighty-five. At her funeral the new organist played perfectly. At the back, someone stood up and left.

Epilogo.3.full: Miss Neeltje Borg dreamed until the last night of her life. She wrote the last dream in her notebook, in the morning, with a trembling hand: *the bog was dry, and there were children playing*. Then she went back to bed, and did not wake again. Her hands were warm.
Epilogo.3.easy: Miss Neeltje Borg had dreams until the last night of her life. In the morning she wrote her last dream in her notebook, with a shaking hand: *the bog was dry, and there were children playing*. Then she went back to bed and never woke up. Her hands were warm.
Epilogo.3.short: Miss Borg dreamed to the end. Her last dream, written with a trembling hand: *the bog was dry, and children were playing*. She went back to bed and did not wake. Her hands were warm.

Epilogo.4.full: Gerrit Tammer died in 1922, in the house on the dyke, with his son Hendrik beside him. On his bedside table he kept two photographs: his father young, spade on his shoulder, and his father old, behind the black peat stall. He never said which of the two he had loved more.
Epilogo.4.easy: Gerrit Tammer died in 1922 in the house on the dyke, with his son Hendrik next to him. On his bedside table there were two photographs: his father when young, with a spade on his shoulder, and his father when old, behind the black peat stall. He never said which one he loved more.
Epilogo.4.short: Gerrit Tammer died in 1922 beside two photographs: his father young with his spade, and his father old at the peat stall. He never said which he loved more.

Epilogo.5.full: Gerrit Tammer died in 1922, in the house on the dyke, with his son Hendrik beside him. He had his father for two years: a forty-year-old peat-cutter, a drunkard and a blasphemer, who called him "old man" and stole his tobacco. It was enough for him.
Epilogo.5.easy: Gerrit Tammer died in 1922 in the house on the dyke, with his son Hendrik next to him. He had his father for two years: a peat-cutter of forty who drank and swore, called him "old man" and stole his tobacco. That was enough for him.
Epilogo.5.short: Gerrit Tammer died in 1922. He had two years with his real father, a forty-year-old drunk who called him "old man" and stole his tobacco. It was enough.

Epilogo.6.full: Gerrit Tammer died in 1922, in the house on the dyke, with his son Hendrik beside him. After the fire he never went back to the Park. He used to say that his father, at least, had died sleeping.
Epilogo.6.easy: Gerrit Tammer died in 1922 in the house on the dyke, with his son Hendrik next to him. After the fire he never went back to the Park. He said that at least his father died in his sleep.
Epilogo.6.short: Gerrit Tammer died in 1922. After the fire he never went back to the Park. His father, he said, at least died sleeping.

Epilogo.7.full: Gerrit Tammer died in 1922, in the house on the dyke, with his son Hendrik beside him. Every Sunday, until the last, he took flowers to the dig in the Park, where his father still sleeps, under two metres of peat, with his hands folded and the burns that do not heal.
Epilogo.7.easy: Gerrit Tammer died in 1922 in the house on the dyke, with his son Hendrik next to him. Every Sunday, until the last one, he took flowers to the dig in the Park. His father is still sleeping there, under two metres of peat, with his hands together and the burns that never heal.
Epilogo.7.short: Gerrit Tammer died in 1922. Every Sunday he brought flowers to the dig, where his father still sleeps, hands folded, the burns unhealed.

Epilogo.8.full: The Watch's lantern, the one Pastor Kalf lit first and {0} carried for years, hangs in the tower, beside the brass ring. Someone lights it every evening.
Epilogo.8.easy: The lantern of the Watch, the one Pastor Kalf lit first and {0} carried for years, hangs in the tower, next to the brass ring. Every evening someone lights it.
Epilogo.8.short: The Watch's lantern, Pastor Kalf's and then {0}'s, hangs by the ring. Someone lights it every evening.

Epilogo.9.full: The Tammer spade, the one {0} took from Gerrit's hands at the cemetery, hangs beside the lantern, its handle worn by three generations of warm hands.

Epilogo.9.short: Beside it hangs the Tammer spade {0} took from Gerrit, worn by three generations of warm hands.

Epilogo.10.full: The council's silver medal is still in the entrance hall of the estate. It has never tarnished.
Epilogo.10.easy: The council's silver medal is still in the hall of the estate. It has never gone dark.
Epilogo.10.short: The council's silver medal still hangs in the hall. It has never tarnished.

Epilogo.11.full: Piet Brink, the editor of the Conservative Report, one winter evening left the paper without his coat and took the dyke road. They saw him go into the bog at the place where he had fallen as a boy, calling for his mother. He did not come out again. The next morning, on the bank, there was a boy of fifteen, wet, barefoot, asking for the widow Brink.
Epilogo.11.easy: One winter evening Piet Brink, the editor of the Conservative Report, left the newspaper office without his coat and walked along the dyke. People saw him walk into the bog at the place where he fell as a boy, calling for his mother. He never came out. Epilogo.11.short: One winter evening Piet Brink walked coatless into the bog where he fell as a boy, calling his mother. Next morning, on the bank, a wet, barefoot boy of fifteen was asking for the widow Brink.

Epilogo.12.full: The descendants of Bruin, Fokke Tammer's dog, still live at the estate: black, big, patient. They bark only at certain people. Nobody ever trained them to.
Epilogo.12.easy: The great-grandchildren of Bruin, Fokke Tammer's dog, still live at the estate. They are black, big and patient. They only bark at some people. Nobody ever taught them to do it.
Epilogo.12.short: Bruin's descendants still live at the estate. They bark only at certain people. Nobody taught them.

Epilogo.13.full: The light bulb above the brass ring, the light company's, has never burnt out. The tower's meter, ever since, has run backwards.
Epilogo.13.easy: The light bulb above the brass ring, from the electric company, has never burnt out. Since then the tower's electricity meter has turned backwards.
Epilogo.13.short: The bulb above the ring has never burnt out. The tower's meter runs backwards.

Epilogo.14.full: Wil Maas lived to ninety and never married. To the last, every evening, before sleeping, she took her grandmother's watch out of her pocket, stopped at a quarter past eleven, and wondered where the stone had come from, if nobody had sent it back. Then she put it away, took her temperature, and wrote it down. Thirty-six point eight, always.
Epilogo.14.easy: Wil Maas lived until she was ninety, and she never married. Until the end, every evening before she slept, she took her grandmother's watch out of her pocket. It was stopped at a quarter past eleven. She wondered where the stone came from, if nobody sent it back. Then she put the watch away, took her temperature and wrote it down. Thirty-six point eight, always.
Epilogo.14.short: Wil Maas lived to ninety, unmarried. Each night she looked at Hester's watch and wondered where the stone had come from, if nobody sent it back. Then she took her temperature. Thirty-six point eight, always.

Epilogo.15.easy: Wil Maas lived until she was ninety, and she never married. Until the end, every evening before she slept, she took her temperature and wrote it down. Thirty-six point eight, always.
