Epilogo.16.full: Siebe the gravedigger's notebook, the one with the faces seen in the water, ended up in the tower with the Register, or else in the stove of his little house. Either way, nobody read it again. The names, though, are still down there.
Epilogo.16.easy: Siebe the gravedigger's notebook, with the faces he saw in the water, went into the tower with the Register, or into the stove of his little house. Either way, nobody read it again. But the names are still down there.
Epilogo.16.short: Siebe's notebook went into the tower or into the stove. Nobody read it again. The names are still down there.

Epilogo.17.full: Marieke, the girl who said no at the altar, left for the city in 1920 and became an operetta singer. She sang out of tune, the critics say, in a moving way.
Epilogo.17.easy: Marieke, the girl who said no at the altar, went to the city in 1920 and became an operetta singer. The critics say she sang out of tune in a beautiful way.
Epilogo.17.short: Marieke, who said no at the altar, became an operetta singer. She sang out of tune, the critics say, movingly.

Epilogo.18.full: Jan Hoek, her fiancé back from Flanders, never wrote to her: on the night of the stone, in his room, there remained only a heap of peat and a pen.
Epilogo.18.easy: Jan Hoek, her fiancé back from Flanders, never wrote to her. On the night of the stone, in his room, there was only a pile of peat and a pen.
Epilogo.18.short: Jan Hoek never wrote to her: on the night of the stone, his room held only peat and a pen.

Epilogo.19.full: Jan Hoek, her fiancé back from Flanders, wrote to her every week, for fifty years, the same letter.
Epilogo.19.easy: Jan Hoek, her fiancé who came back from Flanders, wrote her the same letter every week for fifty years.
Epilogo.19.short: Jan Hoek wrote her the same letter every week for fifty years.

Epilogo.20.full: Jan and Marieke Hoek had three children, healthy, serene, excellent at school. None of the three, as a child, ever had a nightmare.
Epilogo.20.easy: Jan and Marieke Hoek had three children. They were healthy, calm and very good at school. None of the three ever had a bad dream as a child.
Epilogo.20.short: Jan and Marieke Hoek had three healthy, serene children. None of them ever had a nightmare.

Epilogo.21.full: Harm Visser, the miller, died in Rotterdam in 1901, poor, drunk and free. Every Christmas he sent a postcard to the estate, always the same: *Thank you for the ticket. We quarrel beautifully here.*
Epilogo.21.easy: Harm Visser, the miller, died in Rotterdam in 1901, poor, drunk and free. Every Christmas he sent a postcard to the estate, always with the same words: *Thank you for the ticket. Here we argue beautifully.*
Epilogo.21.short: Harm Visser died in Rotterdam in 1901, poor, drunk and free. Every Christmas: *Thank you for the ticket. We quarrel beautifully here.*

Epilogo.22.full: The iron chains that Lambert the master builder put round the tower are still there. They rust only on the side facing the bog.
Epilogo.22.easy: The iron chains that Lambert the master builder put around the tower are still there. They only rust on the side that faces the bog.
Epilogo.22.short: Lambert's chains still circle the tower. They rust only on the bog side.

Epilogo.23.full: The Van Dam boy, the one who got everything wrong, became the most disorderly mechanic in the province, and the best loved. When someone asked him how he managed to make so many mistakes, he answered that making mistakes was the only way he knew of being sure he was himself.
Epilogo.23.easy: The Van Dam boy, the one who did everything wrong, became the messiest mechanic in the province, and the most loved. When people asked him how he could make so many mistakes, he said that mistakes were the only way he knew to be sure he was still himself.
Epilogo.23.short: Kees Van Dam became the province's messiest, best-loved mechanic. Mistakes, he said, were the only way he knew to be sure he was himself.

FinaleFuoco.3.full: We did not vote. While we were in the tower, down in the village the Watch had already decided for everyone. Hendrik Tammer and twenty or so men, the ones who had never drunk, went to the dyke with the light company's cans of paraffin and set fire to the bog in ten different places, all together, at three in the morning.
FinaleFuoco.3.easy: We did not vote. While we were in the tower, down in the village the Watch had already decided for everyone. Hendrik Tammer and about twenty men, the ones who never drank the water, went to the dyke with cans of paraffin from the electric company. At three in the morning they set fire to the bog in ten different places, all at the same time.
FinaleFuoco.3.short: We never voted. The Watch decided for everyone: at three in the morning Hendrik Tammer and twenty men who had never drunk set the bog alight in ten places at once.

FinaleFuoco.4.full: Peat burns in a way one does not forget. It makes no tall flames: it smokes, it smoulders, it eats the earth from beneath, metres deep, with nothing showing on the surface but a grey veil and a sweetish smell. It cannot be put out. It cannot be stopped. The firemen from the city came, looked, and left again.
FinaleFuoco.4.easy: Peat burns in a way you never forget. There are no high flames. It smokes and burns slowly, and it eats the ground from below, many metres deep. On top you see only a grey cloud and you smell something sweet. You cannot put it out. You cannot stop it. The firemen from the city came, looked and went away.
FinaleFuoco.4.short: Peat burns unforgettably: no flames, only smoke and a sweet smell, while it eats the earth from below. It cannot be stopped. The city firemen came, looked, and left.

FinaleFuoco.5.full: The Brunveen bog burned underground for seven years. With everything that was in it.
FinaleFuoco.5.easy: The Brunveen bog burned under the ground for seven years. With everything that was inside it.
FinaleFuoco.5.short: The bog burned underground for seven years. With everything in it.

FinaleFuoco.6.full: The Neighbours did not run. They went to the dyke, that first morning, all together, in silence, and sat on the bank to watch the smoke, the way one keeps vigil over a relative. Many stayed there until they began to dry and crack, one by one, like Fokke. The others went back to the village, as kind as before. They never said a word to those who had lit the fire. They only, for seven years, wished them good morning.
FinaleFuoco.6.easy: The Neighbours did not run away. On the first morning they all went to the dyke together, in silence, and sat on the bank to watch the smoke, like people sitting with a dying relative. Many of them stayed there until they started to dry and crack, one by one, like Fokke. The others went back to the village, as kind as before. They never said a word to the people who lit the fire. For seven years they only said good morning to them.
FinaleFuoco.6.short: The Neighbours did not run. They sat on the dyke watching the smoke like mourners. Many stayed until they dried and cracked, like Fokke. The rest went home, kind as ever, and for seven years wished the fire-setters good morning.

FinaleFuoco.7.full: I still measure temperatures. But when, at night, the wind carries the smell of burning peat into the village, I cannot sleep. I think of those who were sleeping down there, and who did not wake in time.
FinaleFuoco.7.easy: I still measure temperatures. But at night, when the wind brings the smell of burning peat into the village, I cannot sleep. I think of the people who were sleeping down there, and who did not wake up in time.
FinaleFuoco.7.short: I still measure temperatures. But when the wind brings the smell of burning peat, I cannot sleep. I think of those sleeping down there, who did not wake in time.

FinaleFuoco.8.full: On the night of the fire {0} did not go down to the village. They spent the night in the tower, at the window, watching the smoke, until dawn, with cold hands resting on the glass. The next morning they had breakfast with us, as always, and asked for the salt. We have never spoken of that night again.
FinaleFuoco.8.easy: On the night of the fire {0} did not go down to the village. They stayed in the tower all night, at the window, watching the smoke until dawn, with cold hands on the glass. The next morning they had breakfast with us, as always, and asked for the salt. We have never talked about that night again.
FinaleFuoco.8.short: On the night of the fire {0} watched the smoke from the tower until dawn, cold hands on the glass. At breakfast they asked for the salt. We have never spoken of that night.

FinaleFuoco.9.full: Old Fokke, the one woken from the peat, had been dead for three years already. Hendrik says he would have been glad. He has never said it in front of his father.
FinaleFuoco.9.easy: Old Fokke, the one they woke from the peat, had already been dead for three years. Hendrik says he would have been happy about it. He has never said so in front of his father.
FinaleFuoco.9.short: Old Fokke, woken from the peat, had died three years before. He would have been glad, says Hendrik. Never in front of his father.

FinaleQuieto.3.full: There was no need to vote. When we came down from the tower, at dawn, the village was awake, and waiting for us under the windows of the estate: the whole village, in silence, hands in their pockets. They wanted nothing. They only wanted us to know.
FinaleQuieto.3.easy: We did not need to vote. When we came down from the tower at dawn, the village was awake. The whole village was waiting for us under the windows of the estate, in silence, with their hands in their pockets. They did not want anything. They only wanted us to know.
FinaleQuieto.3.short: No vote was needed. At dawn the whole village stood silent under the estate's windows, hands in pockets. They wanted nothing. Only for us to know.

FinaleQuieto.4.full: I have redone the sums of the Register. In Brunveen there are few of us left: the family of the estate, Trijntje Kalf, Miss Borg, Hendrik Tammer, me, and a handful of stubborn old folk who drink only gin. The others, all the others, are them. The mayor, the councillors, the teachers, the schoolchildren, the soldiers from the memorial. The village is theirs, and has been for longer than we want to admit. We are the last.
FinaleQuieto.4.easy: I have done the sums of the Register again. There are only a few of us left in Brunveen: the family of the estate, Trijntje Kalf, Miss Borg, Hendrik Tammer, me, and a few stubborn old people who only drink gin. All the others are them. The mayor, the councillors, the teachers, the schoolchildren, the soldiers from the memorial. The village belongs to them, and it has for longer than we want to say. We are the last ones.
FinaleQuieto.4.short: I have redone the sums. We are few: the estate, Trijntje, Miss Borg, Hendrik, me, and a few old gin-drinkers. Everyone else is them, and has been for longer than we admit. We are the last.

FinaleQuieto.5.full: They do us no harm. They never have. They bring us fruit, mend our tiles, greet us by name, and wait. They have time: they have always had more of it than us. One at a time, partly from tiredness, partly from loneliness, partly because sleep, in the end, is sweet, we too will drink.
FinaleQuieto.5.easy: They do not hurt us. They never have. They bring us fruit, repair our roofs, say hello to us by name, and wait. They have time: they always had more time than us. One by one, because we are tired, because we are lonely, because in the end sleep is sweet, we will drink too.
FinaleQuieto.5.short: They do us no harm. They bring fruit, mend our roofs, and wait. They have time. One by one, from tiredness, from loneliness, because sleep is sweet, we too will drink.

FinaleQuieto.6.full: This morning, on waking, I took my temperature, as I do every day. Thirty-five point nine. I put the thermometer back in its case and wrote the number here, without comment. My father measured. My grandmother counted. I, from today, wait.
FinaleQuieto.6.easy: This morning, when I woke up, I took my temperature as I do every day. Thirty-five point nine. I put the thermometer back in its box and wrote the number here, with no comment. My father measured. My grandmother counted. From today, I wait.
FinaleQuieto.6.short: This morning: thirty-five point nine. I wrote it here without comment. My father measured. My grandmother counted. From today, I wait.

FinaleQuieto.7.full: At the estate, {0} treats us with infinite gentleness. They bring breakfast in bed, mend the shutters, read to us in the evening, when we cannot sleep. They have never asked us to drink. They know there is no need: one has only to wait.
FinaleQuieto.7.easy: At the estate, {0} is endlessly gentle with us. They bring us breakfast in bed, repair the shutters, and read to us in the evening when we cannot sleep. They have never asked us to drink. They know they do not need to: they only have to wait.
FinaleQuieto.7.short: At the estate {0} is endlessly gentle: breakfast in bed, mended shutters, reading to us at night. They never ask us to drink. They need only wait.

FinaleQuieto.8.full: The council's medal, in the entrance hall, shines more than ever. The mayor comes to polish it in person, once a month, and each time stays to dinner.
FinaleQuieto.8.easy: The council's medal, in the entrance hall, shines more than ever. The mayor comes to polish it himself once a month, and every time he stays for dinner.
FinaleQuieto.8.short: The council's medal shines as never before. The mayor polishes it himself each month, and stays to dinner.

FinaleReduce.3.full: We stayed at the tower window until dawn, watching the bog. The snow, at the place of the light, still would not settle. Towards seven the water moved. Out of the water came, slowly, knee-deep, a person we knew: {0}, the real person, the one who had been sleeping under the peat since the night of the party. White skin, purple lips, chattering teeth.
FinaleReduce.3.easy: We stayed at the window of the tower until dawn, watching the bog. At the place where the light was, the snow still did not stay. At about seven the water moved. Slowly, with water up to the knees, a person we knew walked out of it: {0}, the real one, who had been sleeping under the peat since the night of the party. White skin, purple lips, teeth chattering.
FinaleReduce.3.short: At dawn, from the tower, we watched the water move at the place of the light. Out of it, knee-deep, came {0}: the real one, asleep under the peat since the party. White, purple-lipped, teeth chattering.

FinaleReduce.4.full: We took {0} home, in blankets, near the fire. I took the temperature every hour: thirty-four. Then thirty-five. Then, at noon, thirty-six point eight. Then the tears came, for no reason.
FinaleReduce.4.easy: We took {0} home in blankets and sat by the fire. I took the temperature every hour: thirty-four. Then thirty-five. Then, at midday, thirty-six point eight. Then the tears came, without a reason.
FinaleReduce.4.short: By the fire, wrapped in blankets: thirty-four, thirty-five, and at noon thirty-six point eight. Then {0} wept, for no reason.

FinaleReduce.5.full: Of the last weeks nothing remains: the party, the days at home, the evenings with the family, the test. All that remains is a very long dream, in which someone with the same face did everything better. It was not unpleasant, they say. Down there there was only a great tiredness.
FinaleReduce.5.easy: Nothing is left of the last weeks: the party, the days at home, the evenings with the family, the test. Only a very long dream is left, where someone with the same face did everything better. It was not unpleasant, they say. Down there, there was only a great tiredness.
FinaleReduce.5.short: The last weeks are gone. Only a long dream remains, where someone with the same face did everything better. Not unpleasant, they say. Just a great tiredness.

FinaleReduce.6.full: The village came to the estate the next day, in silence, with flowers. Not for the one who had come back: for the other. They left the flowers on the dyke, at the place of the light, and went home.
FinaleReduce.6.easy: The next day the village came to the estate in silence, with flowers. Not for the person who came back, but for the other one. They left the flowers on the dyke, at the place where the light was, and went home.
FinaleReduce.6.short: Next day the village came with flowers. Not for the one who returned: for the other. They left them at the place of the light.

FinaleReduce.7.full: The other, down there, is sleeping now. It has taken the place of the one it gave back. The sum, at least this one, adds up.
FinaleReduce.7.easy: The other one, down there, is sleeping now. It has taken the place of the person it gave back. At least this sum adds up.
FinaleReduce.7.short: The other sleeps down there now, in the place of the one it gave back. This sum, at least, adds up.

FinaleReduce.8.full: The stone has stayed at the estate, in its felt box, warm. Nobody has had the courage to decide what to do with it, since. Every so often, at night, the one who came back from the bog goes down to the laboratory and rests a hand on it, for a long time. They say that is how they remember the dream.
FinaleReduce.8.easy: The stone is still at the estate, warm, in its felt box. Since then nobody has been brave enough to decide what to do with it. Sometimes, at night, the person who came back from the bog goes down to the laboratory and puts a hand on it for a long time. They say that this is how they remember the dream.
FinaleReduce.8.short: The stone stays warm in its box. Nobody dares decide its fate. Some nights the one who returned rests a hand on it for a long time, to remember the dream.

FinaleReduce.9.full: The stone has stayed in the bog, at the place of the light. The one who came back goes there every Sunday, at dawn, and stands on the dyke watching the water. They say they are not homesick. They say they only want to remember what it was like to be at peace.
FinaleReduce.9.easy: The stone is still in the bog, at the place where the light was. Every Sunday at dawn, the person who came back goes there and stands on the dyke, looking at the water. They say they do not miss it. They say they only want to remember how it felt to be at peace.
FinaleReduce.9.short: The stone stays in the bog. Every Sunday at dawn the one who returned stands on the dyke watching the water, not homesick, they say: only remembering peace.

FinaleSpezzata.3.full: Jaap Mol's hammer passed from hand to hand, and in the end someone raised it. A single blow, precise, like Jaap's. The stone did not split: it opened, like a fruit, and inside it was empty. A smell of bog filled the room, then nothing. It was cold, for the first time.
FinaleSpezzata.3.easy: Jaap Mol's hammer went from hand to hand, and in the end someone lifted it. One exact blow, like Jaap's. The stone did not break into pieces: it opened like a fruit, and it was empty inside. The room filled with the smell of the bog, and then there was nothing. For the first time, the stone was cold.
FinaleSpezzata.3.short: One precise blow of Jaap Mol's hammer. The stone opened like a fruit, empty inside. A smell of bog, then nothing. For the first time, it was cold.

FinaleSpezzata.4.full: At dawn I went down to the village with my bag. It was no use. In every house, in the beds, on the chairs, behind the shop counters, there were heaps of black, wet peat, with clothes in them, spectacles, false teeth, wedding rings. Mayor Bram Wessel, at the Town Hall, sitting at his desk. The bank cashier. The librarian. The three boys from the memorial. All those who had drunk, all those who had come back from the bog a little different, those of fifty years ago and those of yesterday.
FinaleSpezzata.4.easy: At dawn I went down to the village with my doctor's bag. It was no use. In every house, in the beds, on the chairs, behind the shop counters, there were piles of black, wet peat, with clothes, glasses, false teeth and wedding rings inside. Mayor Bram Wessel at his desk in the Town Hall. The bank cashier. The librarian. The three boys from the memorial. Everyone who had drunk, everyone who had come back from the bog a little different, from fifty years ago or from yesterday.
FinaleSpezzata.4.short: At dawn my doctor's bag was useless. In beds, on chairs, behind counters: heaps of wet black peat, with clothes, spectacles, wedding rings. The mayor at his desk. The cashier. The librarian. The three boys. All who had drunk, all who had come back changed.

FinaleSpezzata.5.full: And at the estate, in {0}'s room, on the pillow, a heap of peat in the shape of a sleeping head.
FinaleSpezzata.5.easy: And at the estate, in {0}'s room, on the pillow, there was a pile of peat shaped like a sleeping head.
FinaleSpezzata.5.short: And in {0}'s room, on the pillow, peat in the shape of a sleeping head.

FinaleSpezzata.6.full: Brunveen is a village of old people, small children and empty houses. I have counted the living: one hundred and twenty. There were nine hundred. The council no longer exists, the school is closed, the bank too. At the market, once again, they quarrel over the price of herring. At the inn they sing out of tune. Last night there was a brawl. I patched up two broken noses and laughed the whole time.
FinaleSpezzata.6.easy: Brunveen is a village of old people, small children and empty houses. I have counted the living: one hundred and twenty. Before there were nine hundred. There is no council now. The school is closed, and so is the bank. At the market people argue again about the price of herring. At the inn they sing out of tune. Last night there was a fight. I fixed two broken noses, and I laughed the whole time.
FinaleSpezzata.6.short: One hundred and twenty living, out of nine hundred. No council, no school, no bank. At the market they quarrel over herring again; at the inn they sing out of tune. Last night I set two broken noses, laughing all the while.

FinaleSpezzata.7.full: Under the peat, in the bog, the sleepers are still sleeping. Without the stone, we do not know whether they will ever wake. Gerrit Tammer, past sixty now, goes there every morning, with his spade, and digs. He says one of them, sooner or later, will open their eyes.
FinaleSpezzata.7.easy: Under the peat, in the bog, the sleepers are still sleeping. Without the stone, we do not know if they will ever wake up. Gerrit Tammer, who is over sixty, goes there every morning with his spade and digs. He says that one day one of them will open their eyes.
FinaleSpezzata.7.short: The sleepers still sleep. Without the stone, perhaps for ever. Gerrit Tammer, past sixty, digs every morning. One of them, he says, will open their eyes.

FinaleSpezzata.8.full: Gerrit, at least, has already woken his own once. He says he knows how it is done.
FinaleSpezzata.8.easy: Gerrit has already woken his own father once. He says he knows how to do it.
FinaleSpezzata.8.short: Gerrit has woken his father once already. He knows how.

FinaleSpezzata.9.full: The Machine, in the tower, still hums, softly, every night at a quarter past eleven. We do not have the courage to switch it off. We do not know what it is waiting for.
FinaleSpezzata.9.easy: The Machine in the tower still hums softly, every night at a quarter past eleven. We are not brave enough to turn it off. We do not know what it is waiting for.
FinaleSpezzata.9.short: Every night at a quarter past eleven, the Machine still hums. We dare not switch it off. We do not know what it waits for.

FinaleRisveglio.3.full: We dug for a month, with Gerrit's spade and two hundred other spades. At first there were few of us: we of the estate, the Watch, Hendrik. Then they came too, the Neighbours, without anyone calling them, spades on their shoulders and sleeves rolled up. They dug beside us, in silence, never tiring. They knew where.
FinaleRisveglio.3.easy: We dug for a month, with Gerrit's spade and two hundred other spades. At the start there were only a few of us: the estate, the Watch, Hendrik. Then the Neighbours came too, though nobody called them, with spades on their shoulders and their sleeves rolled up. They dug next to us in silence and never got tired. They knew where to dig.
FinaleRisveglio.3.short: We dug for a month. At first only the estate, the Watch and Hendrik. Then the Neighbours came, uncalled, with their spades, and dug beside us in silence, tireless. They knew where.

FinaleRisveglio.4.full: We brought them out in their hundreds: white, cold, asleep, in the clothes of fifty years ago, of thirty years ago, of last week. The miller's wife. Mrs Wessel, the mayor's mother. Mrs Mulder, whom her husband believed was in Rotterdam with him. They all woke, slowly, within a few days, in the school gymnasium turned into a hospital, under blankets, with me and Trijntje Kalf taking temperatures.
FinaleRisveglio.4.easy: We took them out by the hundred: white, cold, asleep, in clothes from fifty years ago, thirty years ago, last week. The miller's wife. Mrs Wessel, the mayor's mother. Mrs Mulder, whose husband thought she was with him in Rotterdam. They all woke up slowly, over a few days, in the school gym, which became a hospital. They lay under blankets, and Trijntje Kalf and I took their temperatures.
FinaleRisveglio.4.short: We brought them out by the hundred, cold and asleep, in the clothes of fifty years ago or last week: the miller's wife, Mrs Wessel, Mrs Mulder. They woke within days in the school gym, while Trijntje and I took temperatures.

FinaleRisveglio.5.full: First of all, Fokke Tammer, young as in 1865, with the burns on his palms. Gerrit watched over him for three days.
FinaleRisveglio.5.easy: The first was Fokke Tammer, as young as in 1865, with the burns on his palms. Gerrit stayed by him for three days.
FinaleRisveglio.5.short: First came Fokke Tammer, young as in 1865, his palms burnt. Gerrit watched over him for three days.

FinaleRisveglio.6.full: Now Brunveen has two of everyone. Two Jan Hoeks, two Piet Brinks, two miller's wives, who do not look at each other and do not speak. The awakened are tired, confused, angry, frightened; they do not know what year it is, do not recognise the streets, weep for children who grew up without them. The Neighbours help them in everything, with infinite patience, the way one helps a sick relative. Nobody can tell any more who is whose family.
FinaleRisveglio.6.easy: Now Brunveen has two of everyone. Two Jan Hoeks, two Piet Brinks, two miller's wives, who do not look at each other and do not talk. The people who woke up are tired, confused, angry and frightened. They do not know what year it is, they do not recognise the streets, and they cry for the children who grew up without them. The Neighbours help them with everything, with endless patience, like you help a sick relative. Nobody knows any more whose family is whose.
FinaleRisveglio.6.short: Now Brunveen has two of everyone, who never look at each other. The awakened are lost, angry, weeping for children grown without them. The Neighbours help them with infinite patience. Nobody can tell whose family is whose.

FinaleRisveglio.7.full: Nobody knows what will happen. I know only that last night, at the inn, a man just woken punched his double, and the double, instead of defending himself, embraced him. They stayed like that, embracing, for a long time, one warm and one cold. Then they ordered two gins.
FinaleRisveglio.7.easy: Nobody knows what will happen. I only know that last night, at the inn, a man who had just woken up hit his double. The double did not fight back. He hugged him. They stayed like that for a long time, one warm and one cold. Then they ordered two gins.
FinaleRisveglio.7.short: Nobody knows what will come. Last night at the inn a man just woken punched his double, who embraced him. They stood a long time like that, one warm, one cold. Then they ordered two gins.

FinaleRisveglio.8.full: At the estate, too, there are now two of {0}. One of the two came out of the peat with memory stopped at the night of the party; the other gave up the room, the clothes, the chair at table, and sleeps on the sofa. They argue about everything. They look less and less alike. This morning, for the first time, the one who sleeps on the sofa sang a wrong note, and laughed.
FinaleRisveglio.8.easy: At the estate too there are two of {0} now. One came out of the peat remembering nothing after the night of the party. The other gave up the bedroom, the clothes and the chair at the table, and now sleeps on the sofa. They argue about everything. Every day they look less alike. This morning, for the first time, the one on the sofa sang a wrong note, and laughed.
FinaleRisveglio.8.short: At the estate there are two of {0} now. One remembers nothing after the party; the other sleeps on the sofa. They argue about everything, and look less alike each day. This morning the one on the sofa sang a wrong note, and laughed.

FinaleRisveglio.9.full: The stone is still at the estate, warm, in its box. The awakened will not go near the laboratory. The Neighbours pass in front of it, now and then, and stop for a moment, the way one does before a church.
FinaleRisveglio.9.easy: The stone is still at the estate, warm, in its box. The people who woke up do not want to go near the laboratory. Sometimes the Neighbours walk past it and stop for a moment, the way you stop in front of a church.
FinaleRisveglio.9.short: The warm stone stays in its box. The awakened shun the laboratory. The Neighbours pause before it, as before a church.

FinaleCerchio.3.full: {0} put the stone on the platform, in the centre of the ring. It was warm, and pulsing, softly. Great-grandfather had written it: *it must go back where it came from*. We did it. At a quarter past eleven the Machine came on: white light, no heat, a hum of bees inside a wall. The stone vanished.
FinaleCerchio.3.easy: {0} put the stone on the platform, in the middle of the ring. It was warm, and it was pulsing softly. The great-grandfather wrote it: *it must go back where it came from*. We did it. At a quarter past eleven the Machine turned on: white light, no heat, a hum like bees inside a wall. The stone disappeared.
FinaleCerchio.3.short: {0} set the warm, pulsing stone on the platform. *It must go back where it came from.* At a quarter past eleven: white light, a hum of bees. The stone was gone.

FinaleCerchio.4.full: I took out the Register and opened it at the first page, grandmother Hester's. *11 November 1865. Night, a quarter past eleven. Saw a white light on the tower of the estate, bright as day. At the same instant, another light just like it in the middle of the bog.* I looked out of the window, towards the bog. Nothing could be seen. Nor should it: that light came on fifty-four years ago.
FinaleCerchio.4.easy: I took out the Register and opened it at the first page, grandmother Hester's page. *11 November 1865. Night, a quarter past eleven. I saw a white light on the tower of the estate, as bright as day. At the same moment, another light just like it in the middle of the bog.* I looked out of the window, at the bog. There was nothing to see. There should not be: that light came on fifty-four years ago.
FinaleCerchio.4.short: I opened the Register at Hester's first page: *11 November 1865, a quarter past eleven. A white light on the tower; at the same instant, another in the bog.* I looked at the bog. Nothing. Of course: that light came on fifty-four years ago.

FinaleCerchio.5.full: Great-grandfather thought that something had come through from the other side, and that it had to go back where it came from. He was wrong only about the direction. The stone did not come from another world, and he did not fetch it. We sent it. Tonight, wanting to free the village from the stone, we sent it to where it all began. Brunveen became what it is because we, fifty-four years later, would send it back. The stone exists in the past because it existed in the future, and in the future because it existed in the past. It comes from nowhere. It goes round in a circle. And we are the point where the circle closes.
FinaleCerchio.5.easy: The great-grandfather thought that something came through from the other side and had to go back where it came from. He was wrong only about the direction. The stone did not come from another world, and he did not bring it here. We sent it. Tonight, trying to free the village from the stone, we sent it to the place where everything began. Brunveen became what it is because we, fifty-four years later, would send the stone back. The stone is in the past because it was in the future, and it is in the future because it was in the past. It does not come from anywhere. It goes round and round in a circle. And we are the point where the circle closes.
FinaleCerchio.5.short: Great-grandfather was wrong only about the direction. Nobody fetched the stone: we sent it. Trying to free Brunveen, we sent it to where it all began. It exists in the past because it existed in the future, and the other way round. It comes from nowhere. It goes in a circle, and we are where the circle closes.

FinaleCerchio.6.full: No more Neighbours will be born. Those who are here will remain, as long as the peat holds: ten years, twenty, fifty. They will crumble one at a time, slowly, like Fokke. The village will have time to say goodbye to them. This morning, at the market, one of them asked me how I was, and for the first time, in its voice, there was something that resembled fear.
FinaleCerchio.6.easy: No new Neighbours will be born. The ones who are here will stay as long as the peat lasts: ten years, twenty, fifty. They will fall apart one at a time, slowly, like Fokke. The village will have time to say goodbye to them. This morning at the market one of them asked me how I was, and for the first time there was something like fear in its voice.
FinaleCerchio.6.short: No more Neighbours will come. Those here will last as long as the peat: ten years, fifty. The village will have time to say goodbye. This morning one asked how I was, and for the first time its voice held something like fear.

FinaleCerchio.7.full: On the table in the tower I left grandmother's watch, stopped at a quarter past eleven. Now I know what time it shows.
FinaleCerchio.7.easy: I left my grandmother's watch on the table in the tower, stopped at a quarter past eleven. Now I know what time it shows.
FinaleCerchio.7.short: I left Hester's watch on the tower table, at a quarter past eleven. Now I know what time it shows.

FinaleCerchio.8.full: {0} was in the room when the stone vanished. They looked at the empty platform for a long time, cold hands at their sides. Then they looked at us, one by one, and said only: "Thank you. Now I know how much time I have." There was no bitterness in their voice. There was, for the first time, something like haste.
FinaleCerchio.8.easy: {0} was in the room when the stone disappeared. They looked at the empty platform for a long time, with their cold hands by their sides. Then they looked at each of us and said only: "Thank you. Now I know how much time I have." There was no anger in their voice. For the first time there was something like hurry.
FinaleCerchio.8.short: {0} watched the empty platform a long time, cold hands at their sides. Then: "Thank you. Now I know how much time I have." No bitterness. For the first time, something like haste.

FinaleCerchio.9.full: The Morning Liberal, which in November had published our statement, published this one too. Below, in small print, a comment from the editor: *If it is true, it is the saddest story I have ever printed. If it is not true, so is it.*
FinaleCerchio.9.easy: The Morning Liberal, which printed our statement in November, printed this one too. Under it, in small letters, the editor wrote: *If it is true, it is the saddest story I have ever printed. If it is not true, it still is.*
FinaleCerchio.9.short: The Morning Liberal printed this too, with the editor's note: *If it is true, it is the saddest story I have ever printed. If not, it still is.*

FinaleSemina.3.full: We carried the stone to the dyke at dawn, in the snow, wrapped in its sack. The whole village was waiting for us. Nobody said a word. When we handed it over, they passed it from hand to hand, with infinite care, down to the bank, and Mayor Bram Wessel waded into the water up to his chest to lay it at the place of the light. The stone sank without a sound. The snow, at last, began to settle.
FinaleSemina.3.easy: At dawn we carried the stone to the dyke in the snow, wrapped in its sack. The whole village was waiting for us. Nobody spoke. When we gave it to them, they passed it from hand to hand, very carefully, down to the bank. Mayor Bram Wessel walked into the water up to his chest and put it down at the place where the light was. The stone sank without a sound. At last the snow began to stay on the ground.
FinaleSemina.3.short: At dawn the silent village passed the stone hand to hand to the bank, and Mayor Bram Wessel waded chest-deep to lay it at the place of the light. It sank without a sound. At last, the snow began to settle.

FinaleSemina.4.full: From that day on the Neighbours no longer crumble. The oldest, those who had begun to dry out, recovered within a week: the cracks closed, the skin grew smooth again. They thanked us, one by one, coming to the estate with flowers. They told us they will not forget it. I believe them: they never forget anything.
FinaleSemina.4.easy: From that day the Neighbours do not fall apart any more. The oldest ones, who had started to dry, got better in a week: the cracks closed and their skin was smooth again. They thanked us one by one, coming to the estate with flowers. They told us they will never forget it. I believe them: they never forget anything.
FinaleSemina.4.short: The Neighbours crumble no more. The oldest healed within a week. They came with flowers to thank us, and said they will never forget. I believe them: they never forget anything.

FinaleSemina.5.full: And the bog begins again. The fountain in the square gives dark water again, fresh, good. The babies born this year drink it from the bottle. The council already has a plan for an aqueduct, to carry Brunveen Water all over the province, and then all over the kingdom, and then who knows.
FinaleSemina.5.easy: And the bog starts again. The fountain in the square gives dark water again, fresh and good. The babies born this year drink it from their bottles. The council already has a plan for a long water pipe, to take Brunveen Water to the whole province, then to the whole kingdom, and then who knows where.
FinaleSemina.5.short: The bog begins again. Dark water flows from the fountain; this year's babies drink it from the bottle. The council plans an aqueduct: the province, the kingdom, and then who knows.

FinaleSemina.6.full: I have decided to stay. Someone has to count. But last night, for the first time in my life, I drank a glass from the fountain. I wanted to know what peace tasted like. It is good. Tomorrow morning I will take my temperature, and write it here, as always. If I do not write it, you will know why.
FinaleSemina.6.easy: I have decided to stay. Someone must count. But last night, for the first time in my life, I drank a glass of water from the fountain. I wanted to know how peace tastes. It is good. Tomorrow morning I will take my temperature and write it here, as always. If I do not write it, you will know why.
FinaleSemina.6.short: I will stay: someone must count. But last night I drank from the fountain, to taste peace. It is good. Tomorrow I will write my temperature here. If I do not, you will know why.

FinaleSemina.7.full: {0} went with me to the fountain, last night. They held the glass for me, kindly, the way one does for a child taking medicine. They said I will not regret it. They said that nobody in Brunveen has ever regretted anything.
FinaleSemina.7.easy: Last night {0} came with me to the fountain. They held the glass for me, kindly, like you do for a child taking medicine. They said I will not be sorry. They said that nobody in Brunveen has ever been sorry about anything.
FinaleSemina.7.short: {0} came with me to the fountain and held the glass, as for a child taking medicine. I will not regret it, they said. Nobody in Brunveen ever regrets anything.

FinaleSemina.8.full: The Machine, in the tower, stayed on for three days after the night of the vote, humming, its platform empty. Then it switched itself off. Since then nobody has tried to turn it on again.
FinaleSemina.8.easy: The Machine in the tower stayed on for three days after the night of the vote, humming, with nothing on the platform. Then it turned itself off. Since then nobody has tried to turn it on.
FinaleSemina.8.short: The Machine hummed for three days over its empty platform, then switched itself off. Nobody has tried it since.

FinaleRegistro.3.full: We voted to do nothing. That is a choice too, the commonest of all. The stone stays in the bog, the sleepers sleep, the Neighbours greet us in the street. The village is quiet. Tomorrow it will be as quiet as today, and the day after, quieter still.
FinaleRegistro.3.easy: We voted to do nothing. That is a choice too, the most common choice of all. The stone stays in the bog, the sleepers sleep, the Neighbours say hello to us in the street. The village is quiet. Tomorrow it will be as quiet as today, and the day after it will be even quieter.
FinaleRegistro.3.short: We voted to do nothing: the commonest choice of all. The stone stays, the sleepers sleep, the Neighbours greet us. Tomorrow will be as quiet as today, and the day after, quieter.

FinaleRegistro.4.full: I close the Register here. Three generations of temperatures, of cold hands, of names with a little cross beside them. My grandmother counted them, my father measured them, I have added them up. The total is of no use if nobody reads it. I leave it to the family of the estate, to keep in the tower, beside the Machine that was of no use and the watch that no longer tells the time.
FinaleRegistro.4.easy: I am closing the Register here. Three generations of temperatures, cold hands and names with a small cross next to them. My grandmother counted them, my father measured them, and I added them up. The total is useless if nobody reads it. I leave it to the family of the estate. They can keep it in the tower, next to the Machine that was no use and the watch that does not tell the time any more.
FinaleRegistro.4.short: I close the Register: three generations of temperatures and crosses. Grandmother counted, father measured, I added up. A total is useless unread. I leave it in the tower, beside the useless Machine and the stopped watch.

FinaleRegistro.5.full: Every now and then, in the evening, I go up on the dyke to look at the bog. The snow, at the place of the light, never settles. Below, in their hundreds, those who sleep go on sleeping, hands folded, preserved as on the day they were taken. Above, those who walk go on walking, kind, healthy, at peace. In fifty years they will crumble, and others will take their place, and nobody in Brunveen will notice.
FinaleRegistro.5.easy: Sometimes, in the evening, I go to the dyke to look at the bog. At the place where the light was, the snow never stays. Below, hundreds of sleepers go on sleeping, with their hands together, kept just as they were on the day they were taken. Above, the ones who walk go on walking: kind, healthy, at peace. In fifty years they will fall apart, others will take their place, and nobody in Brunveen will notice.
FinaleRegistro.5.short: Some evenings I watch the bog from the dyke. Below, hundreds sleep on, preserved. Above, the others walk on, kind and at peace. In fifty years others will take their place, and nobody will notice.

FinaleRegistro.6.full: I do not know if we were wrong. But for the first time in my life, closing this notebook, I feel quiet too. And that, more than anything else, frightens me.
FinaleRegistro.6.easy: I do not know if we made a mistake. But for the first time in my life, as I close this notebook, I feel quiet too. And that frightens me more than anything else.
FinaleRegistro.6.short: I do not know if we were wrong. But closing this notebook, I feel quiet too. That frightens me most of all.

FinaleRegistro.7.full: {0}, after the vote, walked me home, in the snow, holding the umbrella over me. At the door they thanked me. For what? "For leaving things as they are," was the answer. "It is the kindest thing one can do."
FinaleRegistro.7.easy: After the vote {0} walked me home in the snow, holding the umbrella for me. At the door they thanked me. For what? "For leaving things as they are," they said. "It is the kindest thing you can do."
FinaleRegistro.7.short: {0} walked me home under an umbrella and thanked me at the door, "for leaving things as they are. It is the kindest thing one can do."

FinaleRegistro.8.full: The family of the estate, at least, never accepted the medal. It is little. But in Brunveen, by now, little is all that is left of our own.
FinaleRegistro.8.easy: At least the family of the estate never accepted the medal. It is not much. But in Brunveen now, not much is all we have left that is ours.
FinaleRegistro.8.short: At least the estate never took the medal. It is little. But little is all that is still ours.
